Title: Parsimonious theorizing
Authors: Diego Jannace, Saeid Kazemi, Arnaldo Camuffo
Affiliations: Entrepreneurship and Family Enterprise INSEAD Singapore Singapore; ION Management Science Lab‐SDA Bocconi Bocconi University Milan Italy; Department of Economics and Decision Sciences HEC Paris Paris France; Department of Management and Technology Bocconi University Milan Italy
Abstract: Abstract Research Summary Entrepreneurs act on theories of value, and the theory‐based view favors simplicity. Yet a theory can be too thin to guide action or too heavy to carry, and simplicity cannot tell which. We model a theory as bundles linking attempted actions, uncertain implementation states, and external conditions to a focal outcome, and make its structure a choice variable. Parsimony then calls for optimal rather than minimal complexity: structure whose contribution to the value of acting justifies its carrying cost. Under the model's assumptions, optimal complexity rises with value at stake, representational capacity, and domain knowledge, and falls with bundle overlap. Theories also change. The entrepreneur's theory shapes her awareness, so some bundles are worth carrying for what they open, while commitments make revision path dependent. Managerial Summary Entrepreneurs often need to explain a future that does not yet exist: what they will try, what must work, and why customers, partners, or investors should care. We show how to weigh the value of linked actions, their possible results, and outside conditions against the effort of understanding, communicating, and testing them. More detail is worthwhile when the potential payoff is greater, the entrepreneur knows the business better, or the team can handle complexity; overlapping ideas add less. As evidence accumulates, the theory may need to expand, shrink, or be rebuilt. Some ideas are worth keeping because they reveal new possibilities. Earlier investments can make changes costly, so a failed test may call for reshaping the idea rather than abandoning it.

Title: XBRL adoption and SEC monitoring
Authors: Minjae Koo, Yinqi Zhang, Meiling Zhao, Yuping Zhao
Abstract: Abstract We examine how disclosure processing costs influence SEC monitoring of firm disclosures by leveraging the mandatory adoption of XBRL—a digital reporting language designed to reduce these costs. Post adoption, both the frequency and quality of SEC comment letters for 10-K filings increase. Additional tests suggest that XBRL enhances SEC monitoring through three channels. First, automated data extraction improves review efficiency, as reflected in more timely comment letters and greater XBRL benefits when the SEC faces tighter resource constraints or uses XBRL analytical tools. Second, standardized reporting strengthens the SEC’s benchmarking ability: firms using more standardized tags and tags more comparable to those of industry peers benefit more. Third, XBRL facilitates SEC scrutiny of complex reporting issues, yielding more frequent and higher-quality comments on noncore earnings accounts and for firms with more footnote tags or complex filings. Overall, our evidence suggests that reduced disclosure processing costs enhance the SEC’s regulatory monitoring.

Title: Juking the Stats: Policing, Misreporting, and Policy Evaluation
Authors: Michael Gibilisco, Carlo M Horz
Affiliations: California Insitute of Technology; Washington University in Saint Louis
Abstract: Abstract We analyze a game-theoretic model of crime and crime reporting to study the quality of crime statistics. An offender potentially engages in illicit behavior; an enforcer chooses effort and how to report outcomes. Because of signaling concerns, the enforcer may misreport. We show that multiple equilibria can exist and characterize when crime is under- or overreported. Increasing the enforcer’s costs of data manipulation can backfire, increasing misreporting in crime statistics. When calculating treatment effects of parameter changes, the effect on reported statistics will not equal the effect on true statistics, and the true effect can be under- or overestimated.

Title: Programmable Repayment: Risk-Sharing and Enforcement Through the Payment Platform
Authors: Kumar Rishabh, Alessandro Di Stefano
Affiliations: University of Lausanne and University of Basel; University of Bern
Abstract: Abstract Payment platforms increasingly offer merchants loans with programmable repayment, deducting a share of merchants’ platform sales toward repayment. The contract transfers part of merchants’ cash-flow risk to the lender and automates collection, but merchants partly control which sales the platform processes. This puts risk-sharing in tension with enforcement. At a major Indian payment platform, merchants accept offers more often when sales are volatile or outside debts are overdue. After disbursal, borrowers’ platform sales fall 12 percent relative to matched controls. Declines are larger among high-volatility merchants and on second loans, so the deduction base shrinks with borrower risk and experience. These larger declines come without detectably greater outside arrears. Declines are smaller where cash is scarce, consistent with diversion. The lender nevertheless earns 9.6 percent annually before costs, above the 6.5 percent Treasury-bill yield. High-volatility merchants generate comparable loan returns, stay longer on the platform, and contribute more rental revenue.

Title: External Enablement Across Types of Environmental Change: Experimental Evidence on Onset Variance Effects
Authors: Jiyoung Kim, Per Davidsson, Denis A. Grégoire
Affiliations: University of Queensland, Queensland, Australia; Jönköping International Business School, Jönköping, Sweden; Australian Centre for Entrepreneurship Research, Queensland University of Technology, Queensland, Australia; HEC Montréal, Québec, Canada
Abstract: A growing research stream applies the external enablement framework (EEF) to capture how macroenvironmental changes benefit entrepreneurial pursuits. To refine and nuance the EEF’s guidance of future research in this domain, we examine the provisionally suggested structural relationships among its constructs. Combining between-subjects experiments and think-aloud protocols, we show that variance in the characteristics of macroenvironmental changes—specifically, their gradual versus radical onset—influences expectations of enablement and does so similarly across types of change. Our results also uncover relationships between macroenvironmental changes and agents beyond what the EEF explicates. We discuss implications for future research on macroenvironmental impact on business.

Title: Correcting the Unobserved Textual Confounding Factors in Regression by BERT and Partially Linear Regression
Authors: Mengke Qiao, Ke-Wei Huang
Affiliations: Culverhouse College of Business, The University of Alabama, Tuscaloosa, Alabama 35487; School of Computing, National University of Singapore, Singapore 119077
Abstract: In the last decade, there has been a surge of text-mining applications in the information systems literature. In these applications, researchers typically construct independent variables from documents by various text-mining techniques. The most prominent example could be using online review sentiments to investigate online word-of-mouth issues. Typically, most documents contain information richer than the independent variable, and researchers may construct control variables from the same documents to alleviate endogeneity issues. However, researchers need to manually craft these variables, and this process may not guarantee that all the important confounding factors are extracted and included in the regression model with a correct functional form. If useful textual information is overlooked and a valid identification strategy is not available, the omitted variable bias may occur. To solve this challenge, we propose a novel model that utilizes text embedding based on the state-of-the-art neural network language model (i.e., bidirectional encoder representations from transformers (BERT)) to automatically create a new control variable vector for controlling latent confounding factors in the absence of a valid identification strategy. Moreover, our approach can be considered a semiparametric approach in that our model contains a linear term of the key independent variable and an unknown functional term of the textual control variables. Our approach extends the semiparametric framework, double machine learning, by introducing a novel Neyman-orthogonal loss function in an integrated deep neural network to minimize the estimation bias. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of controlling textual control variables by text embedding and improving the estimation performance by the novel loss function. This paper was accepted by Anindya Ghose, information systems. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.04758 .
Accepting Editor: This paper was accepted by Anindya Ghose, information systems.

Title: Reducing Risk Through Trade Credit: Theory and Evidence from Dual-Channel Suppliers
Authors: Jie Ning, Sammi Y. Tang, Jing Wu, Jiaqi Zhu
Affiliations: Department of Operations, Case Western Reserve University, Cleveland, Ohio 44106; Department of Management, University of Miami, Coral Gables, Florida 33146; CUHK Business School, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong; Tilburg School of Economics and Management, Tilburg University, Tilburg 5037AB, Netherlands
Abstract: Trade credit is traditionally viewed as increasing supplier risk, because delayed payments expose suppliers to buyer uncertainties. Using a stylized game-theoretic model, we show that this conventional wisdom can be overturned when a supplier is dual channel: operating a direct channel that sells to end customers in addition to an indirect channel that sells to an industry peer who serves the same market. Compared with zero trade credit provision where the supplier requires cash on delivery (COD), we observe empirically that high trade credit provision can lead to lower risk for the dual-channel supplier. We propose a possible mechanism for this risk mitigation effect—pooling: When the market overlap between the supplier and its peer buyer is sufficiently high, the random split of the overlapping market creates negative association between the supplier’s direct channel sales and the buyer’s trade credit payment. Trade credit does not always mitigate risk for dual-channel suppliers. If the supplier’s debt level is high, our theory predicts that trade credit exacerbates risk. We find empirical evidence consistent with our theoretical predictions using data on U.S. manufacturing firms that sell to their industry peers. The positive association between trade credit provision and bankruptcy risk is dampened or even reversed once a supplier begins selling to peer firms. This risk mitigation effect is stronger among suppliers with lower leverage and greater market overlap with their buyers. For highly financially constrained suppliers, trade credit provision is associated with an increase in bankruptcy risk after the supplier becomes dual channel. This paper was accepted by Jayashankar Swaminathan, operations management. Supplemental Material: The online appendices and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.03142 .
Accepting Editor: This paper was accepted by Jayashankar Swaminathan, operations management.

Title: Echoes of Discord: The Effects of Global Conflicts and Disputes on Entrepreneurship
Authors: Astrid Marinoni
Affiliations: Scheller College of Business, Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, Georgia 30308
Abstract: Mixed-nationality founding teams bring together heterogeneous, hard-to-replicate bundles of human capital and country-specific ties through their cross-national networks, providing a distinctive foundation for building successful ventures. Yet these connections may be vulnerable to nonmarket shocks. This study examines whether geopolitical conflicts and disputes between the countries of origin of immigrant founders affect the formation of new ventures. Leveraging data on the founders of start-ups established in Great Britain and global information on conflicts and disputes, I find that such tensions reduce the likelihood that nationals of hostile countries cofound firms together. The evidence is more consistent with social mechanisms and, particularly, the erosion of interpersonal relationships than with diminished access to cross-country resources or the loss of entrepreneurial opportunities. Start-ups of both low and high quality are affected, including in sectors that depend heavily on skilled human capital, such as high-tech and business services. The negative effect is substantially attenuated for nationality pairs that are heavily colocated across local areas and for founders with prior social exposure to individuals from the opposing nationality, indicating that interpersonal ties can buffer against geopolitical shocks. Conflicts do not affect the exit of existing firms, and the decline in mixed-nationality entrepreneurship is not offset by alternative team configurations such as solo ventures or those formed with conationals, natives, or individuals from third-party countries. This paper was accepted by Alfonso Gambardella, business strategy. Funding: I gratefully acknowledge funding from the Institute for Leadership and Social Impact at Georgia Institute of Technology. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.04559 .
Accepting Editor: This paper was accepted by Alfonso Gambardella, business strategy.

Title: Inferential Theory for Pricing Errors with Latent Factors and Firm Characteristics
Authors: Jungjun Choi, Ming Yuan
Affiliations: Department of Computer Science and Statistics, University of Rhode Island, Kingston, Rhode Island 02881; Department of Statistics, Columbia University, New York, New York 10027
Abstract: We study factor models that combine latent factors with firm characteristics and propose a new framework for modeling, estimating, and inferring pricing errors. Following Zhang (2024), our approach decomposes mispricing into two distinct components: inside alpha, explained by firm characteristics but orthogonal to factor exposures, and outside alpha, orthogonal to both factors and characteristics. Our model generalizes those developed recently such as Kelly et al. (2019) and Zhang (2024), resolving issues of orthogonality, basis dependence, and unit sensitivity. Methodologically, we develop estimators grounded in low-rank methods with explicit debiasing, providing closed-form solutions and a rigorous inferential theory that accommodates a growing number of characteristics and relaxes standard assumptions on sample dimensions. Empirically, using U.S. stock returns from 2000 to 2019, we document strong evidence of both inside and outside alphas, with the former showing industry-level comovements and the latter reflecting idiosyncratic shocks beyond firm fundamentals. Our framework thus unifies statistical and characteristic-based approaches to factor modeling, offering both theoretical advances and new insights into the structure of pricing errors. This paper was accepted by Lukas Schmid, finance. Funding: This research was supported by the National Science Foundation [Grant DMS-2052955]. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.04971 .

Title: Tax-induced Corporate In-kind Donations: Equilibrium Analysis and Policy Design
Authors: Lusheng Shao, Nan Zhang, Baozhuang Niu, H. Sebastian Heese
Affiliations: The University of Melbourne, Faculty of Business and Economics, Melbourne, Victoria, Australia; South China University of Technology, School of Business Administration, Guangzhou, China; North Carolina State University Poole College of Management, Business Management, Raleigh, North Carolina, United States
Abstract: Problem definition: Food-sector firms often make in-kind donations to help alleviate food insecurity. For example, major retailers such as Walmart and Kroger routinely donate products to food banks. To encourage such donations, many governments offer tax incentives to donor firms. We examine how tax incentives affect firms’ operational and donation decisions, profits and consumer surplus, and we investigate the optimal design of such incentives. Methodology/results: We develop an analytical model to study a firm’s operational and in-kind donation decisions under capacity constraints, in a setting where consumers with heterogeneous valuations can either purchase a product from the firm or attempt to obtain a donated product from charitable organizations. Among other findings, we identify a threshold of the tax incentive rate above which the firm is willing to donate. While the firm always benefits from more generous incentives, consumer surplus follows a U-shaped relationship with respect to the incentive rate: a moderate incentive may result in lower consumer surplus than no incentive at all. Further, the optimal tax policy depends on the government’s emphasis on social welfare, with donation tax incentives becoming desirable only when sufficient weight is placed on social welfare. These findings remain robust when accounting for competition from fringe firms and consumer heterogeneity in the acceptance of donated products. Finally, as an alternative policy intervention, government’s direct market entry can be optimal at intermediate levels of social welfare concern. Managerial implications: Our results provide guidance for governments that design tax policies to incentivize in-kind donations and alleviate food insecurity. Importantly, our results suggest that donation tax policies may have unintended adverse effects on consumers, and when weighing social welfare against tax revenue, it may be optimal for governments to avoid such policies.

Title: Online Allocation of Throughput-Constrained Resources Using Proxy Assignments
Authors: Chamsi Hssaine, Huseyin Topaloglu, Garrett van Ryzin
Affiliations: University of Southern California Marshall School of Business, Data Sciences and Operations, Los Angeles, California, United States; Cornell University, School of Operations Research and Information Engineering, Ithaca, New York, United States; Amazon.com Inc, SCOT, New York, New York, United States
Abstract: Problem definition: We study a variation of the canonical online resource allocation problem in which resources are throughput, rather than budget, constrained. As in the classical setting, the decision-maker must assign sequentially arriving jobs to one of multiple available resources. However, in addition to the assignment costs incurred from these decisions, the decision-maker is also penalized for deviating from exogenous, time-varying target assignment rates for each resource, which represent the resources’ respective throughput capacities throughout the horizon. The goal is to minimize the total expected assignment and deviation penalty costs incurred throughout the horizon when the distribution of assignment costs is unknown. Methodology/results: We first show that naive extensions of state-of-the-art algorithms for classical budget-constrained resource allocation problems can fail dramatically when applied to throughput-constrained resource allocation. We then propose a novel “proxy assignment“ primal-dual algorithm that uses current arrivals to simulate the effect of future arrivals. We prove that our algorithm achieves the optimal $O(\sqrt{T})$ regret bound when the assignment costs of the arriving jobs are drawn i.i.d. from a fixed distribution. We demonstrate the practical performance of our approach by conducting numerical experiments on synthetic datasets, as well as real-world datasets from retail fulfillment operations. Managerial implications: Our framework applies to many practical settings where resource capacity is throughput-based and potentially time-varying, such as assigning jobs to a pool of workers where staffing levels change over time, or assigning shipments to trucks whose departure times are scheduled throughout the day. In contrast to traditional online resource allocation, the financial costs of assignments must be balanced against the cost of deviating from target consumption rates. Our work provides decision-makers with the tools to efficiently manage this trade-off.

Title: Throttling Equilibria in Auction Markets
Authors: Xi Chen, Christian Kroer, Rachitesh Kumar
Affiliations: Columbia University, Computer Science Department, New York, New York, United States; Columbia University, IEOR, New York, New York, United States; Carnegie Mellon University, Tepper School of Business, Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, United States
Abstract: Throttling is a popular method of budget management for online ad auctions in which the platform modulates the participation probability of an advertiser in order to smoothly spend her budget across many auctions. In this work, we investigate the setting in which all of the advertisers simultaneously employ throttling to manage their budgets, and we do so for both first-price and second-price auctions. We analyze the structural and computational properties of the resulting equilibria. For first-price auctions, we show that a unique equilibrium always exists, is well-behaved and can be computed efficiently via tatonnement-style decentralized dynamics. In contrast, for second-price auctions, we prove that even though an equilibrium always exists, the problem of finding even an approximate equilibrium is PPAD-complete, there can be multiple equilibria, and it is NP-hard to find the revenue maximizing one. We also compare the equilibrium outcomes of throttling to those of multiplicative pacing, which is the other most popular and well-studied method of budget management. Finally, we characterize the Price of Anarchy of these equilibria for liquid welfare by showing that it is at most 2 for both first-price and second-price auctions, and demonstrating that our bound is tight.

Title: Embedded in Two Worlds: How Incumbents’ Brokerage Affects Adaptation When Old and New Supply Networks Coexist
Authors: Jongyoun Baek, Andrew V. Shipilov, Nathan R. Furr
Affiliations: INSEAD, EFE, Fontainebleau, Île-de-France, France; INSEAD, Strategy, Fontainebleau, France
Abstract: The development of new technology architectures often opens up new markets within an existing industry. Incumbents face the decision of whether to enter the new technology market and how to do so. As incumbents attempt to enter the new market, they can become embedded in two buyer-supplier networks, one for the old and the other for new technologies. We argue that brokers have an advantage in this process because they have developed capabilities to integrate suppliers of new technology components or develop unique component combinations for the new technology products. In a study of the U.S. automotive industry between 2012 and 2022, we find that brokerage in the old technology network is positively associated with successful entry into the new technology (i.e., number and performance of new technology models). Surprisingly, brokerage in the old technology network had a stronger positive impact than brokerage in the new technology network on incumbents’ entry into the new technology market for electric vehicles.

Title: Democratic Organizing and Contemporary Managerial Talent Markets: Internal Promotion or External Hiring?
Authors: Aleksandra Gregoric, Takao Kato, Casper B. L. Larsen
Affiliations: Copenhagen Business School, Department of Accounting, Center for Corporate Governance and Owner-Managed Firms, Frederiksberg, Denmark; Colgate University, Department of Economics, Hamilton, New York, United States; Copenhagen Business School, Department of Accounting, Center for Corporate Governance, Frederiksberg, Capital Region, Denmark
Abstract: We develop and empirically examine a theoretical framework explaining the relationship between democratic organizing and firms’ propensity to staff management positions through internal promotion rather than external hiring. Conventionally, the advantages of promoting through internal labor markets (ILM) have rested on the assumption that workers value intra-firm careers and anticipate remaining with the same employer for a longer term. These advantages may prove harder to attain in contemporary labor markets, given that declining tenure and workers’ growing preference for inter-firm careers possibly reduce the information advantage of ILM and undermine internal candidate retention. We propose that firms with more democratic organizing are less susceptible to these ILM challenges, enjoy higher benefits from recruiting internally and are thus more likely to fill management positions through internal promotion. Using longitudinal employer-employee linked data for Danish firms from 2001 to 2017, we find that firms with worker board representation (WBR), one form of more democratic organizing, are more likely than firms without WBR to fill management positions through internal promotion rather than external hiring. This association is stronger where (i) worker representatives have broader intra-firm experience and are more likely to possess promotion-relevant information; (ii) more managers and professionals have peers serving as worker representatives on the board. These results are consistent with a higher economic viability of internal promotion in firms with more democratic organizing, and largely inconsistent with the conventional account of powerful workers distorting firms’ hiring choices. Interviews with worker directors and human resource professionals illustrate the proposed mechanisms.

Title: Does training in AI affect PhD students' careers? Evidence from France
Authors: Pierre Boutros, Eliana Diodati, Michele Pezzoni, Fabiana Visentin

Title: Consumer sickness behavior: A model for understanding consumption during illness
Authors: Felipe M. Affonso
Affiliations: Spears School of Business Oklahoma State University Stillwater Oklahoma USA
Abstract: Abstract Illness is a near‐universal and economically consequential consumer state, yet consumer theory has no framework for how being sick changes consumption. Prior work has focused on external pandemic responses and not the internal biological state of being sick, and little research connects the biological mechanisms of illness (inflammation, cytokine activation) to systematic change in consumer behavior. Drawing on converging evidence from immunology, neuroscience, and consumer behavior, we develop the Consumer Sickness Behavior (CSB) model. The model proposes that illness activates an adaptive motivational program with three psychological mediators: motivational reprioritization, risk‐perception recalibration, and effort‐value recalibration. It predicts a distinctive differential‐effects pattern, the simultaneous suppression of exploratory and social consumption and amplification of comfort‐ and safety‐seeking, that neither a single feeling state nor fatigue produces. By treating illness as a compound psychological state, in which acute inflammation produces feelings and motivational changes together, CSB explains marketplace patterns that no account based on a single feeling or on fatigue predicts and offers implications for marketing, consumer welfare, and public health.

Title: Theory‐based foundations of Bayesian entrepreneurship
Authors: Joshua S. Gans, Erin L. Scott, Scott Stern
Affiliations: Rotman School of Management University of Toronto Toronto Ontario Canada; Sloan School of Management Massachusetts Institute of Technology Cambridge Massachusetts USA; NBER Cambridge Massachusetts USA
Abstract: Abstract Research Summary Entrepreneurs can observe the same evidence yet reach different conclusions about an opportunity. We connect the theory‐based view with Bayesian Entrepreneurship by separating a qualitative theory of value creation—the mechanisms it admits, what it rules out, and where it applies—from the probabilistic beliefs needed to use it. The separation explains why actors disagree despite shared evidence, why different disagreements call for different experiments, and why an experiment can improve prediction without separating theories. It also distinguishes disagreement about an opportunity from differences in costs, constraints, or capabilities. When evidence is thin, a more focused theory can make acting worthwhile sooner without being more accurate. A worked theory card for Vanguard shows how to diagnose disagreement, and we outline tests of the resulting hypotheses. Managerial Summary Founders, investors, and mentors often read the same evidence differently because they hold different theories of how a venture will create value, not because one side lacks information. Before asking for “more traction,” they should state the founder's theory and its strongest rival, then locate the disagreement: whether a mechanism matters, how strong it is, which market conditions will arise, whether lessons transfer between settings, or how predictable results are. Each calls for a different test. When the parties share a forecast but differ in costs, contracts, or capabilities, the remedy is a change in terms or staging rather than another test. A worked example for Vanguard shows the method. Focused theories can justify acting sooner, but focus does not make them right.

Title: The reversal of gender disparities in the retention and promotion of Big Four auditors
Authors: Jade Huayu Chen, Nicholas Hallman, Jayanthi Sunder
Abstract: Popular media and academic research have long characterized the Big Four audit firms as boys’ clubs that fail to equitably retain and promote women. Using data on more than 150,000 rank-and-file auditors, we show that women did face significantly lower rates of retention and promotion throughout the 1990s and 2000s. These disparities reversed during the mid-2010s, however, and female auditors now enjoy higher rates of retention and promotion than their male colleagues. We examine three drivers: increasing female representation on client audit committees, growing client emphasis on diversity in hiring and vendor selection, and the introduction of Form AP, which made lead audit partner identities public for the first time. Only Form AP significantly predicts the reversal when controlling for the other two. Consistent with Form AP’s salience, the reversal is absent among professionals with no Form AP exposure, muted where exposure is partial, and delayed in Big Four tax practices.

Title: The metro crew scheduling problem with train service segmentation: Formulations and a column generation-based algorithm
Authors: Jue Zhou, Xiaoming Xu, Jiancheng Long

Title: Generative AI And Creative Goods: Market Expansion, Crowd-Out, and Copyright
Authors: Samuel G Goldberg, H Tai Lam
Affiliations: Stanford Graduate School of Business, Stanford University; Anderson School of Management, University of California , Los Angeles
Abstract: Abstract We study how generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) affects creative goods markets using data from a large stock images marketplace. In December 2022, the platform announced it would allow artists to sell GenAI-produced images, subject to two conditions: all GenAI images must be labeled, and GenAI would be prohibited in certain markets. We exploit this policy variation using a difference-in-differences design. We estimate a 136% increase in image production and 47% increase in active artists, accompanied by a 15% decline in non-GenAI production and 29% decline in non-GenAI active artists. On the demand side, total sales increase by 82%, but non-GenAI sales fall by 28% and non-GenAI sales rates decline by 3 percentage points. We use image embeddings to develop novel measures of image quality, characteristics, and market composition.We find that quality (measured as predicted sales probability) increases by 9 percentage points overall and 2 percentage points for non-GenAI content, suggesting low-quality non-GenAI artists exit. Our product characteristic measures indicate that GenAI production is heavily concentrated in characteristic space, potentially limiting the value of these images to the market. Non-GenAI production responds to GenAI by differentiating into niches. We discuss implications for copyright policy and the longer-run sustainability of original creative work.

Title: International Power
Authors: Ernest Liu, David Y Yang
Affiliations: Princeton University and NBER; Harvard University, NBER, BREAD, CIFAR and J-PAL
Abstract: Abstract An interconnected world increases economic efficiency while giving certain countries leverage over others. We aim to describe and understand international power stemming from trade. Using an illustrative model of trade with possibilities of bilateral disputes and ex-post hold-ups, we highlight that bilateral asymmetry in import dependence can be a source of power towards one another. We construct the model-implied measure of international power — asymmetric bilateral import dependence, weighted inversely by sectoral trade elasticities — across country pairs over the past 20 years. Combining this measure with comprehensive data on bilateral engagement events and a high-frequency measure of bilateral geopolitical relationships, we examine the consequences and strategic causes of international power. We present two main empirical results. First, increases in international power between countries — which raise the credibility of threats of trade disruptions — induce more bilateral engagement and negotiations. Second, evidence suggests that worsened geopolitical relationships — in anticipation of future disputes — prompt countries to build up greater international power through adjusting trade activities.

Title: Fine Stratification of Survey Experiments
Authors: Max Cytrynbaum
Affiliations: Yale University
Abstract: Abstract This paper studies a two-stage model of experimentation, where the researcher first samples representative experimental participants from an eligible pool, then assigns each sampled unit to treatment or control, using matched k-tuples randomization at both stages. To implement such designs, we develop a fast algorithm for matching units into k-tuples for any k ≥ 2 and any dimension of covariates. By surveying 200 recent experimental working papers, we estimate that our algorithm newly enables multivariate fine stratification with provable match quality guarantees in about 48% of recent papers. We show that finely stratified sampling and assignment both nonparametrically reduce the variance of treatment effect estimation, with the gains from stratified sampling increasing in the size of the eligible pool and how well covariates predict treatment effect heterogeneity. We develop new inference methods that fully exploit the efficiency gains from both design stages, allowing researchers to report smaller standard errors if they designed a representative experiment. An application to nine published experiments quantifies the efficiency gains.

Title: The Labor Demand and Labor Supply Channels of Monetary Policy
Authors: Sebastian Graves, Christopher Huckfeldt, Eric T Swanson
Affiliations: University of Cambridge; Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System; University of California , Irvine
Abstract: Abstract Monetary policy is typically understood to affect employment through labor demand, with the role of labor supply receiving less consideration. We estimate the response of labor market flows to high-frequency changes in interest rates around FOMC announcements and Fed Chair speeches, and find that a contractionary monetary policy shock leads to a significant increase in labor supply: workers reduce the rate at which they quit jobs to nonemployment, and non-employed individuals increase their job-seeking behavior. These effects are quantitatively important: holding supply-driven labor market flows constant, the decline in employment from a contractionary monetary policy shock would be twice as large. To interpret our findings, we estimate a heterogeneous agent model with frictional labor markets and an active extensive margin of labor supply. The model rationalizes existing estimates of modest labor supply responses to idiosyncratic transfers with our new evidence of a large labor supply response to an aggregate shock.

Title: Breaking Gender Norms: A Dynamic Perspective on Entering Gender-Atypical Occupations
Authors: Sophie Schellhammer, Florian Kunze
Affiliations: University of Konstanz
Abstract: Occupational gender segregation remains a defining feature of labor markets worldwide, and efforts to recruit individuals into gender-atypical occupations often fail because newcomers drop out shortly after entry. Understanding what drives this early attrition requires examining the day-to-day experiences of newcomers whose gender is underrepresented in their occupation, especially during the critical first weeks of organizational socialization. Integrating role congruity theory with a dynamic work-events perspective, we propose that gender-atypical newcomers experience an intensifying trajectory of perceived negative work events over time, and that this intensifying trajectory undermines their task mastery and heightens their turnover intention. Results from a longitudinal field study applying a repeated-measures design to 673 newcomers across 88 occupations over 12 weeks support these predictions. Newcomers working in gender-atypical occupations experienced a significant increase in negative work events over time, with this effect being significantly stronger for men in female-dominated occupations than for women in male-dominated occupations. Furthermore, steeper negative work event trajectories were associated with lower task mastery and higher turnover intentions. These findings advance dissimilarity research by uncovering the dynamic mechanism through which gender dissimilarity translates into adverse adjustment outcomes and contribute to the anchoring events literature by demonstrating the disproportionate and lasting influence of early negative experiences at the very outset of a professional career.

Title: Commentary: Abortion Attitudes and Laws Are About Gender Beliefs and Gender Inequality
Authors: P. J. Henry, Kate Hawks
Affiliations: Psychology Department, New York University Abu Dhabi
Abstract: Brandt and Maner’s (2024) article in Psychological Science linked opposition to abortion with evolutionary pressures arising from high-mortality environments. Extending their analysis, we argue that such approaches overlook the critical role of gender beliefs and gender inequality in understanding abortion attitudes and laws. Using cross-national data and reproducing Brandt and Maner’s methodology, we show that when controlling for indices of gender inequality and gender-role beliefs, the previously observed relationship between mortality risk and abortion restrictiveness disappears. These results suggest that attitudes and laws concerning abortion are more robustly related to gender, rather than to ecological imperatives. We discuss the implications for evolutionary theory, gender equality, and public policy.

Title: Scalable Just-in-Time Price Elasticity Estimation
Authors: Jingbo Wang, Yufeng Huang
Affiliations: Department of Marketing, Chinese University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong; Simon Business School, University of Rochester, Rochester, New York 14627
Abstract: This paper presents a scalable, nonparametric approach to estimating point-wise price elasticities designed for real-time pricing decisions. A key challenge in these settings is correcting for price endogeneity while remaining computationally efficient. We address this by leveraging nonparametric control functions to decompose the identification of causal elasticities into a sequence of scalable intermediate prediction tasks. We implement this framework with bootstrap averaged (bagged) nearest neighbors, which admits a closed-form representation that enables scalable, real-time implementation. We establish uniform consistency of our estimator and show in Monte Carlo simulations that it robustly recovers local elasticities across a diverse range of data-generating processes. We demonstrate the method’s practical usefulness by applying it to the New York City ride-sharing market, recovering substantial spatial-temporal heterogeneity in price elasticity and updating citywide elasticity estimates in less than one minute, which provide a “just-in-time” input for algorithmic pricing systems. This paper was accepted by Raphael Thomadsen, marketing. Funding: J. Wang acknowledges financial support from the Research Grants Council of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region, China [Grant 14508924]. Title: Machine Learning Vast Dynamic Conditional Covariance Matrices: The Spirit of “Divide and Conquer”
Authors: Zhoufan Zhu, Ke Zhu
Affiliations: Wang Yanan Institute for Studies in Economics, Xiamen University, Xiamen 361005, China; and Department of Finance, School of Economics, Xiamen University, Xiamen 361005, China; Department of Statistics and Actuarial Science, The University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong
Abstract: Large-scale portfolio selection requires accurate forecasts of high-dimensional dynamic conditional covariance matrices (CCMs). This task is challenging because the number of covariance elements grows quickly with the number of assets, whereas the available time-series observations are limited and noisy. In this paper, we propose a novel graph-based quantiled (GRAND) CCM estimator in the spirit of “divide and conquer.” By extracting information from the extensive asset features, the GRAND method leverages a new graph-based deep learning network, called the self-grouping autoencoder (SGA), to learn the conditional quantiles of returns. Using those learned conditional quantiles, the GRAND method further learns (co)variances of CCM element-wisely via the quantiled conditional moment (QCM) method, and finally, it makes the resulting assembled CCM estimator positive semidefinite through a projection. Because of the use of the SGA network and the QCM method in an element-wise way, the GRAND method is blessing dimensionality in learning the CCM of a large-scale portfolio, while keeping the computation manageable and maintaining causal semantics. From an extensive empirical analysis of the Chinese stock market, we show that the GRAND method can produce much better tangency portfolios than its competitors, and provide dynamic causal graphs to study variance and quantile connectedness of all stocks for interpreting systemic risk and forecasting the business cycle. This paper was accepted by Kay Giesecke, finance. Title: Online Job Selection: Reward Rate vs. Remaining Value
Authors: Mohammad Reza Aminian, Will Ma, Linwei Xin
Affiliations: Booth School of Business, University of Chicago, Chicago, Illinois 60637; Graduate School of Business, Columbia University, New York, New York 10027; School of Operations Research and Information Engineering, Cornell University, Ithaca, New York 14853
Abstract: High-throughput systems, such as cloud spot markets, adaptive large language model inference, and order consolidation in logistics, operate under capacity constraints. In these settings, decision makers must allocate fixed resources among a stream of requests with heterogeneous reward rates and service durations. A critical tension arises when capacity is saturated; the system must decide whether to continue serving an active job to harvest its remaining value or to preempt it in favor of a new arrival. This trade-off is especially subtle when a new job offers a lower immediate reward rate but a longer service duration, potentially outweighing a high-rate job near completion. To address this challenge, we introduce a general and parsimonious online allocation framework for capacity-constrained resources, where preemption is nonresumable and yields partial rewards. This abstraction captures the essential dynamics of modern resource management problems, including but not limited to those discussed earlier. We derive intuitive index-based policies and provide constant-factor competitive-ratio guarantees for their performance without requiring any forecasts of future demand. In particular, we show that two naive index-based policies have competitive ratios of 1/2 and [Formula: see text]. Our main methodological contribution is to develop a flexible framework for defining “quasiutilities” that couples the states of an online algorithm versus an offline algorithm, which reduces the design of online index-based policies to an offline geometrical problem. The framework allows us to optimize the index function, leading to an exponential-index-based policy that has an improved competitive ratio of 0.68. We also consider various extensions and prove that most of our analyses are tight. Finally, we conduct a concise numerical study to demonstrate the strong empirical performance of the proposed policies under nonworst-case stochastic demand sequences. Title: When GenAI Increases Inequality: Evidence from a University Debating Competition
Authors: Antonio Roldán-Monés
Affiliations: School of Politics, Economics and Global Affairs (IESPEGA), IE University, 28046 Madrid, Spain
Abstract: Research on Generative AI (GenAI) and work reports both productivity-compressing and inequality-expanding effects, leaving open a central question for organizations: Who benefits from GenAI and on which specific tasks? I address this question through a randomized controlled trial in competitive university debating, where participants are randomly assigned access to GenAI. Although most previous experimental work examines the impact of GenAI on written activities and across individuals, this setting allows me to study the impact of GenAI on a knowledge-intensive spoken activity and to identify heterogeneous effects across subtasks. I find that GenAI expands performance inequality in this setting. Consistent with recent theories on GenAI and work, results show that high-ability participants experience significantly larger gains from GenAI usage than their lower-ability counterparts in judgment-intensive subtasks, whereas lower-ability individuals only improve their performance in less expert components of debating, where GenAI can be used as a substitute. If these inequality-expanding effects generalize to similar spoken settings where complex ideas must be internalized and explained, rather than simply written, they would have important implications for understanding the impact of GenAI on work and inequality. This paper was accepted by Maria Guadalupe, business strategy. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.01063 .

Title: Carbon home bias
Authors: Patrick Bolton, Marc Eskildsen, Marcin Kacperczyk
Abstract: We undertake a global analysis of institutional investor portfolios and find widespread underweighting of companies with higher carbon emissions, both in levels and intensities. This underweighting is largely driven by foreign companies with high carbon emissions, both at the intensive (tilting) and extensive (exclusion) margins. Domestic firms with high emissions are overweighted but by a smaller magnitude. These results reveal a bias for domestic companies with high carbon emissions. The carbon home bias is stronger in settings where institutions have tighter business connections, in countries with weaker social norms regarding climate crisis, and where the political environment is more polarized.

Title: The term structure of the price of variance risk
Authors: Marianne Andries, Thomas M Eisenbach, R Jay Kahn, Martin C Schmalz
Affiliations: Department of Economics, University of Southern California , Los Angeles, CA; Federal Reserve Bank of New York , New York, NY; Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System; Saïd Business School, University of Oxford , Oxford; Centre for Economic Policy Research , London; European Corporate Governance Institute , Brussels
Abstract: Abstract We empirically investigate the term structure of variance risk pricing and how it varies over time. We estimate the aversion to variance risk in a stochastic-volatility option pricing model separately for options of different maturities and find that variance risk pricing decreases in absolute value with maturity but remains significantly different from zero up to the nine-month horizon. We find consistent non-parametric results using estimates from Sharpe ratios of delta-neutral straddles. We further show that the term structure is downward sloping both during normal times and in times of stress, when required compensation for variance risk increases and its term structure steepens further.

Title: Secured lending versus leasing: the role of asset management in capital structure
Authors: Anna Maria C Menichini, Maria Grazia Romano
Affiliations: Department of Economics and Statistics, University of Salerno , Fisciano (SA), 84084; CSEF , Via Cintia, Monte S. Angelo, Napoli, 80126
Abstract: Abstract We propose a theory of leasing where incentive problems in asset use and maintenance, along with borrowing constraints, shape firms’ renting decision. When secured lending finances asset purchases but the owner’s uncontractible maintenance determines its residual value, collateral constraints endogenously arise due to privately unprofitable maintenance, causing asset depletion and credit rationing. Leasing contracts bundling financing with maintenance restore maintenance incentives, but create agency problems on the lessee, who may choose insufficient care in asset usage. We find that leasing mitigates credit rationing and facilitates secured lending. However, contrary to conventional wisdom, it may be non-monotone in financing constraints, explaining small firms limited reliance on it. We provide novel testable predictions regarding the use of leasing in different industries.

Title: Machines could not compete with Chinese labor: evidence from US firms’ innovation
Authors: Jan Bena, Elena Simintzi
Affiliations: Sauder School of Business, University of British Columbia , Vancouver, V6T 1Z2; Kenan-Flagler Business School, University of North Carolina , Chapel Hill, NC 27599; CEPR, 2 Coldbath Square, London, EC1R 5HL; ECGI, The Royal Academies of Belgium, Palace of the Academies, Rue Ducale 1 Hertogsstraat, 1000 Brussels
Abstract: Abstract We study how multinational firms’ access to offshore labor affects their decisions to develop new production technologies. The 1999 US–China bilateral agreement improved contracting institutions in China, reducing uncertainty for US multinationals and enabling cheaper labor sourcing through foreign direct investment. Using data from US parent companies and their Chinese subsidiaries, we show that US firms expanded their Chinese operations and increased subsidiaries’ profitability post-agreement. Our novel measure reveals that US multinationals reduced process innovations after the agreement. These findings highlight the impact of cross-border labor sourcing on domestic technological development, highlighting that production and technological choices of multinationals are jointly determined.

Title: Non-bank lending during crises
Authors: Iñaki Aldasoro, Sebastian Doerr, Haonan Zhou
Affiliations: Bank for International Settlements (BIS) , Basel; Centre for Economic Policy Research (CEPR) , London; Faculty of Business and Economics, University of Hong Kong , Hong Kong
Abstract: Abstract For a large sample of countries, this article shows that non-banks curtail their syndicated lending by significantly more than banks during financial crises in borrower countries. Differences in the value of lending relationships explain most of the gap. Relationships with non-banks are less valuable in general and thereby do not improve borrowers’ access to credit during crises. Non-banks are also less likely to form lasting relationships with borrowers. These findings imply that the rise of non-banks could increase the importance of transaction-based lenders and exacerbate the repercussions of financial shocks.

Title: Social transmission bias: evidence from an online investor platform
Authors: Pengfei Sui, Baolian Wang
Affiliations: Shenzhen Finance Institute, School of Management and Economics, The Chinese University of Hong Kong , Shenzhen; Warrington College of Business, University of Florida , Gainesville, FL
Abstract: Abstract Using data from a Twitter-like investor social platform, we document evidence consistent with self-enhancing transmission bias. We find investors are more likely to post about their better-performing stocks. Their followers are more likely to buy the posted stocks than other non-posted stocks. The effect of the postings on follow-up purchases is consistent with an attention-based interpretation: the postings bring the discussed stocks into the followers’ choice set and increase their purchases. We also find that postings’ effect on follow-up purchases is related to postings’ perceived credibility. The performance-postings relationship is stronger among more volatile stocks and the relationship between postings and follow-up purchases is stronger among stocks with higher recent returns, shedding light on the spread of high-variance and extrapolative strategies. We also document that the social network features influential nodes.

Title: Environmental, Social, and Governance Ratings of Environmental, Social, and Governance Index Providers
Authors: Sonakshi Agrawal, Lisa Yao Liu, Shivaram Rajgopal, Suhas A. Sridharan, Yifan Yan, Teri Lombardi Yohn
Affiliations: Columbia University; Emory University
Abstract: ABSTRACT We explore the role of ESG raters’ business models in the production of their ratings, noting that increasingly ESG raters not only produce ESG ratings but also construct and sell ESG indices. We examine whether index licensing incentives are associated with how ESG ratings relate to stock returns. By comparing ratings across raters for the same firm, we control for fundamental ESG performance. We find that raters with strong index licensing incentives assign higher ESG ratings to firms with better stock performance compared to raters with weaker licensing incentives, and that this association is concentrated among index-eligible firms. We further show that index construction is significantly associated with stock returns, and that the high-incentive rater adjusts its ratings following index composition changes, whereas the low-incentive rater does not. Our findings highlight the need for greater transparency in the incentives of ESG rating producers. JEL Classifications: G24; M14; M40; M41; M48; Q56.

Title: Rational Information Acquisition Screens
Authors: Paul E. Fischer, Mirko S. Heinle, Jung Min Kim, Christina Zhu
Affiliations: University of Pennsylvania; Northwestern University
Abstract: ABSTRACT We develop and empirically test a model of information acquisition in capital markets. In the model, investors are uncertain about the returns to acquiring private information before they acquire it. This results in a novel reason for why past price movements affect future capital market outcomes: investors use public information, including past prices, as a screen to estimate the returns to acquiring private information and efficiently allocate their limited information-processing capacity across firms. The model predicts that larger unexplained price movements lead to more private information acquisition, higher future price volatility, and higher future expected trading volume. Using fine-grained data measuring information acquisition on EDGAR and Bloomberg, we provide empirical evidence in support of the model’s predictions. Data Availability: All data are available from the sources cited in the text. JEL Classifications: D83; G12; G14; M41.

Title: Confident and Well‐Connected: The Interplay of Line Managers' HR Self‐Efficacy, Brokerage, and HRM Implementation
Authors: Budy Purnawanto, Huadong Yang, Salma Raheem, Julia Brennecke
Affiliations: Management School University of Liverpool Liverpool UK; College of Business University of Doha for Science and Technology Doha Qatar; Carl von Ossietzky Universität Oldenburg Oldenburg Germany
Abstract: ABSTRACT HRM implementation, defined as line managers' execution of core HRM tasks, has been identified as a key challenge in realizing the competitive advantages associated with HRM. Integrating social cognitive and social network theories, we investigate the joint effect of line managers' HR self‐efficacy (i.e., their confidence in their ability to effectively perform HRM‐related tasks) and their positions as brokers (i.e., their role as intermediaries between otherwise disconnected contacts) in HR advice networks on HRM implementation and establish a link to team performance. Multilevel analyses were conducted using multisource survey data from 88 line managers, their 325 subordinates, and 69 of the line managers' direct superiors across six Indonesian firms. The findings reveal an inverted U‐shaped relationship between self‐efficacy and HRM implementation, with medium levels of self‐efficacy linked to more effective HRM implementation than either low or high levels. Moreover, line managers' positions as HR information brokers moderate the inverted U‐shaped relationship: The curve remains steeper at low levels of brokerage, but becomes shallower at high levels. Finally, HRM implementation mediates the joint effect of self‐efficacy and HR information brokerage on team performance. Taken together, these findings challenge the assumption of a linear relationship between HR self‐efficacy and HRM implementation, enrich understanding of the social foundations of line managers' HRM implementation, and contribute to broader discussions on the enablers and effects of HRM implementation.

Title: Opt-in queue regulation via coarse correlated equilibrium
Authors: Hung Q. Nguyen

CHILE
Authors: Efstathios Avdis, Sergei Glebkin
Affiliations: University of Alberta; INSEAD
Abstract: Abstract We introduce CHILE, an asset-pricing framework with asymmetric information, general utility functions, and arbitrary payoffs. It features a large economy (LE) with continuous-and-heterogeneous information (CHI). The defining feature of this information structure is that the total amount of information stays finite as the economy grows large. We use the framework to study how concentration—the presence of market participants of different sizes—affects market quality, namely liquidity and information efficiency. Greater concentration proves a double-edged sword: it raises liquidity but harms information efficiency. (JEL D01, D53, D82, E19, G12, G14)

Title: Fintech Expansion
Authors: Jing Huang
Affiliations: Texas A&M University
Abstract: Abstract I study credit market outcomes with different competing lending technologies: a fintech lender that learns from data and can seize on-platform sales, and a banking sector that relies on physical collateral. Despite flexible information acquisition technology, endogenous fintech learning is surprisingly coarse, with a single threshold that screens out low-quality borrowers. As fintech lending technology improves, better enforcement harms, while better information technology benefits traditional banking sector profits. Big data technology enables the fintech to leverage data from its early-stage operations in unbanked markets to develop predictive models that support expansion into wealthier markets. (JEL G21, L13, L52, O33, O36)

Title: Coming Clean on Hidden Ties: How Transparency in Related‐Party Transactions Shapes Business Group Internal Organization
Authors: Marina Gama, Rodrigo DeMello, Aldo Musacchio, Tobias Parente
Affiliations: São Paulo School of Business Administration (FGV‐SP); Bentley University; Brandeis University; University of São Paulo (PPGA/FEA‐USP)
Abstract: Abstract This study demonstrates that transparency reforms trigger organizational restructuring within pyramidal business groups rather than simply eliminating opacity. Building on pyramidal ownership theory, we argue that enhanced disclosure alters the relative value of security benefits and diversion across hierarchical layers and jurisdictions. Exploiting the 2008 Brazilian reform of related‐party transaction disclosure as a natural experiment and leveraging a unique dataset covering both publicly traded and privately owned business groups, we show that increased transparency shapes the top layers of the pyramid to maximize security benefits. At the same time, to partially offset the loss of private benefits of control due to increased diversion costs, we find that groups increase the number of offshore affiliates to relocate diversion‐prone activities to jurisdictions with weaker disclosure regimes. These findings contribute to related literature by demonstrating that transparency reforms trigger organizational adaptation across both hierarchical and geographic dimensions.

Title: Evaluating the Ecological Validity and Mechanism of a Generative Model-Based Decomposition of Affective Variability
Authors: Ryan Yan Yan, Don Chamith Halahakoon, Michael Browning
Affiliations: Department of Psychiatry, University of Oxford; Department of Psychology, Stanford University
Abstract: Affective variability is a pervasive phenomenon with important implications for cognition, behavior, and well-being. Yet the broad concept of variability may conflate distinct processes, such as transient fluctuations versus more sustained shifts. Computational approaches like reinforcement learning (RL) offer a mechanistic framework for these processes, but they are often studied in artificial settings, raising questions about ecological validity. We combined an RL task with real-world experience sampling from 332 adult Prolific participants. Using a Bayesian filter, we decomposed affective variability into short-lived affective noise and longer-term affective volatility . In the RL task, noise was driven by recent outcomes, whereas volatility reflected more distant ones. Notably, task-based noise and volatility selectively mapped onto their real-world experience-sampling method (ESM) counterparts, whereas conventional measures did not show such specificity. These findings provide a mechanistic account of distinct timescales underlying affective variability and demonstrate the ecological validity of laboratory tasks for studying real-world affect dynamics.

Title: Movies’ Content Features Predict the Personalities of Their Fans
Authors: Gideon Nave, Peter J. Rentfrow, Sudeep Bhatia
Affiliations: Department of Marketing, The Wharton School, University of Pennsylvania; Department of Psychology, University of Cambridge; Department of Psychology, Korea University; Department of Psychology, The Wharton School, University of Pennsylvania
Abstract: Movies are a central form of entertainment and cultural expression, yet little is known about how their content aligns with the psychological traits of their audiences. We link movie characteristics and contents with the aggregate Big Five personalities of social-media users from a large, international sample who “liked” them. Movie content, captured by text keywords, predicts aggregate audience personalities beyond genre, demographics, and attributes like quality and popularity. An online experiment ( N = 1,018 adults) demonstrates that these content-based personality predictions are behaviorally relevant for choices and evaluations involving new movies and participants. We further provide fine-grained mappings between personality and movie features, including quality, popularity, genre, psychological themes, and unique concepts. Our findings reveal systematic links between personality and movie preferences, showing that people favor content that resonates with their thoughts, emotions, and behaviors. This research enables scalable, automated audience psychographic assessment based on content features, offering insights into personality-driven media preferences.

Title: Efficient and Flexible Large Language Model–Generated Content Detection
Authors: Wan Tian, Zhongfeng Qin, Yijie Peng
Affiliations: School of Economics and Management, Beihang University, Beijing 100191, China; and Wangxuan Institute of Computer Technology, Peking University, Beijing 100871, China; and Advanced Institute of Information Technology, Peking University, Beijing 311215, China; and Key Laboratory of Complex System Analysis, Management and Decision (Beihang University), Ministry of Education, Beijing 100191, China; Department of AI for Management, School of Management and Engineering, School of Computer Science, Nanjing University, Nanjing 210008, China; and Wuhan Institute for Artificial Intelligence, Peking University, Wuhan 100080, China; and Xiangjiang Laboratory, Changsha 410205, China
Abstract: We propose an efficient content detection method generated by large language models (LLMs), referred to as Mahalanobis distance–based confidence score (MDCS)–based detection (MDCSD), that fully harnesses the universality of LLMs across multiple splits. Its essence lies in utilizing the MDCS of the text as the ultimate discriminative feature. The prerequisite for computing the MDCS is the efficient joint estimation of the precision matrices corresponding to multiple splits. We provide regularization techniques for constructing the joint estimator and offer corresponding computationally feasible optimization algorithms. The sparsity and consistency of the joint estimator are demonstrated. Based on offset Rademacher complexity, we further derive the optimal excess risk bound for the detection problem. Superiority of MDCSD is validated on the recently released Human ChatGPT Comparison Corpus data set. History: Accepted by Ram Ramesh, Area Editor for Data Science and Machine Learning. Supplemental Material: The software that supports the findings of this study is available within the paper and its Supplemental Information ( https://pubsonline.informs.org/doi/suppl/10.1287/ijoc.2024.0877 ) as well as from the IJOC GitHub software repository ( https://github.com/INFORMSJoC/2024.0877 ). The complete IJOC Software and Data Repository is available at https://informsjoc.github.io/ .

Title: Understanding the Prompting Effects of Chain-of-Thought on Human Collaboration with Generative AI
Authors: Xusen Cheng, Lu Gao, Qiguang Yang, Xin (Robert) Luo
Affiliations: Renmin University of China, School of Information, Beijing, China; Renmin University of China, School of Journalism and Communication, Beijing, China; Hong Kong Metropolitan University, Lee Shau Kee School of Business and Administration, Hong Kong, Hong Kong
Abstract: It is well established that Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning improves model performance in Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI). Far less understood is whether presenting CoT reasoning in AI-enabled interfaces enhances users’ perceived trust in GenAI’s competence in performing tasks. Drawing on the Heuristic-Systematic Model, we develop a theoretical framework in which CoT presence and quality trigger either heuristic perceptions of transparency or systematic perceptions of diagnosticity and germane cognitive load, with distinct mechanisms across task-difficulty conditions. Across a series of online experiments, we identify two key findings. First, high-quality CoT consistently enhances perceived trust in GenAI’s ability to generate correct outputs, regardless of task difficulty. Notably, under high-difficulty conditions, users’ trust in GenAI is primarily driven by the greater germane cognitive load perceived from high-quality CoT, whereas under low-difficulty conditions, trust is primarily driven by perceived transparency or diagnosticity. Second, low-quality CoT reduces users’ competence trust in GenAI that generates incorrect outputs only under low-difficulty conditions and only when users engage in careful processing, operating through perceived diagnosticity. Yet, under high-difficulty conditions, low-quality CoT amplifies trust via perceived transparency. By disentangling the cognitive pathways through which CoT shapes competence trust in GenAI and by identifying task difficulty as a critical boundary condition, these findings deepen our understanding of transparent reasoning in AI interfaces and offer valuable insights for deploying CoT in GenAI systems.

Title: Platform Information Design and Competitive Price Targeting
Authors: Ruiqi Wu, Yufeng Huang, Nan Li
Affiliations: University of Delaware, Alfred Lerner College of Business & Economics, Newark, Delaware, United States; University of Rochester, Simon Business School, Rochester, New York, 14627, United States; Tongji University School of Economics and Management, Advanced Institute of Business, Shanghai, 200092, China
Abstract: We study platform information design, in which a platform provides information about individual consumers, enabling sellers to set targeted prices. Because targetable information partitions the market and might intensify seller competition, what information should be provided remains an empirical question. We collect novel microdata from Steam, the dominant PC video game platform, and use granular consumer purchase and usage data to estimate their heterogeneous demand for video games. We then develop an equilibrium targeted pricing model to simulate counterfactual outcomes under all possible information designs. We demonstrate that the profit-maximizing information design—which distinguishes heterogeneous consumer types while accounting for the design’s equilibrium impact—yields substantially higher profits compared to demand-based heuristics that ignore the equilibrium impact.

Title: Widely Used Measures of Overconfidence Are Confounded with Ability
Authors: Stephen A. Spiller
Affiliations: Anderson School of Management, University of California, Los Angeles, Los Angeles, California 90095
Abstract: Measures of overconfidence are used both to assess biases in people’s beliefs regarding their own abilities and to identify correlates of those biases. Proposed correlates of overconfidence include narcissism, social status, (low) task anxiety, savings, planning, and many more. Research on these correlates typically explicitly or implicitly claims that the associations with overconfidence are not attributable to ability (i.e., latent inputs enabling successful task performance, including inputs that vary across people, states, or contexts). I argue that several typical approaches used to measure overconfidence are not sufficient to support such claims. This argument follows from two underappreciated properties of these measures of overconfidence. First, performance is an imperfect measure of ability: accounting for performance does not sufficiently account for ability. Second, self-evaluations of performance should reflect ability in addition to performance: because performance is ambiguous, people should incorporate prior beliefs about their ability. These properties imply that multiple commonly used measures of overconfidence are confounded with ability. I support these analytical results by reexamining previously published findings. In the first analysis, I find that overconfidence predicts subsequent performance, consistent with measures of overconfidence serving as a signal of ability. In the second set of analyses, I find that some purported associations between overconfidence and other constructs could be attributed to ability instead. I close with recommendations to recognize and reduce the potential for mistaken inferences. When research indicates that differences in overconfidence are associated with other behaviors, beliefs, or evaluations, researchers should account for the possibility that differences in ability could provide a sufficient explanation. This paper was accepted by Jack Soll, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Funding: This work was supported by the UCLA Anderson Morrison Center for Marketing and Data Analytics. Title: Determinants of Norm Compliance: Moral Similarity and Group Identification
Authors: Alexander Schneeberger, Erin Krupka
Affiliations: Department of Corporate Development and Business Ethics, Faculty of Management, Economics and Social Sciences, University of Cologne, Cologne NRW 50923, Germany; and Max Planck Institute for Behavioral Economics, Bonn NRW 53113, Germany; School of Information, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, Michigan 48109; and Institute for the Study of Labor, Bonn NRW 53113, Germany
Abstract: What determines whether someone complies with a social norm? The social identity approach offers a mechanism for norm compliance: A person who feels similar to a group identifies more with that group and, in turn, complies with the group’s norms. Using an experiment, we test whether similarity in values increases identification and adherence to a group rule. To do so, we varied the similarity/dissimilarity between the values of an individual and members of a social group and measured group identification and rule compliance. We find that moral similarity in progressivism increases group identification, and group identification can increase compliance with rules from the social group. However, our results also suggest that this relationship can be disrupted. Because of our design and empirically verified in our study, social norms do not differ between treatments. As a consequence, observed behavior changes are attributable to increased group norm sensitivity and not changes in group norms. We advance the study of social identity by testing a causal pathway between group identification, group norm sensitivity, and behavior change. Our contribution to the management literature is to extend the empirical rationale, and cautionary notes, for investing in value-alignment between individuals and organizations. This paper was accepted by Marie Claire Villeval, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Title: Screening, Investment Incentives, and the Welfare Trade-Offs of Privacy
Authors: Anastasios Dosis, Casey Rothschild
Affiliations: ESSEC Business School, 95021 Cergy, France; and THEMA, 95021 Cergy, France; Wellesley College, Wellesley, Massachusetts 02481
Abstract: This paper studies how information disclosure affects investment incentives and contracting efficiency. We analyze a class of principal-agent models in which information helps the principal screen the agent but also facilitates surplus appropriation, thereby weakening the agent’s incentive to invest before contracting. Efficient privacy regimes balance these two forces. Along the frontier of efficient information policies, more privacy is associated with stronger investment incentives and higher agent payoff. We characterize conditions under which full privacy, full disclosure, or intermediate privacy is efficient. The results provide guidance for intellectual property and innovation policy by identifying when additional privacy fosters or hinders economic efficiency and innovation. Title: Gatekeepers and Kingmakers: Do Superplatforms Distort Digital Competition?
Authors: Umit G. Gurun, Zheng Liu, Steven Chong Xiao
Affiliations: Naveen Jindal School of Management, University of Texas at Dallas, Richardson, Texas 75080; Metropolitan College, Boston University, Boston, Massachusetts 02215
Abstract: The rising dominance of superplatforms raises concerns about conflicts of interest and externalities on innovation, because they act as both marketplace gatekeepers and strategic investors. Studying Google’s dual role via Google Ventures (GV) and the Android marketplace, we find Google-backed startups receive 115% more reviews, 12% higher ratings, and 77% fewer bug complaints than their iOS counterparts—despite no major app updates. These gains are consistent with selective review removal and platform promotion. Using a difference-in-differences approach with iOS versions as controls, we isolate treatment from selection effects. Our findings challenge platform neutrality and highlight subtle mechanisms of competitive distortion. This paper was accepted by D. J. Wu, information systems.
