Title: How Not to Overpackage: AI for Sustainability in HelloFresh’s Service Supply Chain
Authors: Evelyn Xiao-Yue Gong, Michael Johnson
Affiliations: Carnegie Mellon University, Tepper School of Business, Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, United States; HelloFresh SE, Global AI, United States
Abstract: Problem definition: Packaging waste is a common challenge faced by meal-kit subscription services. Before shipping each box, providers must decide how much and what type of insulated packaging to use. While these materials are essential for preserving product quality, excessive use increases material waste and carbon emissions. As the industry leader, HelloFresh is committed to improving the environmental sustainability of its supply chain. Methodology/results: This paper introduces the Contextual Packaging problem and develops an online-learning method that leverages the problem structure to efficiently mitigate overpackaging. Our algorithm, Contextual Frontier-Preserving Elimination (CFPE), takes into account weather, transit conditions, box contents, and other contextual information to adaptively select the packaging configuration for each box. The algorithm achieves theoretically optimal performance, with an Õ(√𝑇) regret bound unattainable by existing methods, where 𝑇 is the horizon length. We conduct numerical experiments on real delivery data from HelloFresh and observe that CFPE rapidly identifies contexts in which the current guidelines lead to overpackaging. Managerial implications: This paper provides a methodological advance for the meal-kit industry by enabling providers to learn high-granularity optimal packaging guidelines from heterogeneous delivery data, a necessary step toward reducing overpackaging. CFPE is a scalable data-driven alternative to the current chamber-experiment practice, and can also be used in conjunction with such experiments to refine packaging guidelines. The method provides a mechanism to systematically reduce environmental impact while maintaining service quality, rather than treating sustainability as a constraint external to operations. The regret improvement CFPE achieves over existing algorithms has a direct operational interpretation: fewer exploratory shipments are needed before the algorithm narrows attention to promising packaging actions. CFPE also facilitates future adoption of greener packaging materials by enabling faster recalibration of packaging guidelines.

Title: Inventory Productivity and Carbon Emissions in Retailing
Authors: Nikolay Osadchiy
Affiliations: Emory University, Goizueta Business School, Atlanta, Georgia, United States
Abstract: Problem definition: Higher inventory productivity is thought to be associated with lower carbon emissions and waste. We test this conventional wisdom using granular emissions data from CDP. Methodology/results: Pairing emissions data with firms’ financials, we show that most of the emission reduction benefits emerge organically with the scale of operations. Using causal inference techniques, we show that, absent the scale, an external shock to inventory productivity results in higher emission intensity in aggregate across scopes, in Scope 3, and its category of purchased goods and services. The effect on Scope 2 emissions is negative and null in Scope 1. The effect is concentrated in the non-essential retail segments, excluding food and beverage, and health and personal care retailers. Managerial implications: All else kept equal, a higher inventory productivity trades off associated profitability benefits with upstream carbon emissions, particularly in the Scope 3 category of purchased goods and services, underscoring the need for holistic implementation of lean practices. We explore the feasibility of carbon pricing as a mechanism to shift the retailers’ calculus to the dual objective of profit maximization and minimization of environmental impact.

Title: Spoofing and Manipulating Order Books with Learning Algorithms
Authors: Alvaro Cartea, Patrick Chang, Gabriel Garcia Arenas
Affiliations: University of Oxford, Mathematics, Oxford, United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland; University of Oxford, Oxford, United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland; Oxford, United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland
Abstract: We propose a dynamic model of the limit order book to derive conditions to test whether it is optimal to manipulate the order book. Our results show that as a market maker becomes more tolerant to bearing inventory risk, optimal strategies that manipulate the book occur more frequently. Manipulation helps to revert inventory to an optimal level and to execute round-trip trades with limit orders at a higher probability than was otherwise likely to occur. Spoofing is a special case of quote-based manipulation where the market maker prefers that the manipulative limit orders are not filled. Overall, if certain conditions hold, then the optimal trading strategy is to manipulate the limit order book. We use high-frequency data to check our conditions and show that the conditions for manipulation hold in Nasdaq’s limit order book.

Title: Hedging by Giving: Spiritual Insurance and Religious Donations
Authors: Yu-Jane Liu, Juanjuan Meng, Dalin Sheng, Guangxin Yang, Yu Zhang
Affiliations: Peking University Guanghua School of Management; Southwestern University of Finance and Economics China Center for Behavioral Economics and Finance; Xiamen University School of Management
Abstract: Abstract We investigate “spiritual insurance”—a mental strategy for coping with risk, where individuals engage in good deeds, including donations, in exchange for perceived blessings and protection. Using bank transactional data, we show that higher income uncertainty and health shocks lead to increased donations, particularly to religious charities. Moreover, individuals who donate to religious charities tend to reduce insurance expenditures. In a field experiment on millions of potential donors through an online platform, we find that spiritual insurance narratives increase giving, providing direct causal evidence for such a motive. Our findings provide new evidence on how spiritual insurance affects household risk-coping behavior.

Title: Adapting to the new abnormal: multinational corporations’ foreign subsidiary investment and country resilience to climate change
Authors: Chang Hoon Oh, Jorge Rivera, Jennifer Oetzel
Abstract: Abstract As climate change (CC) increasingly disrupts infrastructure, supply chains, labor availability, and public services, multinational corporations (MNCs) face growing uncertainty when selecting locations for foreign expansion. We examine whether host-country CC resilience has become an important determinant of international investment and how firm capabilities shape this relationship. Drawing on socio-ecological resilience theory and the resilience and turbulence framework, we analyze Global Fortune 500 firms investing across 155 countries between 2003 and 2017. We find that MNCs establish more wholly owned subsidiaries in countries with higher CC resilience, indicating that resilience is emerging as a strategic location-specific advantage. This relationship is stronger for firms with well-developed ESG capabilities and prior experience operating in resilient countries, but weaker for firms with greater financial slack. Our findings suggest that managers should incorporate CC resilience into location decisions alongside traditional economic and institutional criteria while considering their firms’ resource and capability profile to assess how effectively they can leverage host-country CC resilience. For policymakers, the results indicate that strengthening CC resilience can improve not only adaptation to CC but also national competitiveness in attracting MNC foreign direct investment. Overall, CC resilience is becoming a strategic determinant of where MNCs choose to invest.

Title: Short-horizon capital in a bank-centered financial system: Japanese mutual fund launches relative to the U.S.
Authors: Toshiki Honda, Alan Guoming Huang, Daisuke Miyakawa, Sho Nishiuchi, Russ Wermers
Abstract: Abstract The median time from launch to peak assets under management (AUM) is nine months for Japanese active domestic equity mutual funds, versus 4.6 years for comparable U.S. funds. Japanese funds also grow much less from launch to peak, as strong initial inflows quickly give way to persistent outflows, while U.S. funds continue to attract net inflows for years. We link this compressed life cycle to Japan’s bank-centered, concentrated distribution system and front-loaded sales compensation. A larger launch size and higher sales load each predict earlier peak AUM in Japan, but not in the U.S.; within Japan, stronger distribution networks are associated with larger launches and earlier peaks, while longer pre-inception sales periods are associated with larger launch sizes and higher sales loads. The evidence shows that the same market-based financial product can follow different life cycles when embedded in different national systems of intermediation and compensation. Japan’s prolonged weak equity-market environment provides an additional context in which investors may reassess newly launched funds as realized performance becomes observable. Our findings suggest that incentives rewarding initial sales can mobilize capital rapidly without generating durable asset retention in an institutional environment such as Japan’s.

Title: Taxing Homeowners Who Can't or Won't Borrow
Authors: Francis Wong
Affiliations: LMU Munich
Abstract: Abstract Using high-frequency administrative data covering millions of US homeowners, I document three novel facts about homeowner responses to property tax increases driven by rising home values. First, non-migrating homeowners cut consumption, exhibit financial distress, and do not borrow against their higher home values. Second, heterogeneity analysis shows that consumption responses do not vary by liquidity, consistent with savings target behavior. In contrast, distress responses are concentrated among liquidity-constrained homeowners. Many homeowners report being debt averse and therefore unwilling to borrow in order to avoid illiquidity and distress. Third, tax hikes induce migration—partly by displacing illiquid homeowners—but do not accelerate neighborhood change. A simple welfare framework reveals that the largest costs of property taxes arise from financial distress, suggesting welfare gains from policies that limit taxes for liquidity-constrained households.

Title: Limits of Disclosure in Search Markets
Authors: Raphael Boleslavsky, Silvana Krasteva
Affiliations: Department of Business Economics and Public Policy, Kelley School of Business, Indiana University; Department of Economics, Texas A&M University
Abstract: Abstract This paper examines competitive information disclosure in search markets with a mix of selective consumers, who search costlessly, and casual consumers, who incur positive search costs. Selective consumers incentivize truthful disclosure; casual consumers, concealment. With both types, the equilibrium features partial disclosure, which persists despite intense competition. Casual consumers may search actively, but only in small markets. While selective consumers benefit from increased competition, casual consumers may be harmed. Changes in search costs have non-monotone effects: the equilibrium approaches full disclosure as the cost approaches zero or the mean valuation. When costs are high, further increases raise equilibrium informativeness and the welfare of selective consumers, while reducing the welfare of casual consumers.

Title: Collateral Demand in Wholesale Funding Markets
Authors: Jamie Coen, Patrick Coen, Anne-Caroline Hüser
Affiliations: Imperial College London , U.K; Warwick Business School , U.K; Bank of England , U.K
Abstract: Abstract Repo markets are systemically important funding markets, but are also used by firms to obtain the assets provided as collateral. We build and structurally estimate a model of trade between heterogeneous firms in the sterling gilt repo market, and show that this collateral demand depresses repo market activity and can impede the transmission of monetary policy. We quantify how well-designed central bank repo facilities can improve outcomes: if the central bank were to lend out the assets on its balance sheet following quantitative easing, transmission and total firm surplus would improve by 20% and 38%, respectively.

Title: Supercharging the Confidence Trap: Too-Big-to-Fail and Man-Made Disasters
Authors: Akhil Bhardwaj, Henk Akkermans, Luk N. Van Wassenhove
Abstract: Man-made disasters are always shocking, especially when they involve loss of life. The shock is even greater when such disasters are attributed to failures in highly regulated organizations like Boeing, long known for engineering excellence and safety. In the spirit of pragmatic inquiry that considers attenuating the likelihood of disasters an urgent and important problem, we explore the underlying dynamics that can lead to such outcomes. We draw on an agent-based modelling approach within a system dynamics framework. We argue that operational and organizational complexity creates barriers to identifying failures that contribute to disasters. A key contributor to this dynamic is the weakening of regulatory oversight, as both regulators and operators fall into a “confidence trap” – a mistaken belief that past risk-taking success justifies continued risk-taking. This dynamic is exacerbated when the organization in question is perceived as “too big to fail,” which shields it from market selection mechanisms. To mitigate these factors, we propose two policy levers. First, we propose financial clawbacks that require executives to return part of their compensation in the event of a disaster. This aligns incentives of the regulator and executives by injecting the latter’s “skin in the game,” and attenuates the moral hazard problem. Second, we propose third-party monitoring and auditing that serve to mitigate regulatory oversight and better utilize expertise. Simulations indicate these levers significantly reduce the likelihood and impact of failures that lead to disasters, offering a robust logic of pursuit.

Title: The Role of Consumer Fairness Seeking in Live-Stream E-Commerce
Authors: Baozhuang Niu, Jianhua Zhang, Qiyang Li, Xinhu Yu, Yulan Wang
Abstract: As live-stream e-commerce rapidly expands and gains popularity among consumers, many brand owners have supplemented their self-owned direct-selling channels with live-stream selling channels to utilize social network effects of key opinion leaders (KOLs). This dual-channel structure creates price discrepancy issues, prompting consumers to raise concerns about price fairness. Therefore, brand owners are motivated to coordinate pricing strategies, balancing cooperation and competition across channels. We build a game-theoretical model to investigate how consumers' peer-induced fairness seeking influences the price decisions of a brand owner (in the direct-selling channel) and the KOL (in the live-stream selling channel). Interestingly, we find that consumers' increased fairness concerns may paradoxically lead to increased prices in both channels, challenging the conventional expectation of price-cutting competition. We further demonstrate that consumers' fairness seeking may either benefit or harm both sellers, depending on the strength of network effects and various factors related to competition intensity. The non-monotonic impacts of consumer fairness seeking are driven by the brand owner's dueling strategic incentives to secure (or relinquish) its direct-selling business to compete with (or favor) the live-stream selling under different situations. Finally, we identify “win-win”, “lose-lose”, and “lose-win” outcomes that consumer fairness seeking can cause for the brand owner and KOL.

Title: Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers-Based Distributed Optimal Power Flow with Fixed- and Finite-Time Update Rules
Authors: Milad Hasanzadeh, Amin Kargarian
Affiliations: Division of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Louisiana State University, Baton Rouge, Louisiana 70803
Abstract: This paper proposes two categories of fixed- and finite-time update rules to enhance the convergence of distributed optimal power flow (OPF) solved using the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM). The first category formulates an update rule for OPF primal variables, starting with an asymptotic update rule, followed by finite-time and fixed-time update rules. These update rules adjust the primal variables using a weighted approach that accelerates the agreement between neighboring OPF subproblems. Stability and convergence are analyzed to guarantee reliable performance. The second category modifies the update rule for dual variables (Lagrangian multipliers) by introducing finite-time and fixed-time update rules, with stability analysis conducted to ensure convergence. These modifications improve the rate at which consensus is achieved among subproblems while maintaining the consistency of dual updates across the network. Case studies confirm that the proposed methods reduce iteration counts and improve ADMM OPF performance, making them effective solutions for accelerating distributed computations. Title: Stockouts and the Success of New Products
Authors: Diego Aparicio, Duncan I. Simester
Affiliations: Georgetown University, Washington, District of Columbia 20057; MIT Sloan School of Management, Cambridge, Massachusetts 02142
Abstract: We investigate how stockouts of existing products influence the success of new product introductions. Our findings reveal that stockouts on incumbent items at the time a new product is launched are associated with higher sales of the new product for at least six months. This positive spillover is specific to new products and is most potent at the start of the product life cycle. To establish causality, we use instrumental variables based on historical stockouts and contemporaneous stockouts in other stores. Analysis of individual-level transaction data corroborates a trial-and-adoption mechanism: Stockouts of existing items prompt consumers to trial the new product, leading to increased repeat purchasing. By identifying inventory as a driver of product trial, this research highlights the importance of strategically timing new product launches and documents a previously unrecognized tradeoff for inventory policies. Title: Deep Tangency Portfolio
Authors: Guanhao Feng, Liang Jiang, Junye Li, Yizhi Song, Yuanzhi Wang
Affiliations: City University of Hong Kong, Kowloon 999077, Hong Kong SAR; International School of Finance, Fudan University, Shanghai 200433, China; School of Management, Fudan University, Shanghai 200433, China; International Business School, Hainan University, Haikou 570228, China; University of Science and Technology of China, Hefei 230026, China
Abstract: We develop a deep learning framework to directly estimate tangency portfolio weights by augmenting benchmark factors with a long-short deep factor derived from high-dimensional characteristics. Guided by a Sharpe ratio maximization objective, the deep factor plays two key roles: (i) providing a natural hedge against benchmark risks and (ii) capturing multimarket signals to enhance the performance of the benchmark. In an empirical application to U.S. corporate bonds using 132 firm-level bond, equity, and option characteristics, the deep factor achieves an out-of-sample Sharpe ratio exceeding one, and the deep tangency portfolio benchmarked against the market factor yields a Sharpe ratio over two, outperforming portfolios spanned by common observable or latent factors. These results demonstrate that bond risk signals are fundamentally dense, requiring the nonlinear integration of multimarket information to span the efficient frontier. Title: Learning from a Biased Sample
Authors: Roshni Sahoo, Lihua Lei, Stefan Wager
Affiliations: Columbia Business School, Columbia University, New York 10027; Graduate School of Business, Stanford University, Palo Alto, California 94305
Abstract: The empirical risk minimization approach to data-driven decision making requires access to training data drawn under the same conditions as those that will be faced when the decision rule is deployed. However, we may be concerned that our training sample is biased in the sense that some groups (characterized by either observable or unobservable attributes) may be under- or over-represented relative to the general population; and in this setting, empirical risk minimization over the training set may fail to yield rules that perform well at deployment. We propose a model of sampling bias called conditional [Formula: see text]-biased sampling, where observed covariates can affect the probability of sample selection arbitrarily much but the amount of unexplained variation in the probability of sample selection is bounded by a constant factor. Applying the distributionally robust optimization framework, we propose a method for learning a decision rule that minimizes the worst-case risk incurred under a family of test distributions that can generate the training distribution under conditional [Formula: see text]-biased sampling. We apply a result of Rockafellar and Uryasev to show that this problem is equivalent to an augmented convex risk minimization problem. We give statistical guarantees for learning a model that is robust to sampling bias via the method of sieves, and propose a deep learning algorithm whose loss function captures our robust learning target. We empirically validate our proposed method in a case study on prediction of mental health scores from health survey data and a case study on intensive care unit length-of-stay prediction. Title: Information Design with Supplemental Investment
Authors: Lin Nan, Lin Qiu, Xiaoyan Wen, Ronghuo Zheng
Affiliations: Purdue University, West Lafayette, Indiana 47907; Texas Christian University, Fort Worth, Texas 76129; University of Texas at Austin, Austin, Texas 78712
Abstract: This paper features a setting with two-dimensional information asymmetry on a firm’s fundamental (good or bad type) and the nature of its supplemental investment (improving upside potential, or mitigating downside risk). We examine the firm’s optimal design of the information system when the system can only address the dimension of fundamental. We show that, with only single-dimensional information asymmetry regarding the firm’s fundamental, greater informativeness on the firm’s fundamental type always improves efficiency. However, with two-dimensional information asymmetry, increasing informativeness about firm fundamental no longer guarantees higher efficiency and can be detrimental. The optimal information system trades off reducing information asymmetry and preserving firms’ incentives to invest, and it could be uninformative or optimistically biased, depending on the level of credit risk, which in our setting is higher when supplemental investment is more likely to improve upside rather than protect downside. Title: Optimal Incentive Design for Decentralized Dynamic Matching Markets
Authors: Chen Chen, Pengyu Qian, Jingwei Zhang
Affiliations: New York University Shanghai, Shanghai 200124, China; Questrom School of Business, Boston University, Boston, Massachusetts 02215; School of Data Science, School of Management and Economics, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen, Guangdong 518172, China
Abstract: In decentralized dynamic matching markets, agents can benefit from sharing resources, but they will collaborate only if properly incentivized. Motivated by applications such as multihospital kidney exchanges and job-hunting markets, this paper proposes novel monetary and nonmonetary mechanisms to incentivize collaboration in such decentralized dynamic markets. We study a model in which multiple self-interested agents manage local multiway dynamic matching problems. Jobs of different types arrive stochastically at each agent, expire after a limited time, and yield rewards when matched. An agent’s job backlog and actions are the agent’s private information, and each agent aims to maximize its long-run average matching reward. We design simple mechanisms that incentivize agents to submit all jobs upon arrival, thereby enabling centralized matching. Our first mechanism, the marginal-value (MV) mechanism, reimburses agents based on the MV of their submitted jobs. This can be implemented in a nonmonetary way by randomly selecting an agent (with a specified probability) to perform a match and collect the associated matching reward. We show that under the MV mechanism, full job submission constitutes an approximate Nash equilibrium—that is, the gain from unilateral deviation vanishes as the number of agents grows. To further eliminate incentives for deviation, we propose a refined mechanism, the MV-plus-credit (MVC) mechanism, and show that, when the number of agents exceeds a constant threshold, full job submission constitutes a stronger oblivious equilibrium. Numerical experiments based on kidney exchange data demonstrate that the gains from deviation under our mechanisms are small even in moderately sized markets. Title: Proximity-Based Delivery Policies: Efficiency, Coverage, and Fairness
Authors: Zhongbin Wang, Shiliang Cui, Yongjian Li, Qian Zhang
Affiliations: College of Management and Economics, Tianjin University, Tianjin 300072, China; McDonough School of Business, Georgetown University, Washington, District of Columbia 20057; Business School, Nankai University, Tianjin 300071, China; School of Management, Xi’an Jiaotong University, Xi’an 710049, China
Abstract: The growing demand for rapid food and grocery delivery has prompted many restaurants and retailers to develop their own on-demand delivery services. Although hiring additional couriers can expand delivery capacity, it is often prohibitively costly. As a cost-effective alternative, we propose a proximity-based delivery (PBD) policy that prioritizes the delivery of orders from customers located closer to the vendor, in contrast to the traditional first-come-first-served (FCFS) approach. We show that PBD can substantially reduce average delivery delays without requiring additional couriers; however, it may raise fairness concerns, because distant customers experience longer wait times, potentially shrinking market coverage and exacerbating service disparities. To address this issue, we introduce an incentive-compatible PBD (IP) policy, where nearby customers are incentivized to pay for priority, whereas distant customers receive compensation to offset longer delays. We demonstrate that this mechanism can restore fairness to levels comparable to FCFS while preserving efficiency, expanding market demand, and enhancing consumer surplus, particularly in moderately dense markets with moderately delay-sensitive customers. We further show that vendors can enhance these benefits through optimal pricing and benefit from less extreme staffing adjustments due to a “pull-to-center” effect. Our findings highlight the operational, economic, and ethical dimensions of proximity-based delivery, and offer a practical framework for balancing speed, profitability, consumer welfare, and equity. Finally, we conduct a mini case study using empirical data to demonstrate the real-world applicability of our approach. This paper was accepted by Jeannette Song, operations management. Funding: Z. Title: The Effect of Cost Elasticity Choice on Loss Reversal
Authors: Edmond Tapero, Dan Weiss
Affiliations: Tel Aviv University
Abstract: ABSTRACT Although the prevalence of losses has been increasing over the years, little is known about how managerial decisions lead to reversing losses back to profits. We find cost elasticity choices, implied by operating actions made in advance, significantly increase the likelihood of loss reversal. We show loss firms with high cost elasticity exhibit significantly higher long-term survival rates and are therefore less likely to exercise the abandonment option than loss firms with low cost elasticity. The contributions are twofold. First, the findings shed light on a mechanism underlying loss reversal. We extend the loss literature by promoting the understanding of how ex ante cost elasticity choices affect the likelihood of loss reversal. Second, the findings enrich the cost accounting literature by demonstrating a unique performance implication of a cost elasticity choice. Title: Disclosing work-from-home flexibility to compete for talent? Evidence from job postings
Authors: Charles Ham, Rebecca N. Hann, Wenfeng Wang, Jingwen Yang
Abstract: Abstract Job postings serve as one of the primary means to communicate with prospective employees, enabling employers to highlight the benefits of the position and attract qualified applicants. As work-from-home flexibility has become increasingly prevalent, this study examines whether employers strategically disclose work-from-home flexibility in their job postings and how this disclosure is associated with hiring outcomes. Using a comprehensive sample of job postings from US employers between 2017 and 2024, we find that employers are more likely to disclose work-from-home flexibility when facing greater labor market competition and that disclosing this flexibility is associated with a higher job vacancy filling rate, especially when work-from-home information is disclosed in a more salient manner. However, we document a positive association between work-from-home disclosures and subsequent employee turnover, suggesting potential costs associated with these disclosures. These findings add to the growing literature on firms’ strategic disclosure targeted towards labor markets.

Title: Deterrence or Backlash? Arrests and the Dynamics of Domestic Violence
Authors: Sofia Amaral, Gordon B. Dahl, Timo Hener, Victoria Kaiser, Helmut Rainer

Title: Book Review: Fayolle, A., Le Pontois, S., & Pelly, R. D. M. (Eds.). Big questions and great answers in entrepreneurship research: Discussing up-to-date methodological and philosophical issues FayolleA.Le PontoisS.PellyR. D. M. (Eds.). (2024). Big questions and great answers in entrepreneurship research: Discussing up-to-date methodological and philosophical issues.Edward Elgar Publishing. 376 pp. ISBN 978 1 80088 865 4
Authors: Pinar Ozcan
Affiliations: Professor of Entrepreneurship and Innovation, Saïd Business School, University of Oxford, Oxford, UK

Title: “Sit Nice!”: Peer Culture, Teacher Capacity, and Joint Socialization Efforts in Preschool
Authors: Casey Stockstill
Affiliations: Dartmouth College
Abstract: Preschools instill soft skills that are crucial to children’s life outcomes. As preschool access expands, research and policy often focus on improving teacher quality. This focus downplays how much teachers’ efforts may depend on children’s peers. Drawing on two years of ethnography, I highlight two important aspects of socialization: teachers’ capacity to deliver messages in the moment, and peers’ tendency to support those messages. I compare socialization processes at two race- and class-segregated preschools. Three interrelated classroom conditions—children’s enrollment, attendance, and challenging behaviors—mattered for socialization interactions. Teachers at both preschools pursued socialization goals of instilling safe and formal classroom behaviors. At the affluent, majority-White preschool, teachers had a greater capacity to coach children in the moment, and peers had a culture of supporting teacher messages. At the low-income, racially diverse preschool, children placed the authority to coach classroom behavior in their teachers, who were pressed for time. I argue that socialization agents jointly influence behavior. In segregated preschools, teachers may shape classroom behavior to unequal extents, preventing early learning settings from disrupting future inequalities.

Title: Cognitive Ambidexterity: Balancing Algorithmic Efficiency and Contextual Judgement in AI-Enabled Decision Systems
Authors: Tahir Abbas Syed
Affiliations: University of Manchester
Abstract: AI-enabled decision systems make algorithmic recommendations appear objective and ready for action before contextual, ethical, and stakeholder concerns are fully considered. This study examines how leaders preserve judgment under these conditions. We develop cognitive ambidexterity as a leader-level meta-cognitive capability through which managers balance algorithmic exploitation with contextual exploration in AI-mediated decisions. Using an exploratory sequential mixed-methods design, we first examine five U.K. procurement and infrastructure organizations and identify four mechanisms of cognitive ambidexterity. We then examine these mechanisms through vignette experiments with managers. The findings show that leaders preserve contextual judgment by treating AI outputs as interpretive cues, calibrating trust under ambiguity, slowing decisions when reflection is needed, and building supports that make algorithmic recommendations contestable. The study extends ambidexterity theory by showing how exploration–exploitation tensions are cognitively regulated when exploitation is embedded in algorithmic decision processes. It also uses leadership cognition and Upper Echelons Theory to explain why leaders differ in their capacity to enact this regulation. Together, these insights position cognitive ambidexterity as a critical leader-level capability for using AI’s efficiency gains while preserving the contextual judgment.

Title: Surprise Resets the Mind: An Adaptive Online Reset in Working Memory Selection
Authors: Jiahan Yu, Jiewei Zheng, Yingtao Fu, Ning Tang, Bin Li, Jifan Zhou, Mowei Shen, Hui Chen
Affiliations: Department of Psychology, Suzhou University of Science and Technology; Department of Psychology and Behavioral Sciences, Zhejiang University; Ningbo Psychiatric Hospital, Ningbo, China; Department of Psychology, Soochow University; The State Key Lab of Brain‑Machine Intelligence, Zhejiang University; Zhejiang Key Laboratory of Neurocognitive Development and Mental Health, Zhejiang University
Abstract: Human cognition rapidly adapts to unexpected events in dynamic environments, but it remains unclear whether expectation violations rapidly influence the selection of attended information into working memory. Using the attribute-amnesia paradigm, we introduced expectation violations during the surprise trial to test whether unexpected changes improve reporting of a target feature that had been attended and used but was normally not reported. Across six experiments (total N = 250 college students, aged 17–27 years; 149 females), expectation violations reliably improved surprise-trial report of this feature, indicating greater availability in working memory. This effect occurred not only when the violation concerned the target, but also when it involved broader contextual or auditory changes, suggesting that the effect cannot be characterized simply as enhanced visual attention to the target. These findings suggest that expectation violations trigger a rapid, flexible adjustment of working-memory selection, highlighting its role in dynamically managing information under uncertainty.

Title: War and Entrepreneurship: A Synthetic Control Study of the Russia-Ukraine Conflict
Authors: David B. Audretsch, Paul P. Momtaz, Hanna Motuzenko, Silvio Vismara
Affiliations: Interim Dean of the Paul O’Neill School of Public and Environmental Affairs, Indiana University, Bloomington, IN, USA; Aspire Lab! University of Klagenfurt, Austria; Martin J. Whitman School of Management, Syracuse University, NY, USA; House of Finance, Endowed Chair of Private Equity, Goethe-Universität Frankfurt am Main, Germany; Department of Management, University of Bergamo, Italy; AXES (Laboratory for the Analysis of CompleX Economic Systems), IMT School for Advanced Studies Lucca, Italy
Abstract: Is war good or bad for entrepreneurship? Entrepreneurs are often situated in extreme environments characterized by violent conflict. Yet existing entrepreneurship scholarship has largely examined war and conflict only at the micro or meso level, leaving the aggregate, macro-level entrepreneurial consequences of large-scale war underexplored. We provide a synthetic control study of entrepreneurial dynamics in the Russo-Ukrainian conflict during 2009 to 2019 as a first step toward bridging this gap. Relative to the synthetic counterfactual, registered LLCs in Ukraine declined by approximately 13% at the 2016 peak (74,000 missing firms) before recovering toward the synthetic trajectory by 2019. Self-employment in Ukraine dropped by approximately 4 percentage points (pp) at the 2015 peak, corresponding to roughly 680,000 Ukrainians no longer self-employed relative to the counterfactual, with partial recovery to a residual shortfall of approximately 280,000 by 2019. For Russia, the gap is delayed but accumulating, widening from −0.4 pp in 2015 to −1.6 pp by 2019. This corresponds to approximately 1.56 million missing LLCs relative to the counterfactual, a 32% relative loss. The contraction in Russian LLCs accumulates rather than attenuates over time. In Ukraine, we also observe a gender gap in post-2014 self-employment deviations from the synthetic counterfactual, with female self-employment falling more than male self-employment. To interpret these findings, we propose a conceptual framework that combines critical-junctures theory with the literature on entrepreneurship under authoritarian and democratic institutional regimes, arguing that the divergent post-2014 institutional trajectories of Russia and Ukraine help explain the contrasting entrepreneurial patterns we observe. JEL Codes: D74, L26, N44, O17

Title: Organizational Goal Hierarchies in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: A Dynamic Behavioral Perspective

Title: Target Firm Material Contract Redactions and Valuation in Acquisitions
Authors: Paul A. Griffin, Hyun A. Hong, Kyungran Lee, Jiwoo Ryou
Affiliations: University of California, Davis; University of California, Riverside; NEOMA Business School; West Virginia University
Abstract: ABSTRACT We study whether and how the SEC’s confidential treatment program, which allows firms to redact proprietary information from material contracts, affects valuation in corporate acquisitions. We find that friendly acquisitions of redacting targets generate significantly higher positive announcement returns for both targets and acquirers compared with acquisitions of nonredacting targets. These positive returns are also more pronounced when targets are likelier to hold valuable proprietary information. In addition, friendly acquisitions of redacting targets achieve better long-term performance and recognize fewer subsequent goodwill impairments compared with acquisitions of nonredacting targets. Our findings of a robust association between target firm material contract redactions and target and acquirer announcement returns are consistent with a dual disclosure perspective, whereby redaction preserves target proprietary value, which is transferred privately to the acquirer through due diligence. Data Availability: Data are available from public sources identified in the paper; some require a subscription. JEL Classifications: D8; M41; M48.

Title: Toward an Integrative Model of Layoff Effects: A Strategic Human Capital Resources Framework
Authors: Kaifeng Jiang, Qianning Liu, Dongyuan Wu, Jie Feng
Affiliations: Guanghua School of Management, Peking University Beijing China; School of Management, Fudan University Shanghai China; School of Management and Labor Relations, Rutgers University New Brunswick New Jersey USA
Abstract: ABSTRACT Despite decades of research yielding rich theoretical insights and empirical evidence, the layoff literature remains fragmented. It lacks an overarching framework integrating findings across levels of analysis (e.g., organizational, group, and individual), stakeholder groups (e.g., layoff decision‐makers, executioners, survivors, and displaced employees), and outcomes from proximal processes to distal performance consequences. This fragmentation impedes understanding of how layoff effects unfold and why they vary across individuals and organizations. We review and synthesize layoff research and integrate insights from recent advancements in the strategic human capital resources literature. Our framework explains how layoffs first trigger an outflow of human capital and then reshape the quality, complementarity, and deployment of remaining human capital resources, while shaping the social‐psychological reactions of stakeholder groups. We further identify layoff characteristics as contingencies that determine whether layoffs produce negative or positive shifts in strategic human capital resources states, shape stakeholder reactions, and condition whether individual outcomes aggregate to the organizational level. In doing so, we delineate the organizational‐, individual‐, and cross‐level pathways through which layoffs influence individual performance and, ultimately, organizational outcomes. We offer implications for firms seeking to plan layoffs strategically, manage social and psychological processes, and leverage human capital resources before, during, and after layoffs.

Title: Optimising intermodal transportation and last-mile delivery: A decomposition approach
Authors: Ioannis Avgerinos, Emmanouil E. Zachariadis, Georgios Zois

Title: An efficient mixed-integer linear programming formulation for solving influence diagrams
Authors: Topias Terho, Fabricio Oliveira, Ahti Salo, Pedro Munari
Abstract: Influence diagrams represent decision-making problems with interdependencies between random events, decisions, and consequences. Traditionally, they have been solved using tailored algorithms that determine the expected utility-maximizing decision strategy. Towards this end, most recent state-of-the-art solution approaches convert them into mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) models that can be solved using off-the-shelf MILP solvers. Computationally, these approaches are most efficient for influence diagrams that represent periodic (or sequential) decision processes, which can be cast as partially observable Markov Decision Processes. However, they are inefficient for problems that lack this periodic structure or whose influence diagrams have large state spaces. The efficient MILP formulation presented in this paper is specifically designed for influence diagrams that are challenging for earlier MILP formulations. Additionally, this formulation can be adapted to optimize conditional value-at-risk and to incorporate chance and logical constraints, thereby retaining the modeling flexibility of MILP-based methods. Finally, computational experiments on a range of problems from the literature are reported to show that the proposed formulation is much more efficient than earlier MILP formulations, particularly in problems which cannot be modeled as partially observable Markov decision processes and which lead to influence diagrams whose decision or chance nodes may have large state spaces.

Title: Unemployment Benefits and Unemployment in the Great Recession: The Role of Equilibrium Effects
Authors: Marcus Hagedorn, Fatih Karahan, Iourii Manovskii, Kurt Mitman
Abstract: Equilibrium labor market theory suggests that unemployment benefit extensions affect unemployment by impacting both job search decisions by the unemployed and job creation decisions by employers. The existing empirical literature focused on the former effect only. We develop a new methodology necessary to incorporate the measurement of the latter effect. Implementing this methodology in the data, we find that benefit extensions raise equilibrium wages and lead to a sharp contraction in vacancy creation and employment and a rise in unemployment.

Title: Intermediate Input Prices and the Labor Share
Authors: Juanma Castro-Vincenzi, Benny Kleinman
Abstract: We argue that the relative price of materials is an important determinant of the labor share of income. When materials and primary inputs are complements and the profit share is positive, a higher price of materials lowers the labor share and raises the profit share of value added, without requiring markups or returns to scale to change. We show that materials-price fluctuations align with U.S. labor-share trends, provide causal evidence on this mechanism across industries and commuting zones, and quantify its importance in a dynamic quantitative model. Finally, we use our mechanism to rationalize differential labor-share trends across countries. Institutional subscribers to the NBER working paper series, and residents of developing countries may download this paper without additional charge at www.nber.org.

Title: Market Response to Racial Uprisings
Authors: Bocar A. Ba, Roman Rivera, Alexander Whitefield
Abstract: Do investors anticipate that demands for racial equity will impact companies? We explore this question in the context of the Black Lives Matter (BLM) movement—the largest racially motivated protest movement in U.S. history—and its effect on the U.S. policing industry using a novel dataset on publicly traded firms contracting with the police. It is unclear whether the BLM uprisings were likely to increase or decrease market valuations of firms contracting heavily with police because of the increased interest in reforming the police, fears over rising crime, and pushes to “defund the police”. We find, in contrast to the predictions of economics experts we surveyed, that in the three weeks following incidents triggering BLM uprisings, policing firms experienced a stock price increase of seven percentage points relative to the stock prices of nonpolicing firms in similar industries. In particular, firms producing surveillance technology and police accountability tools experienced higher returns following BLM activism–related events. Furthermore, policing firms’ fundamentals, such as sales, improved after the murder of George Floyd, suggesting that policing firms’ future performances bore out investors' positive expectations following incidents triggering BLM uprisings. Our research shows how—despite BLM’s calls to reduce investment in policing and explore alternative public safety approaches—the financial market has translated high-profile violence against Black civilians and calls for systemic change into shareholder gains and additional revenues for police suppliers.

Title: Giving More in a Non-Native Language: The Effect of Language on Monetary Donations
Authors: Marie Ozanne, Archer Yue Pan, Xinlian Zhang, Kaitlin Woolley
Affiliations: Cornell University Assistant professor of services management, , Ithaca, NY 14853; Wayne State University Assistant professor of marketing, , Detroit, MI, 48201; Cornell University PhD student in services management, , Ithaca, NY 14853; Cornell University Professor of marketing, , Ithaca, NY 14853
Abstract: Abstract How does the language of a charitable appeal, whether communicated in a potential donor’s native or non-native (but proficient) language, influence monetary donations? Whereas research finds that people behave more morally in their native (vs. non-native) language, eight preregistered experiments (N = 7,447) and one archival analysis (N = 3,142) find that people donate less in response to appeals in their native language. People facing a donation decision need to determine whether and how much to give, with the appropriate action varying across situations. Situational considerations that inform this decision are more accessible in a native language, making donation decisions seem less diagnostic of the self, reducing giving. Consistent with this process, perceived self-diagnosticity mediates the effect of language on donations, and manipulating self-diagnosticity attenuates this effect. Reconciling these findings with prior research, the relationship between language and moral behavior depends on the type of moral decision under consideration: a native language promotes adherence to moral rules when decisions involve moral violations (stealing; lying), but reduces giving for donation decisions, which we refer to as moral aspirations. Beyond advancing theory on language, self-diagnosticity, and moral behavior, this research offers practical guidance to maximize charitable giving when communicating with multilingual audiences.

Title: Cooperative Needs and Competitive Opportunities: Lobbying for Technology and the Expropriation of Knowledge
Authors: Michael Park
Affiliations: INSEAD, France
Abstract: Despite the importance of regulations regarding new technologies, there has been limited research on the competitive dynamics that may unfold among firms engaged in lobbying. In this article, I explore the potential for knowledge expropriation when firms lobby for technology-related regulations. I propose a framework that distinguishes two processes underlying knowledge expropriation—knowledge leakage and uptake—and argue that employing lobbyists creates opportunities for both. Given the different roles of internal and external lobbyists, I predict that increases in internal lobbyists will lead to a greater risk of leakage, while increases in external lobbyists will give rise to more opportunities for uptake. I test these predictions on a unique dataset of U.S. firms that employed lobbyists to influence technology policy and the patents for which those firms applied. I use an embedding approach on the text of patents to directly detect both knowledge leakage and uptake. Overall, the results suggest that lobbying enables opportunities for knowledge expropriation because firms share information that is useful, reliable, timely, and therefore strategically valuable to competitors. In this way, my study identifies a new competitive dynamic at the intersection of firms’ political and innovation strategy.

Title: The Relationship Between a Salesperson’s Past and Future Performance
Authors: Melissa Baucum, Alex R. Zablah, Nawar N. Chaker, Johannes Habel
Abstract: A salesperson’s past performance is widely assumed to predict their future performance, and thus often guides managerial decision-making. Contrary to that assumption, this study uncovers why and under what conditions past performance becomes a less reliable predictor of future performance. A grounded theory study in a solution-selling context reveals that recent wins generate after-sales workload that lowers the odds of converting the next lead, particularly when those wins are complex, as occurs when customer relationships are new or procurement is formalized. Analysis of seven years of CRM data covering 3,669 sales leads at a Fortune 500 firm confirms that the link between past and future wins weakens as recent wins grow in complexity. Behavioral experiments causally confirm this attenuation effect, showing recent wins reduce effort on the next lead when those wins are complex. Finally, a single-dataset meta-analysis offers convergent evidence for workload as the underlying mechanism, revealing the relationship also weakens when workload is decoupled from winning and rooted in organizational change instead. For managers, these findings imply that using past performance to guide forecasting, quota setting, and coaching risks suboptimal decisions. They also underscore the importance of resourcing salespeople to balance after-sales responsibilities with new business development.

Title: Causal Inference With Endogenous Price Response
Authors: Przemyslaw Jeziorski, Dingzhe Leng, Stephan Seiler
Abstract: The authors study the estimation of causal treatment effects on demand when treatment is randomly assigned but prices adjust in response to treatment. They show that regressions of demand on treatment or on treatment and price lead to biased estimates of the direct treatment effect. The sign of the bias in both cases depends on the sign of the correlation of price with treatment, and the two biases point in the same direction. In most cases including an endogenous price control reduces bias but does not remove it. The authors also show how to test whether bias from an endogenous price response arises and how to recover an unbiased direct treatment effect using a price instrument. They apply the approach to the estimation of feature advertising effects across several product categories using supermarket scanner data and show that the bias when not instrumenting price can be substantial.

Title: Making the Shelf Work for You: How Shelf Dimensions and Brand Types Influence the Shelf Placement Effect on Product Performance
Authors: Kristopher O. Keller, Arjen van Lin
Abstract: This study examines how vertical and horizontal shelf position and shelf space affect product sales, and how these effects vary across brand types and shelf dimensions. Using sales data and detailed planogram changes from a leading convenience-store retailer, the analysis distinguishes primary NBs (market-leading national brands), secondary NBs (other nationally distributed brands), and PLs (private labels), and compares tall versus short and wide versus narrow shelves. On tall shelves, primary and secondary NBs perform best between the middle and top, whereas vertical position has little effect for PLs. On short shelves, NBs perform better toward the top and bottom, while PLs tend to perform better near the top. On wide shelves, primary NBs perform best slightly left of center, while horizontal position has little effect for secondary NBs and PLs. On narrow shelves, primary NBs perform best near the center, PLs left of center, and secondary NBs show only modest differences across positions. More shelf space increases sales most strongly for PLs. A shelf-optimization analysis suggests substantial model-implied sales improvements from shelf rearrangement. Overall, the findings help retailers assess and justify requests for contested premium positions and shelf space by showing which brand types benefit most across shelf types.

Title: It’s a System: Shareholder Activism, Corporate Harm, and the Role of Regulators, NGOs, and Media
Authors: Mark R. DesJardine, Jinyuan Song, Yifan Wei
Affiliations: Tuck School of Business, Dartmouth College; The University of Tennessee, Knoxville; Simon Fraser University
Abstract: Research on shareholder activism has focused largely on the direct, dyadic relationship between activists and the firms they target, leaving open a broader question: When does activism actually change corporate behavior? We argue that the answer depends on the wider system of stakeholders surrounding the firm. Integrating stakeholder influence research with institutional theory, we theorize that shareholder demands more effectively motivate organizational change when other actors in the institutional environment reinforce the issues those demands raise. We test this in the context of environmental and social (E&S) shareholder proposals, asking whether they reduce firms’ stakeholder violations, which are regulator-sanctioned acts of misconduct that can harm non-shareholding stakeholders. Using data on E&S proposals at 428 U.S. firms from 2007 to 2021 , we find that proposals reduce stakeholder violations, and that this effect operates through managerial receptivity, defined as a firm’s behavioral pattern of engaging rather than resisting activist demands. Critically, this relationship is amplified when firms face greater scrutiny from two institutional pillars: regulative pressure from regulators and cultural-cognitive pressure from NGOs. By showing that non-shareholding stakeholders condition whether shareholder activism translates into reduced corporate harm, we move beyond the activist–firm dyad and offer a systems-level account of when, and through what mechanisms, shareholder activism succeeds in achieving its aims.

Title: Stakeholder Governance
Authors: Romain Boulongne, Ryan Federo, Ruth V. Aguilera, Pascual Berrone, Maurizio Zollo
Affiliations: IESE Business School; Universitat Autònoma de Barcelona; Northeastern University; Imperial College London
Abstract: Stakeholder governance has become central to debates about stakeholder capitalism, yet research remains fragmented about the configurations through which non-shareholder stakeholders gain authority and firms become credibly bound to stakeholder claims. We systematically review 171 articles in management and related fields to develop a framework organized around stakeholder authority (i.e., the participatory rights or recognized standing through which stakeholders can engage in governance), and firm commitment (i.e., the obligations organizations assume toward stakeholder claims in ways that are costly to reverse or ignore). We identify five recurring configurations: (a) disclosure and evaluation; (b) monitoring and verification; (c) contracting, formal rules, and adjudication; (d) governance rights; and (e) rule-making rights. These configurations generally move from informational authority and very weak firm commitment to constitutional authority and very strong firm commitment. We also identify two off-diagonal configurations—constrained authority and embedded commitment—that reveal how authority and commitment need not align. Our framework distinguishes stakeholder governance that remains largely symbolic from arrangements that create durable constraints on organizational discretion. We conclude by outlining a research agenda on institutional settings, organizational forms, transitions across governance configurations, and the implications of learning dynamics for stakeholder authority and commitment.

Title: Why Time Management Leads to Well-Being (and Performance)
Authors: Brad Aeon
Affiliations: Highline
Abstract: Time management is usually seen as a way to get more done. Yet research suggests that it is more strongly associated with well-being than with performance. Why time management improves well-being and why the benefits vary remain unclear. This article proposes three pathways linking time management to well-being and productivity. First, structure brings order to daily life by giving people a sense of control and predictability. Second, synchrony aligns activities with social and biological rhythms, reducing conflict and strengthening social ties. And third, concordance aligns activities with personal values and long-term goals, giving daily life meaning and strengthening the connection between present and future selves. These benefits depend on both individual practices and organizational conditions. Fragmented work, excessive demands on people’s time, and a focus on short-term results can obstruct the pathways. An imbalance among the pathways can also turn otherwise useful time management practices into sources of strain. By distinguishing these mechanisms and their limits, the framework helps explain why time management can improve well-being and productivity in some circumstances, have little effect in others, and sometimes make things worse.

Title: The Role of Synchrony in the Interpersonal Effectiveness of Operations Management
Authors: Vaneet Kaur, David A. Waldman, Salome Opoku, Shardul Phadnis
Abstract: To achieve a more central role in the top management of firms, the evolution of operations managers involves transitioning from largely isolated technical expertise into leadership excellence that is characterized by interpersonal effectiveness. Grounded in the rich behavioral Operations Management (OM) literature, this conceptual study draws on insights from neuroscience. We argue that success in this expanded role depends on balancing OM’s traditional focus on analytical rigor and the intuitive/emotional demands of senior leadership through a framework that integrates intrapersonal and interpersonal synchrony. Intrapersonal synchrony involves the neural capacity that enables a manager to achieve the cognitive and behavioral attributes that are associated with interpersonal synchrony. We explore how interventions like neurofeedback, along with organizational and cultural context factors, can help to develop or maximize these two forms of synchrony. Thus, an alignment of individual capacity, along with a supportive organizational and cultural context, is likely to help operations managers to move beyond a rigid analytic approach toward a broader strategic perspective based on interpersonal effectiveness, and thereby transcend technical gatekeeping and be more integrated into the strategic efforts of firms. In doing so, the study highlights the potential of neuroscience to provide insights into human aspects of managerial decision-making, which have been recognized in OM since the field’s inception over a century ago.

Title: Financing Selection Under Procurement Decentralization with a Quality-Uncertain Supplier
Authors: Zhiping Lin, Qi Zhang, Di Xu, Ruixia Shi, Gangshu (George) Cai
Abstract: This article investigates how financing choice interacts with outsourcing structure and endogenous quality when a capital-constrained supplier exerts unobservable effort to improve component quality. We consider two common outsourcing structures: consignment, in which the OEM contracts directly with the supplier while outsourcing assembly to a contract manufacturer (CM), and turnkey (i.e., procurement decentralization), in which the CM intermediates component procurement. In each structure, the supplier can be financed either by a bank (bank finance) or by its downstream buyer (buyer finance). Our analysis delivers several main insights. First, we identify a Supplier’s Collateral Paradox : a higher collateral value can reduce the supplier’s equilibrium profit even as it improves product quality and increases total supply chain profit, because downstream firms exploit the supplier’s improved reliability to extract surplus. Second, we establish a Financier’s Advantage : the downstream firm always prefers to provide buyer finance itself (the OEM under consignment and the CM under turnkey), whereas the supplier always prefers bank finance. Third, the performance implications of buyer finance depend critically on the outsourcing structure: under consignment, buyer finance strictly dominates bank finance by yielding higher equilibrium quality and greater supply chain efficiency, and the OEM fully extracts the CM’s surplus, while under turnkey, buyer finance improves quality and efficiency only when the supplier’s collateral is sufficiently high, whereas when collateral is low, bank finance can deliver higher quality and greater supply chain efficiency, reflecting the CM’s intermediary role and the resulting amplification of triple marginalization. Fourth, compared with the case without capital constraints, capital constraints alter the extent of firms’ relative procurement preferences between consignment and turnkey. We further demonstrate the robustness of these findings under five extensions—financing of effort cost, imperfect inspection, stochastic market demand, CM pricing power, and quality-dependent production cost. Overall, the results highlight that financing authority and outsourcing structure jointly shape incentives, surplus allocation, and quality outcomes in outsourced supply chains.

Title: A Framework Addressing Supply Chain Carbon Emissions: Measurement, Reporting, and Reduction
Authors: Jing Wu, Yilin Shi, Yi Liao
Abstract: This paper honors Professor Christopher S. Tang’s seminal contributions to sustainable operations management by examining the pivotal yet underappreciated role of supply chains in global carbon emissions. Despite the critical importance of supply chains in contributing to overall carbon footprints, current efforts to address these emissions are often overshadowed by more visible direct emissions (Scope 1) and energy-related emissions (Scope 2). To bridge this gap, we propose an integrated measurement-reporting-reduction framework for managing supply chain carbon emissions (upstream Scope 3). Drawing on the literature, we introduce methodologies for carbon measurement (e.g., EEIO models, LCA, machine learning, and blockchain), determinants and consequences of disclosure, and strategies for reduction. In addition, we present case studies of two industrial firms, Tongwei (a Chinese photovoltaic leader) and Siemens (a German multinational technology firm), to illustrate how firms with distinct institutional contexts implement the framework in practice, highlighting the strengths, challenges, and implications. We conclude with research questions on whether disclosure mandates and carbon border measures lead to real abatement or merely shift emissions across suppliers and borders.

Title: Crossing platforms, connecting modalities: A multisource and multimodal interactive neural network for enhanced revenue prediction in service operations
Authors: Jie Mu, Jian Xu, Hengyun Li, Liangfei Qiu, Xiaowei Mei
Abstract: Demand and revenue prediction is critical in the hotel industry, where fixed capacity and perishable inventory make profitability highly dependent on the effective alignment of pricing, staffing, and procurement decisions with expected market demand and financial outcomes. Accurate forecasts, therefore, serve as a foundation for service operations, enabling managers to balance cost efficiency with service quality. Online reviews have become a valuable source of information for revenue prediction, as they capture customer perceptions of service quality and influence booking intentions. Beyond numerical ratings, reviews often combine textual narratives and visual content, offering rich multimodal signals about customers’ service experiences. Together, these cues provide more comprehensive insights into consumer evaluations than either modality alone. Yet most existing approaches still rely primarily on numerical indicators or text, overlooking both the visual dimension of reviews and the complementary perspectives available across platforms. This narrow focus reduces predictive accuracy and weakens the operational relevance of current models. To address this gap, this paper uses consumer multimodal reviews as the primary data source and examines hotel revenue prediction through the lens of the consumer purchase decision process. We propose a theoretical framework based on this process to guide the design of our prediction model, thereby enhancing the accuracy of RevPAR predictions. The resulting model, termed the multisource and multimodal interactive neural network (MMINN), leverages cross-platform multimodal reviews to predict hotel RevPAR with greater precision. Our findings show that integrating textual and visual information and capturing their interactions improves prediction accuracy. Incorporating cross-platform reviews further enhances predictive power by using a cross-attention mechanism to fuse multisource features. Moreover, focusing on multigranular customer attention-related factors at both the review and platform levels allows the model to capture differences in the informational contributions of different reviews and platforms, which further strengthens revenue prediction. This research provides actionable insights for hotels by supporting revenue management, staffing, marketing, and investment strategies while enhancing competitiveness and customer satisfaction, thereby generating potential economic value for hotels. It also contributes to the service operations and revenue management literature by demonstrating the value of multisource multimodal data integration for advancing revenue prediction.

Title: Estimating censored demand in family planning supply chains: forecast accuracy, inventory implications, and public health outcomes
Authors: Harsha Chamara Hewage, Bahman Rostami-Tabar, Aris Syntetos, Federico Liberatore, Glenn R. Milano
Abstract: Lost sales due to stockouts and service interruptions create a major challenge for demand forecasting in family planning supply chains. When demand is censored, forecasts become biased, reinforcing cycles of understocking and unmet need. Existing models often ignore this distortion or treat all censoring mechanisms uniformly, limiting their decision relevance in operational settings. We propose the Truncated Conformal Kalman Filter (TCKF), a novel forecasting framework that integrates a Tobit Kalman Filter with conformal prediction. Unlike existing approaches, TCKF explicitly distinguishes between partial censoring (stockouts) and full censoring (interruptions or no-stock-received periods), enabling context-sensitive state updates. It also adapts to prolonged uncertainty through dynamic process-noise inflation and generates distribution-free prediction intervals, avoiding restrictive assumptions about error distributions. We evaluate performance using both synthetic and real-world data from the family planning program in Côte d’Ivoire, and we assess the impact on public health outcomes. Across both settings, TCKF consistently outperforms benchmark methods in forecast accuracy, considering both point and probabilistic forecasts, as well as in downstream inventory performance. Moreover, our results show how improvements in forecast accuracy can translate into better product availability and enhanced public health outcomes. This work bridges a critical gap between forecasting and inventory control and offers a scalable solution for supply chains facing censored demand.

Title: Assessing the Quality of Illegal Copies and its Impact on Revenues and Distribution
Authors: Anthony Koschmann, Yi Qian
Abstract: Conventional wisdom holds that illegal copies cannibalize legitimate sales, even though previous research has found mixed effects, with illegal copies acting as both a substitute and a complement. Yet relatively little is known about how variation in piracy quality affects market outcomes over a product’s lifecycle. Building on product uncertainty and production quality, we propose that higher quality copies benefit sales when product uncertainty is higher (during product launch) but hurt sales when product uncertainty is lower (during post-launch). We examine this question in the context of motion pictures by constructing an objective measure of piracy quality from technical signals embedded in pirated files, combining this data with box office performance, screen availability, and online piracy activity. An econometric framework jointly models movie screens, revenues, illegal downloads, and available illegal copies with piracy quality in both the launch and post-launch periods. We find that at launch, when less information is known about a movie, higher quality illegal copies demonstrate a positive sampling effect on revenues. In the post-launch period, however, higher quality illegal copies exhibit a negative substitution effect on revenues. The findings have operations implications, as producers can alleviate product uncertainty through some higher quality samples at product launch, while diluting the piracy market with lower quality post-launch.

Title: Sample Range as Subjective Variability and Implications for Experience-Based Decision Making
Authors: Tianwei Liu, Benjamin Scheibehenne
Affiliations: Department of Business and Economics, Karlsruhe Institute of Technology, 76131 Karlsruhe, Germany
Abstract: Variance and standard deviation are common metrics of statistical variability in the management and decision-making literature. In everyday contexts, however, information about sample range prevails. Range is arguably easier to comprehend and compute than variance, yet it often yields equivalent judgments about variability. Hence, we reason that decision makers often rely on range to judge variability. We test this hypothesis across four behavioral experiments (total n = 1,093). When comparing the variability of two number sets, decision makers predominantly based their judgments on sample range rather than sample variance when the two metrics disagree (experiment 1). Sample range tends to increase with sample size, whereas sample variance does not. Consistent with the range as variability hypothesis, decision makers perceived distributions as more variable after observing larger samples (experiment 2). This perceived variability, in turn, influenced risky decisions, as larger sample sizes led to decreased valuations of uncertain rewards for risk-averse decision makers (experiment 3). In further support of the hypothesis, when asked to mentally simulate new samples from a previously experienced distribution, participants generated more numbers within the observed range and fewer numbers outside of it than the true distribution implies (experiment 4). To model the data, we propose a “cognitive fence” idea as a potential psychological explanation for how experience shapes subjective variability. We conclude by discussing implications for research on overconfidence, distributional learning, risk perception, and communication. This paper was accepted by Jack Soll, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.05050 .
Accepting Editor: This paper was accepted by Jack Soll, behavioral economics and decision analysis.

Title: Adaptive Preference Elicitation in Preference Robust CPT-Based Shortfall
Authors: Sainan Zhang, Erick Delage, Huifu Xu
Affiliations: Shatin, Hong Kong; HEC Montréal, Management Sciences, Montreal, H3T 2A7, Canada; The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Department of Systems Engineering and Engineering Management, Hong Kong, Shatin, N.T., Shatin, N.T., Hong Kong
Abstract: This paper investigates the cumulative prospect theory (CPT)-based shortfall risk measure where the value (utility) function and the distortion (probability weighting) functions are ambiguous. We propose a worst-case CPT-based shortfall risk measure where the capital requirement is based on the worst-case value function and distortion functions from an ambiguity set constructed with user-specific information (e.g., preference between risky and certain lotteries) and well-known general information such as the S-shape of the value functions. When the underlying random loss is discretely distributed and parameters in pairs of lotteries remain undetermined, we demonstrate that the worst-case value function and the distortion functions have a piecewise linear structure. Based on this observation, we develop an adaptive preference elicitation approach extended from the well-known polyhedral method to simultaneously elicit the distortion functions and the positive and negative parts of the value function by solving a sequence of mixed-integer linear programs. Based on the elicited distortion, we design new queries to construct a feasible set of the holistic value functions. The proposed framework iteratively shrinks the ambiguity set through designed queries, yielding a computationally implementable robust CPT-based shortfall risk measure. To examine the in-sample and out-of-sample performance of the elicited CPT-based preference functions and the resulting preference robust shortfall risk measure, we conduct numerical experiments under an S-shaped value function and inverse S-shaped distortion functions and report the corresponding results.

Title: Column Elimination: An Iterative Approach to Solving Arc-Flow Formulations
Authors: Anthony Karahalios, Willem-Jan Van Hoeve
Affiliations: Naval Postgraduate School, Operations Research, Monterey, California, United States; Carnegie Mellon University, Tepper School of Business, Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, United States
Abstract: We present column elimination as a general framework for solving problems whose solutions can be represented as a collection of decision sequences. We show how such problems can be modeled as arc-flow formulations, using a dynamic program to represent the set of feasible decision sequences and their costs, and an integer linear program over the corresponding state-transition graph. Because the exact arc-flow formulation can be exponentially large, we introduce relaxed dynamic programs to compactly represent a superset of the feasible decision sequences. Column elimination solves the exact model by starting with a relaxed dynamic program, which induces a relaxed arc-flow formulation, and iteratively refining the relaxation by eliminating infeasible sequences in optimal solutions. Doing so, we generalize earlier approaches that were developed for decision-diagram based network models. We apply our general column elimination framework to three new applications: the vehicle routing problem with time windows, the pickup-and-delivery problem with time windows, and the graph multicoloring problem. The computational results show that column elimination is competitive with or outperforms state-of-the-art methods, closing several previously open benchmark instances across these domains, including one vehicle routing problem with time windows on 1,000 locations.

Title: Statistical Efficiency of Distributional Temporal Difference Learning and Freedman’s Inequality in Hilbert Spaces
Authors: Yang Peng, Liangyu Zhang, Zhihua Zhang
Affiliations: Tsinghua University, Yau Mathematical Sciences Center, Beijing, Beijing, China; Shanghai University of Finance and Economics, School of Statistics and Data Science, Shanghai, China; Peking University, School of Mathematical Sciences, Beijing, Beijing, China
Abstract: Distributional reinforcement learning (DRL) has achieved empirical success in various domains. One core task in DRL is distributional policy evaluation, which involves estimating the return distribution η π for a given policy π. Distributional temporal difference (TD) learning has been accordingly proposed, which extends the classic TD learning in RL. In this paper, we focus on the non-asymptotic statistical rates of distributional TD learning. To facilitate theoretical analysis, we propose non-parametric distributional TD learning (NTD). For a γ-discounted tabular Markov decision process, we show that for NTD with a fixed-distribution generative model (at time t ∈ ℕ, sample one state s t ~ μ with μ min := min s∈S μ(s) > 0 and observe a single transition from s t ), we need Õ(ε −2 μ min −1 (1−γ) −3 ) interactions with the environment to achieve an ε-optimal estimator with high probability when the estimation error is measured by the supremum 1-Wasserstein distance. This sample complexity bound is minimax optimal up to logarithmic factors. In addition, we revisit categorical distributional TD learning (CTD), showing that the same non-asymptotic convergence bounds hold for CTD. We also extend our analysis to the more general setting where the data-generating process is Markovian. In the Markovian setting, we propose variance-reduced variants of NTD and CTD and show that both can achieve a sample complexity bound matching the state-of-the-art statistical results for classic policy evaluation. We validate our theoretical results through numerical experiments on an inventory management problem, illustrating the practical utility of distributional policy evaluation in risk-sensitive decision-making. To achieve the sharp statistical rates, we establish a novel Freedman’s inequality in Hilbert spaces. This new Freedman’s inequality would be of independent interest for statistical analysis of various infinite-dimensional online learning problems.

Title: Dual Active Learning for Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback
Authors: Pangpang Liu, Chengchun Shi, Will Wei Sun
