Affiliations: Purdue University, West Lafayette, Indiana, United States; LSE, London, London, United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland; Purdue University, management, West Lafayette, Indiana, United States
Abstract: Aligning large language models (LLMs) with human preferences is critical to recent advances in generative artificial intelligence. Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) is widely applied to achieve this objective. A key step in RLHF is to learn the reward function from human feedback. However, human feedback is costly and time-consuming, making it essential to collect high-quality conversation data for human teachers to label. Additionally, different human teachers have different levels of expertise. It is thus critical to query the most appropriate teacher for their opinions. In this paper, we use offline reinforcement learning (RL) to formulate the alignment problem. Motivated by the idea of $D$-optimal design, we first propose a dual active reward learning algorithm for the simultaneous selection of conversations and teachers. Next, we apply pessimistic RL to solve the alignment problem, based on the learned reward estimator. Theoretically, we show that the reward estimator obtained through our proposed adaptive selection strategy achieves minimal generalized variance asymptotically, and prove that the sub-optimality of our pessimistic policy scales as $O(1/\sqrt{T})$ with a given sample budget $T$. Through simulations and experiments on LLMs, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our algorithm and its superiority over state-of-the-art.

Title: A Continuous-Knapsack-Based Framework for Constrained Static Assortment Optimization
Authors: Hongbin Zhang, Yanzhi Li, Woonghee Tim Huh
Affiliations: University of British Columbia, Vancouver, Canada; City University of Hong Kong, Kowloon, Hong Kong; The University of British Columbia, Sauder School of Business, Vancouver, Canada
Abstract: We consider the constrained static assortment optimization problem under the Multinomial Logit (MNL) model and its extensions, including the Customized Assortment Problem (CAP) and the joint assortment and pricing problem. Building on the knapsack formulation of MNL assortment planning, we introduce a novel concept, termed the modified reduced profit, defined as the maximum attainable value of the knapsack model for a given item set under a fixed no-purchase probability. We show that this modified reduced profit is a continuous-knapsack value function and is monotone and submodular. This structural property leads to a general approximation framework. In particular, if maximizing the continuous-knapsack value function over a downward-closed family L admits an α-approximation algorithm, then our MNL-THR algorithm achieves an α(1 − ϵ)-approximation through a geometric search over the no-purchase probability. As important special cases, cardinality, budget, and matroid constraints yield a (1 − 1/e)(1 − ϵ) guarantee. We further extend the framework to the CAP and the joint pricing and assortment problem, showing that the underlying submodularity structure is preserved. Finally, we develop faster approximation algorithms that avoid the geometric search and achieve a (1 − 1/e)/2 guarantee under the three commonly studied constraint families, providing a trade-off between computational efficiency and solution quality

Title: Institutional reform and persistent innovation: Novel evidence from a quasi-natural experiment in pilot free trade zones
Authors: Hao Wang, Ying Jiang

Title: Challenges, opportunities, and policies for dual use innovation
Authors: Matthijs J. Janssen, Bart Hollants, Maryse M.H. Chappin, Ellen H.M. Moors

Title: Dismantling organized crime's “protective umbrella”: How the downfall of corrupt officials fuels urban entrepreneurship in China
Authors: Yong Ma, Yanfang Wan, Xifen Lin

Title: Social Capital and the Boundary of the Firm: Evidence from Relationship-Specific Investments
Authors: Jarrad Harford, Xing Li, Jiaren Pang, Haibin Wu, Liu Zheng
Affiliations: University of Washington Foster School of Business; University of Science and Technology of China Faculty of Business for Science and Technology, School of Management; Tsinghua University School of Economics and Management; City University of Hong Kong College of Business
Abstract: Abstract We investigate the role of social capital in mitigating hold-up problems along the supply chain. We find that supplier firms are more willing to make relationship-specific investments (proxied by their citations to customers’ patents) when transacting with customers headquartered in high social capital areas. This effect is more pronounced when the potential for expropriation by the customer is greatest: when the supplier has a weak bargaining position, faces high asset specificity, or the customer is in poor financial condition. High social capital firms are less vertically integrated and are more likely to form (longer-lasting) trading relationships with each other.
Journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis

Title: Attentive Options Traders: Textual Changes to 10-Ks and Option Volatility Smirk
Authors: Hua Cheng, Steve Liu, Zheng Qiao, Z. Jay Wang
Affiliations: Sun Yat-sen University International School of Business and Finance and University of Texas at Austin; University of Rhode Island College of Business; Xi’an Jiaotong University School of Management; University of Oregon Lundquist College of Business
Abstract: Abstract In contrast to the “lazy prices” phenomenon in the stock market, more 10-K textual changes lead to larger increases in volatility smirks—consistent with options traders buying more out-of-the-money put options based on negative information disclosed in textual changes. Moreover, the lazy-prices effect is mainly driven by stocks with tradable options, suggesting that limits to arbitrage lead to a delayed response of stock prices. Finally, the return predictability of textual changes is stronger for stocks with larger option volatility smirk changes. Sophisticated options traders, therefore, demonstrate superior skills at extracting relevant information from public filings.
Journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis

Title: Blockchain Currency Markets
Authors: Angelo Ranaldo, Ganesh Viswanath-Natraj, Junxuan Wang
Affiliations: University of Basel and Swiss Finance Institute; Warwick Business School and Gillmore Centre for Financial Technology; Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)
Abstract: Abstract We conduct the first comprehensive study of blockchain currencies—stablecoins pegged to fiat currencies and traded on decentralized exchanges (DEXs). Using transaction-level data linked to wallet characteristics, we show that prices in these markets are generally efficient, though constrained by blockchain frictions such as gas fees and Ether volatility. DEX rates closely track traditional currency markets through arbitrage and informed trading. Traders with substantial market share and access to primary markets exert greater price impact, reflecting informational advantages. While blockchain markets may improve access for customers excluded from traditional venues, their scalability depends on addressing frictions inherent to decentralized trading.
Journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis

Title: Mutual Fund Strategy: Swing for the Fences or Bat for Average
Authors: John Chalmers, Arash Dayani
Affiliations: University of Oregon Charles H. Lundquist College of Business; Clemson University Wilbur O. and Ann Powers College of Business
Abstract: Abstract We document two distinct mutual fund strategies: “Swinging for the Fences” (SF), in which managers hold stocks with extreme style-adjusted returns on either tail of the return distribution, and “Batting for Average” (BA), in which managers seek stocks with consistently moderate performance. We provide evidence that these strategies are persistent and deliberate. Existing measures of active management and known asset-pricing factors do not explain the strategies. SF attracts more flow, particularly when funds mention specific stock holdings in shareholder reports. SF funds charge higher fees and hold riskier portfolios; yet, they fail to deliver higher risk-adjusted returns. In falsification tests, SF strategies are not present in passive funds, supporting our conclusion that SF and BA are intentional strategies.
Journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis

Title: The Sensitivity of Cash Saving to the Cost of Capital
Authors: Viral V. Acharya, Soku Byoun, Zhaoxia Xu
Affiliations: New York University Stern School of Business; Baylor University Hankamer School of Business; University of New South Wales School of Banking and Finance
Abstract: Abstract We show that with a time-varying cost of capital (COC), firms save from external capital when the firm-specific COC is low to hedge against future underinvestment risks associated with a higher COC. This hedging motive drives the sensitivity of cash saving to the COC for both financially constrained and currently unconstrained firms. This sensitivity is especially pronounced among firms that face a higher COC when in need of external finance. Firms with high hedging motives issue excess capital to save cash when the COC is lower and use cash savings for future investment.
Journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis

Title: Politically Polarized Depositors
Authors: Jinoug Jeung
Affiliations: The Chinese University of Hong Kong CUHK Business School
Abstract: Abstract Exploiting an exogenous increase in public awareness of banks’ lending to the gun industry, this article documents significant deposit outflows from gun lenders. These outflows are stronger in Democratic-leaning markets and for Republican-leaning lenders. In contrast, anti-gun lenders experience limited and insignificant outflows, consistent with policy alignment with depositor values. Outflows tighten funding constraints, prompting gun lenders to reduce deposit spreads and branches in Democratic-leaning markets. While large gun lenders remain resilient, small gun lenders significantly reduce their CRA loan volumes. The findings highlight political value misalignment as a driver of depositor behavior and its real effects on bank operations.
Journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis

Title: Intra-Household Risk Sharing in Collective Portfolio Choice Models
Authors: Joachim Inkmann, Alexander Michaelides, Yuxin Zhang
Affiliations: University of Melbourne Department of Finance; Imperial College London Department of Finance; University of Nottingham Ningbo China Department of Finance, Accounting and Economics
Abstract: Abstract Using a calibrated, collective life-cycle portfolio choice model for a dual-income couple, we show that an increase in the ability to share risk within the household due to a mean-preserving spread in the partners’ coefficients of relative risk aversion leads to a substantial increase in financial risk-taking. Importantly, we show that risk sharing has a larger economic impact on portfolio choice than risk diversification. While unitary models usually do not fully replicate the optimal portfolio choice of collective models, we propose approximations that work reasonably well for moderate background risk. We provide strong empirical support for our key findings.
Journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis

Title: Operational Proximity and Cross-Border Shareholder Monitoring
Authors: Fariborz Moshirian, Peter Pham, Jenny Jihyun Tak
Affiliations: University of New South Wales – Kensington Campus School of Banking and Finance; The University of Sydney Business School; The University of Manchester Alliance Manchester Business School
Abstract: Abstract Using U.S. mutual funds’ international voting records, we investigate whether proximity to firm operations promotes active monitoring by foreign investors. To identify monitoring effects, we exploit variations in proximity arising from existing portfolio firms’ actions. We find that after a non-U.S. firm expands operations into the United States, U.S. funds cast more dissenting votes at the firm’s shareholder meetings, especially in response to poor performance and close-call proposals. The increase in dissent voting is consistent with funds becoming more engaged shareholders as they gain better information. Our findings suggest that cross-border economic activities facilitate the global dissemination of best-practice shareholder activism.
Journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis

Title: Trust in Cultural Institutions and Interfirm Cooperation: Evidence from Religious Scandals
Authors: Quentin Dupont, Kayla M. Freeman
Affiliations: Georgetown University McDonough School of Business; Colorado State University College of Business and University of Georgia Terry College of Business
Abstract: Abstract We study how trust in cultural institutions affects cooperation between firms, employing local religious scandals for identification. We focus on trade credit as a trust-intensive aspect of supply chain relationships. In a triple-difference estimation, we find that firms located in scandal areas where the affected religion is prominent reduce trade credit to customers (relative to sales) by 5 percentage points. Consistent with the scandal damaging local norms of cooperation, results are stronger in relationships with limited history, greater geographic barriers, or transaction complexity. Our findings offer novel causal evidence of the influence of local culture on interfirm relationships.
Journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis

Title: When Is the Price of Analysts’ Disagreement Risk Positive?
Authors: Alexander David, Amel Farhat
Affiliations: University of Calgary Haskayne School of Business; University of Sherbrooke
Abstract: Abstract We provide robust evidence that the price of analysts’ disagreement risk in the cross section of stock returns changes sign; it is positive (negative) in periods of high (low) disagreement. We construct a general equilibrium model in which analysts have heterogeneous beliefs about aggregate earnings growth. Each asset’s risk premium depends on i) the market portfolio, ii) the macroeconomic factor, and iii) a “squared-beta” factor. i) decreases and iii) increases with disagreement as investors choose lower cash flow beta assets during periods of high disagreement. We find support for such a flight-to-safety in the data.
Journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis

Title: Get the Money Somehow: The Effect of Missing Performance Goals on Insider Trading
Authors: Meng Gao
Affiliations: University of Connecticut School of Business
Abstract: Abstract This article uses a regression discontinuity design to identify the effect of compensation shocks on insider trading. I find that CEOs who narrowly miss relative performance goals and hence suffer a loss in compensation subsequently earn higher abnormal profits from their insider trades than otherwise similar CEOs who narrowly beat such goals. CEOs who narrowly miss relative performance goals also become less likely to provide earnings and sales guidance. These results suggest that managers can use insider trading to make up for compensation losses due to missing relative performance goals, which could reduce the incentive effect of performance-based pay.
Journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis

Title: Appointing Charity Directors in Response to ESG Incidents
Authors: Marina Gertsberg, Hae Won (Henny) Jung, Yuyang Zhang
Affiliations: University of Melbourne Department of Finance; University of Sydney School of Finance
Abstract: Abstract This article examines how companies respond to negative ESG incidents by appointing directors with charitable organization experience. Firms are more likely to make these appointments following high-profile ESG incidents, especially those involving social issues. The market reacts positively, particularly when directors’ biographies emphasize their charity experience. Using the local supply of charity directors as an instrumental variable, we show that incidents, particularly workforce-related incidents, decline after these appointments, with effects driven by nonoverboarded directors. Overall, our study documents a value-enhancing human capital channel through which firms address ESG concerns.
Journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis

Title: Do Banks Overreact to Disaster Risk?
Authors: Qianqian Huang, Feng Jiang, Yuhai Xuan, Tao Yuan
Affiliations: City University of Hong Kong; University at Buffalo; University of California Irvine The Paul Merage School of Business; City University of Macau School of Finance
Abstract: Abstract We examine how banks respond to natural disasters when borrowers are in proximity to affected areas. We find robust evidence that banks impose significantly higher loan spreads on firms in these areas following a disaster compared to other borrowers. This effect diminishes over time and is stronger for loans with concentrated syndicates, disasters with greater media coverage, and cases in which loan officers are geographically closer to disaster sites. The increased financing costs result in capital constraints for affected firms. Overall, our findings highlight a salience bias in banks’ evaluation of borrowers’ disaster risk, with adverse effects on borrowing firms.
Journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis

Title: Measuring the Cost of Regulation: A Text-Based Approach
Authors: Charles W. Calomiris, Harry Mamaysky, Ruoke Yang
Affiliations: Andersen Institute for Finance and Economics and National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER); Columbia University Business School; U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission
Abstract: Abstract We derive a measure of firm-level regulatory exposure from corporate earnings calls text and study its effects on growth, leverage, profitability, and equity returns. Higher regulatory exposure results in slower sales and asset growth, lower leverage, reduced profitability, and higher post-call equity returns. Most of these effects are mitigated for larger firms. We validate our measure by showing its explanatory power for cross-sectional stock returns during the 2016 Presidential election.
Journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis

Title: Bond Convenience Yields in the Eurozone Currency Union
Authors: Zhengyang Jiang, Hanno Lustig, Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh, Mindy Z Xiaolan
Affiliations: Kellogg School of Management, Northwestern University, NBER; Graduate School of Business, Stanford University, NBER, SIEPR; Columbia Business School, Columbia University, NBER, CEPR; McCombs School of Business, University of Texas at Austin
Abstract: Abstract In a monetary union, the risk-free rate cannot adjust to country-level fiscal positions, leaving only default spreads and convenience yields to respond. Empirically, we find that convenience yields explain a large share of the variation in eurozone (EZ) sovereign bond yields. EZ sovereign bonds earn larger convenience yields when their governments run larger surpluses. Since convenience yields generate substantial seigniorage revenue from debt issuance, our estimates imply economically large fiscal costs from low convenience yields for peripheral countries in the EZ.

Title: The Effect of Primary Dealer Constraints on Intermediation in the Treasury Market
Authors: Falk Bräuning, Hillary Stein
Affiliations: Federal Reserve Bank of Boston
Abstract: Abstract Using confidential microdata, we show that shocks to primary dealers’ constraints have significant effects on the U.S. Treasury securities market. We consider two types of constraints: the supplementary leverage ratio and trading desk value-at-risk constraints. In response to tighter constraints, dealers reduce their Treasury positions, triggering a reduction in aggregate turnover and an increase in dealer intermediation margin. Impaired intermediation also amplifies the yield response to net demand shifts and weakens Treasury auction outcomes. Our estimates suggest that the (shadow) cost of dealer constraints is as high as 9% of dealers’ profit margins.

Title: Mutual Fund Flows and the Supply of Capital in Municipal Financing
Authors: Manuel Adelino, Sophia Chiyoung Cheong, Jaewon Choi, Ji Yeol Jimmy Oh
Affiliations: Duke University, CEPR and NBER; Hang Seng University of Hong Kong , Hong Kong; Seoul National University; Korea University Business School
Abstract: Abstract This paper investigates how capital supply from mutual funds affects municipal bond financing, making three key contributions. First, we introduce an identification strategy using the rule-based update of Morningstar ratings for 5-year-old funds, isolating supply-side effects from fund and issuer fundamentals. The results indicate that exogenous fund flows increase bond issuance probability and decrease yields. Second, these fund flows lead to more issuances when funds and issuers are connected through underwriters, highlighting relationship lending in municipal bond financing. Third, municipal issuers leverage favorable financing conditions for new issuance of revenue bonds, which translates into higher local house prices.

Title: Convenience Yield, Inflation Expectations, and Public Debt Growth
Authors: Julie Zhiyu Fu, Jian Li, Yinxi Xie
Affiliations: Olin Business School at Washington University in St. Louis; Columbia Business School; Indiana University Bloomington
Abstract: Abstract We present new facts on how convenience yields fluctuate with macroeconomic variables and fiscal policy: the convenience yield of long-term Treasuries is negatively correlated with inflation expectations, and inflation expectations predict future debt-to-GDP growth. To rationalize these findings, we incorporate the convenience yield into a macro-finance model with endogenous fiscal policy. The government finances deficit shocks partially through higher inflation and partially through more future borrowing, which reduces the convenience yield today. The feedback loop between the convenience yield and future debt supply amplifies the effect of fiscal shocks. We further verify this channel using empirically constructed exogenous deficit shocks.

Title: Treasury Reuse and the Demand for Safe Assets
Authors: Sebastian Infante, Zack Saravay
Affiliations: Federal Reserve Board
Abstract: Abstract We theoretically and empirically show how the reuse of Treasury securities as collateral alleviates safe asset scarcity. Our model characterizes how reuse allows intermediaries to efficiently reallocate the safety benefits of long-term Treasury securities to a broader investor base. By reusing Treasury securities, intermediaries can access more collateral to create safe assets without interest rate risk. When the demand for safe assets is high, intermediaries increase reuse, distributing safe asset benefits to investors that value safety the most. Using supervisory data to calculate a dealer-level measure of reuse called the “collateral multiplier,” we empirically confirm the model’s main predictions.

Title: Do Municipal Bond Investors Pay a Convenience Premium to Avoid Taxes?
Authors: Matthias Fleckenstein, Francis A Longstaff
Affiliations: Lerner College of Business and Economics, University of Delaware; UCLA Anderson School of Management, University of California at Los Angeles and the National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER)
Abstract: Abstract We study the valuation of state-issued tax-exempt municipal bonds and find that there are significant convenience premia in their prices. These premia parallel those identified in Treasury markets. We find evidence that these premia are tax related. Specifically, the premia are related to measures of tax and fiscal uncertainty, forecast flows into state municipal bond funds, and are directly linked to outmigration from high-tax to low-tax states and to other measures of tax aversion such as IRA and retirement plan contributions. These results suggest that investors are willing to pay a substantial premium to avoid taxes.

Title: Corrigendum to “Where do ideas go? A spatial analysis of the patenting impact of publicly funded basic science” [Res. Policy (2026)105528]
Authors: Laura Toschi, Federico Munari, Maurizio Sobrero, Hérica Morais Righi, Sebastiano Leonelli

Title: Trended Momentum
Authors: Charlie Xiaowu Cai, Peng Li, Kevin Keasey
Affiliations: University of Liverpool Management School; University of Bath School of Management; University of Leeds Leeds University Business School
Abstract: Abstract Drawing on cognitive psychology and behavioral theories of pattern recognition and heuristic processing, we offer a new perspective on momentum by highlighting how clear price trends shape investor expectations. Trend clarity (TC) materially strengthens momentum returns: the highest trend-clarity quintile earns annualized returns of 12.68%, compared with 6.90% for a conventional momentum strategy. We also show that TC affects momentum trading intensity within Hong and Stein’s (1999) multiperiod return-chasing model. Additional tests indicate that trading on clear trends is a central feature of momentum, distinct from existing explanations and observable across asset classes and global markets.
Journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis

Title: Prospect Theory and Currency Returns: Empirical Evidence
Authors: Qi Xu, Roman Kozhan, Mark P. Taylor
Affiliations: Zhejiang University: School of Economics and Academy of Financial Research; University of Warwick: Warwick Business School; Washington University in Saint Louis
Abstract: Abstract We empirically investigate the role of prospect theory in the foreign exchange market. A currency-level measure of prospect-theory value, constructed from the historical distribution of exchange rate returns, negatively forecasts future currency excess returns. A long–short strategy based on this measure yields approximately 5% per annum. Predictability is stronger when arbitrage is limited. Bank order flow is positively associated with prospect-theory value, with inter-dealer and proprietary trading primarily driving this relation. Funds trade against prospect-theory value, acting as arbitrageurs. Overall, our findings suggest that investors evaluate currencies based on historical return distributions, consistent with prospect theory.
Journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis

Title: Temporal tradeoffs and contracting dynamics in buyer–supplier agreements
Authors: Jeffrey J. Reuer, Toby X. Li
Affiliations: Mitch Daniels School of Business Purdue University West Lafayette Indiana USA; Mays Business School Texas A&M University College Station Texas USA
Abstract: Abstract Research Summary We examine temporal tradeoffs and contracting dynamics in buyer–supplier agreements by investigating how suppliers' contractual terms change when contracting with initial clients versus new clients in the future. We use information economics and research on certifications in interorganizational relationships to delve into the mechanisms leading to potential improvements in suppliers' contractual terms. We situate the empirical analysis in the context of onshore oil and gas drilling projects to examine the liabilities for project‐related risks that startup drillers assume when contracting with client producers. Evidence indicates that when drillers initially work for prominent client producers, the drillers assume more risks in these first contracts, but fewer risks in subsequent agreements with other client producers. We argue and show that the degree to which a specific driller obtains better terms in future deals owing to its initial client's prominence will be attenuated when subsequent clients have more information on the value of the driller's resources and capabilities. Specifically, the resulting reduction in risks borne by the driller will be smaller when the driller was founded by a serial entrepreneur and when the subsequent client is vertically integrated into drilling operations. Managerial Summary This study examines the contracting dynamics that startups experience as suppliers in buyer–supplier agreements. Startups often bear more risk in initial deals to build credibility, especially when contracting with prominent clients, and such affiliations can then lead to improved terms for startups in subsequent contracts with other clients. However, this follow‐on benefit of working with a prominent client depends upon whether subsequent clients have more information on the startup's resources and capabilities. In particular, the risk‐reduction effect of working with an initial client that is prominent will be smaller for those startups founded by serial entrepreneurs. It will also be smaller when the subsequent client is vertically integrated into the value chain activities carried out by the startup. Using data from startups in the oil and gas drilling industry, we illustrate the dynamics and tradeoffs that startup drillers encounter when contracting with established client producers.

Title: Supplemental Material for Are Situational Judgment Tests Really Less Fakable? A Meta-Analysis
Authors: Liyan Xi, Filip Lievens, Qingxiong (Derek) Weng

Title: Rising Wages and the Decline of Low-Wage Work
Authors: Clem Aeppli, Soohyun Roh, Nathan Wilmers
Affiliations: MIT
Abstract: From 2014 to 2024, the share of U.S. hourly workers paid below $15 in real terms fell by two-thirds, from 38 percent to 13 percent. Why? We first distinguish the entry and exit of employers—wherein high-paying employers have supplanted low-paying ones—from organizational changes among incumbent employers. Organizational changes can be imposed on employers by external constraints, like labor market tightness, or emerge from the pursuit of new opportunities. Using panel data drawn from administrative records and job reviews, we bring this framework to bear on the recent wage gains at the bottom of the labor market. Contrary to predictions of creative destruction, we can trace only a small amount of these wage gains to the disappearance of low-wage organizations. Instead, the main driver of rising pay was low- and middle-paying incumbent employers of low-wage occupations increasing pay. These gains in low-wage occupations were associated with tightening labor markets and increased minimum wages. But over and above these external constraints, employers also pursued new opportunities for reorganizing work in low-skill jobs. Notwithstanding organizational inertia, major gains for workers’ pay can come from changes in existing workplaces.

Title: Examining Negative Asymmetry in Employee Social Networks: A Meta-Analysis
Authors: Kameron M. Carter, Hamed Ghahremani, Eean R. Crawford, Prasad Balkundi, Robert J. Barrett
Affiliations: Old Dominion University; Louisiana State University New Orleans; University of Iowa; University at Buffalo (SUNY); Midway University
Abstract: Two decades have passed since Labianca and Brass introduced social ledger theory with its focal assumption of negative asymmetry—that the social liabilities created by negative workplace ties are more strongly related to employee outcomes than the social assets created by positive workplace ties. Yet widespread conclusions that negative workplace ties are more consequential have exceeded a surprisingly limited base of empirical tests. This article uses meta-analysis to examine this largely untested assumption by offering 22 original meta-analytic estimates drawn from 248 effect sizes across 71 samples representing 13,369 employees. At the bivariate level, both positive and negative ties have significant relationships with employee outcomes. However, evidence consistent with negative asymmetry emerged only for out-degree ties predicting task performance. In contrast, evidence more consistent with positive asymmetry emerged for in-degree ties predicting task performance and for both in-degree and out-degree ties predicting organizational attachment, although the relationships between in-degree ties and attachment are relatively small. Considerable variation exists around the effect sizes constituting these patterns, suggesting that future research is needed to consider moderating factors that may shift the relative importance of negative versus positive ties. We discuss the implications for refining social ledger theory and for helping practitioners managing social assets and liabilities in organizations.

Title: Production Rate Control in Condition-Based Maintenance Planning
Authors: Luuk Pentinga, Onur A. Kilic, Jasper Veldman, Ruud Teunter
Affiliations: University of Groningen Faculty of Economics and Business, Operations, Groningen, Groningen, 9747 AE, Netherlands; University of Groningen Faculty of Economics and Business, Operations, Groningen, Groningen, Netherlands; Universityof Groningen, Economics and Business Operations, Groningen, Netherlands; Universityof Groningen, Zernike Complex, Groningen, 9700 AV, Netherlands
Abstract: Problem description: Production assets deteriorate over time as they operate and require maintenance to prevent failures and costly downtime. In many systems, the rate of deterioration depends on the production rate. Hence, production and maintenance decisions should be coordinated in response to the system's deterioration state. In this study, we analyze integrated condition-based maintenance and production control policies for systems where the production rate influences both revenue generation and the deterioration process. Methodology/results: We study the integrated condition-based maintenance and production control problem under general assumptions regarding the deterioration process, maintenance costs, system revenue, and their dependence on the deterioration level and the production rate. Exploiting the renewal–reward structure of the system, we develop an approach to compute profit-maximizing policies through solving a sequence of simpler parametric optimization problems. This approach also enables us to characterize the structure of optimal policies. We show that control-limit policies remain optimal even when the production rate is controllable, and may involve multiple thresholds when maintenance costs are piecewise constant in the deterioration state. We further derive bounds on optimal production rates and identify conditions under which the optimal production rate is monotone in the deterioration state. Through numerical experiments, we illustrate that integrated production and maintenance control policies can substantially outperform policies that rely on fixed production rates, particularly in systems where maintenance costs are high, revenue generation and deterioration dynamics strongly depend on the deterioration state, and the deterioration process is highly uncertain. Managerial implications: For systems with controllable production rates and condition monitoring infrastructure, coordinating production and maintenance decisions can improve profitability. Our approach establishes policies that help managers optimally determine when to maintain production assets and how to adjust production rates based on real-time condition information to maximize profit.

Title: Price Competition Under Platform-Mediated Search: A Consider-Then-Choose Framework
Authors: Chamsi Hssaine, Vijay Kamble, Sid Banerjee
Affiliations: University of Southern California Marshall School of Business, Data Sciences and Operations, Los Angeles, California, United States; University of Illinois at Chicago, Department of Information and Decision Sciences, Chicago, Illinois, United States; Cornell University, School of Operations Research and Information Engineering, Ithaca, New York, United States
Abstract: Problem definition: We study the problem of predicting price equilibria on e-commerce platforms where sellers compete across multiple attributes (e.g., price, average rating, delivery speed). In these settings, a platform’s design choices — such as its display ranking, filtering tools, and promotional badges — critically shape customer search and purchase behavior, which in turn determine sellers’ equilibrium pricing strategies. Our goal is to develop a tractable framework that allows a platform to anticipate the market impact of its design interventions. Methodology/results: We consider a behavioral model — Consider-then-Choose with Lexicographic Choice (CLC) — specifically tailored to platform-mediated search. We establish that any local Nash equilibrium admits a sequential-move characterization; this yields a tractable procedure for computation under an interpretable sufficient condition, which we term gradient dominance. We further prove that under gradient dominance, simple, decentralized gradient-based algorithms converge to an equilibrium, providing platforms with a method for simulating market outcomes. Finally, we use our framework to study how platform design affects market outcomes. Managerial implications: Our framework applies to any platform in which sellers compete on multiple attributes and customer choice is guided by the platform’s interface. In these environments, sellers’ pricing strategies must be understood not in isolation, but as a response to the platform’s design. Our work provides platform operators with a rigorous toolbox to efficiently evaluate how changes to interface design, information disclosure, and ranking policies can affect competitive outcomes.

Title: Artificial Intelligence Along the Supply Chain
Authors: Ling Cen, Yanru Han, Jiaping Qiu, Jing Wu
Affiliations: The Chinese University of Hong Kong Business School, Finance, Hong Kong, Hong Kong; Stevens Institute of Technology, Business, Hoboken, New Jersey, United States; McMaster University DeGroote School of Business, Business, Hamilton, Canada; Chinese University of Hong Kong, Decisions, Operations and Technology, New Territories, Hong Kong
Abstract: Problem definition: The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) is revolutionizing production and operational models, yet whether and how AI technologies diffuse across economically linked firms, especially partners along supply chains, remains underexplored. Methodology/results: This paper documents the diffusion of AI technologies along supply chains where principal customers’ AI adoption significantly predicts dependent suppliers’ subsequent adoption. We establish the causal effect of this diffusion through rigorous and comprehensive empirical strategies that address endogeneity concerns, including placebo tests, selection tests, and an identification strategy based on the random H-1B visa lottery outcome. The diffusion mechanism is primarily driven by learning rather than catering, with suppliers acquiring specific AI applications from customers. The learning effect is stronger in relationships with higher relationship-specific investments and more frequent interactions. Suppliers experiencing AI diffusion achieve substantial economic benefits through quality improvement and cost reduction. Managerial implications: For corporate managers, our findings demonstrate that supply chain relationships serve as critical conduits for building AI capabilities, particularly for resource-constrained smaller suppliers, highlighting the strategic value of cultivating partnerships with technologically advanced firms. For policymakers, our results reveal supply chains as natural mechanisms for democratizing AI access, suggesting that policies supporting supply chain integration and knowledge sharing could accelerate the broader diffusion of AI benefits across the economy and society.

Title: The Impact of Heat Hazard on Gig Economy Workers: Evidence from An On-demand Food Delivery Platform
Authors: Run Ge, Susan Feng Lu, Wenzheng Mao
Affiliations: Central University of Finance and Economics, School of Public Finance and Taxation, Beijing, Beijing, China; University of Toronto - St George Campus, Rotman School of Management, Toronto, Canada; Tongji University, Advanced Institute of Business, Shanghai, Shanghai, China
Abstract: Problem definition: This paper examines how extreme heat affects gig workers in on-demand delivery systems, focusing on food delivery couriers who face sustained outdoor exposure while operating in a time-sensitive platform environment. Methodology/results: We combine detailed operational data from a major food delivery platform in China with high-frequency weather data from July and August 2015. To account for non-random work participation, we estimate a two-step Heckman selection model at the courier-hour level. We define extreme heat using the “danger” and “extreme danger” categories of the heat index. Our estimates capture the overall effect of heat hazard in the platform environment, including consumer-demand and platform-operating responses. We find that, during extreme heat, couriers accept 9.9% more orders per hour and work 7.4% longer, but also experience a 23.8% higher share of delayed orders relative to the sample mean. Hourly income rises by 9.3%, or about 1 RMB per hour. Furthermore, by integrating our findings with medical research on the impact of heat on human health, we provide illustrative estimates of the health costs associated with heat exposure for couriers under different scenarios and insurance schemes. Managerial implications: Our findings show that extreme heat creates a tension between short-run service expansion and worker well-being in on-demand delivery systems. While platforms may benefit from stronger demand during hot periods, couriers bear greater workload, delay risk, and heat-related burden. These results highlight the need for heat-aware operating policies, worker-support measures, and stronger institutional protections as climate extremes become more frequent.

Title: On the (In)Efficiency of Sustainability-Linked Loans
Authors: Vernon Hsu, Guoming Lai, Guitian Liang, Yang Li
Affiliations: The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Department of Decision Sciences and Managerial Economics, Shatin, New Territories, Hong Kong; University of Texas at Austin, McCombs School of Business, United States; Jinan University, School of Management, Guangzhou, China; Western University Ivey Business School, Management Science, London, Canada
Abstract: Problem definition: Sustainability-linked loans (SLLs) are designed to reward firms with cheaper financing when sustainability performance targets (SPTs) are met. Yet empirical evidence shows no meaningful interest rate reductions, mixed sustainability outcomes, and participation concentrated among firms with low ESG risk. Regulators have criticized weak financial incentives and questioned whether targets are sufficiently ambitious. If SLLs neither lower borrowing costs nor reliably improve sustainability, how do they actually operate, what limits their effectiveness, and how should they be designed to achieve efficient sustainability while remaining viable in competitive credit markets? Methodology/results: We develop a production–financing model in which sustainability investments increase consumer willingness to pay but must be financed under credit-risk premiums. We show that standard SLLs function through coercive enforcement rather than discounted capital: banks set ambitious SPTs backed by penalty rates that redirect all borrower surplus toward sustainability without lowering borrowing costs. This mechanism explains the absence of rate reductions and the increase in loan sizes. However, it creates a viability concern. When firms can access ordinary loans that preserve positive profit, they choose not to participate in SLLs. The sustainability advantage of standard SLLs thus collapses under competition—rationalizing selective adoption and limited impact. Government subsidies can restore participation but introduce calibration risk because subsidies and SPTs are determined separately. We propose refined SLLs that integrate enforcement with financing-friction mitigation via target-contingent rebates. Refined SLLs implement the highest sustainability level supported by consumer willingness to pay while preserving competitive viability. They dominate standard SLLs when financing frictions are severe and outperform subsidized SLLs when subsidies are not precisely aligned with financing frictions. Managerial implications: Effective sustainability-linked finance depends not on nominal interest discounts but on coordinated contract design that jointly secures commitment, preserves participation, and aligns financing costs with economically efficient sustainability investment.

Title: OM Forum—Viewing Knowledge Creation as a Supply Chain – Scholarly Purpose in the Age of AI
Authors: Jing-Sheng Song
Affiliations: Duke University, Fuqua School of Business, Durham, North Carolina, United States
Abstract: Problem definition: Operations management scholars face questions about where to contribute and whether specialized work can sustain a meaningful career when its immediate audience is small. Advances in artificial intelligence (AI) add uncertainty about the value of analytical expertise. Methodology/results: Building on a 2017 MSOM Distinguished Fellow address, this Forum article views knowledge creation as a supply chain of complementary contributions. It shifts attention from the reach of an individual paper to the capabilities and connections that sustain collective progress. Four lessons follow: specialization can serve a collective purpose; usable connections are part of a contribution; feedback and inquiry renew capabilities; and faster individual tasks do not necessarily improve the whole process. Examples from inventory management and process flexibility illustrate cumulative contributions, while medical research, soccer, and photography connect the perspective to renewal, participation, and purpose. The AI discussion emphasizes research questions and parsimonious modeling, and uses coding and numerical experiments to explain shifting bottlenecks and complementarities. Managerial implications: Researchers can identify what their work enables and choose collaborators who supply missing capabilities. Doctoral training can combine methodological depth with practice in evaluating and connecting contributions. Editors and research leaders can assess work within its stated scope while supporting renewal and reuse. Researchers and managers in companies, public agencies, and nonprofits can pair operational goals with reusable learning and feedback. These recommendations do not require every project to span the full process or promise a large, immediate impact.
