Title: Production Function Estimation With Factor‐Augmenting Technology: An Application to Markups
Authors: Mert Demirer
Affiliations: Sloan School of Management, Massachusetts Institute of Technology
Abstract: I develop a new method for estimating production functions with labor‐augmenting technology and apply it to markup estimation. The method imposes limited parametric restrictions and generalizes prior approaches that rely on the CES production function. I first extend the canonical Olley–Pakes framework assumptions to multidimensional productivity and then develop an identification strategy based on a control variable approach and first‐order conditions. I use this method to estimate output elasticities and markups in manufacturing industries in the US and four developing countries. I find that neglecting labor‐augmenting productivity underestimates capital elasticity, overestimates variable input elasticity, and overestimates markups in all countries.

Title: Intermediate Input Substitutability
Authors: Alessandra Peter, Cian Ruane
Affiliations: Department of Economics, New York University; Irish Economic Analysis Division, Economics and Statistics Department, Central Bank of Ireland
Abstract: We estimate long‐run elasticities of substitution between intermediate inputs for Indian manufacturing plants. India's trade liberalization in the early 1990s provides an ideal natural policy experiment, with permanent and heterogeneous tariff reductions inducing changes in relative prices which we use for identification. We find a high degree of substitutability at the plant‐level between 8 broad categories of material inputs, significantly above the Cobb–Douglas benchmark of 1. In contrast, when considering shorter time horizons or more transitory shocks to relative prices, we find evidence of much lower elasticities. Using our long‐run elasticities in a quantitative model, we find that misallocation of intermediate inputs causes a reduction in aggregate output of 29%–3.5 times larger relative to a standard calibration with complementary inputs.

Title: Comment on ‘Selection and Comparative Advantage in Technology Adoption’ by Tavneet Suri
Authors: Emilia Tjernström, Dalia Ghanem, Aleksandr Michuda, Oscar Barriga-Cabanillas, Travis J. Lybbert, Jeffrey D. Michler
Affiliations: Department of Economics, Macquarie University; Monash Business School; Department of Agricultural and Resource Economics, University of California, Davis; Department of Economics, Swarthmore College; Poverty and Equity Global Practice, The World Bank; Department of Agricultural and Applied Economics, University of Arizona
Abstract: This paper illustrates and addresses weak identification in the correlated random coefficient (CRC) model that Suri (2011) uses to study agricultural technology adoption. Using the publicly available data set, which differs slightly from the version used in Suri (2011), we obtain different point estimates for the paper's main CRC model. To understand why these differences are as large as they are, we recast the CRC model as a more general random coefficient model in which the returns to hybrid adoption are restricted to be linear in comparative advantage. This reveals that the key structural parameter in the CRC model ( ϕ ), which governs the relationship between baseline productivity and the returns to adoption, is prone to a weak‐identification problem. We then propose a procedure to conduct weak‐identification robust inference on ϕ using test inversion. Our weak‐identification robust confidence intervals contain the original Suri (2011) point estimates, which suggests that the difference in results may be attributable to a combination of minor data differences and weak identification.

Title: Informal Redistribution Through Work
Authors: Elisa Macchi, Jeremia Stalder
Affiliations: Department of Economics, Brown University; Department of Economics, University of St. Gallen
Abstract: We investigate work as informal redistribution, leveraging field experiments and firm‐level survey data from Kampala, Uganda. Employers and workers consistently choose redistribution through work over cash transfers, revealing a willingness to pay for work. By randomizing work tasks—some designed to have zero marginal product—we find that production value does not explain these choices: employers pay for zero‐value work. These patterns are also inconsistent with other relational benefits, such as social image concerns or networking. Instead, motivations are normative. Experimental evidence reveals an internalized norm for redistribution through work rooted in incentive arguments on the demand side—as employers stop requiring work only when workers have verifiable emergencies—and in reciprocity and dignity from earning on the supply side. The norm shapes both the organization and measurement of production: failing to account for redistribution through work makes firms appear significantly larger and less productive than they are.

Title: Extreme Value Theory With Heterogeneous Agents
Authors: Sephorah Mangin
Affiliations: Research School of Economics, Australian National University
Abstract: Extreme value processes feature in any economic model in which agents receive a number of draws from some distribution of values and we examine the behavior of the maximum value in the limit as the number of draws becomes large. This paper asks: Do the average outcomes of such processes change when different agents receive a different number of draws? To answer this, we allow the number of draws an agent receives from the underlying distribution of values (e.g., productivities, ideas, or utility shocks) to be given by a search technology , which reflects heterogeneity in the expected number of draws across different types of agents. We derive a new class of extreme value distributions that generalizes the three standard distributions (Fréchet, Gumbel, Weibull) by incorporating heterogeneity across agents. We generalize a result from Gabaix, Laibson, Li, Li, Resnick, and de Vries (2016) regarding extreme value outcomes and consider applications to aggregate productivity, markups, and social networks.

Title: Two‐Sided Markets Shaped by Platform‐Guided Search
Authors: Kwok Hao Lee, Leon Musolff
Affiliations: Department of Strategy and Policy, National University of Singapore (NUS) Business School; Business Economics and Public Policy Department, The Wharton School, The University of Pennsylvania
Abstract: This paper investigates concerns that vertically integrated platforms like Amazon steer demand toward their own offers via algorithmic prominence, potentially harming consumers. On Amazon, for each product, the Buybox prominence algorithm selects one seller to feature, influencing which offers consumers consider. Using novel Amazon sales and Buybox (prominence) data, we estimate a structural model capturing the effects of such algorithmic prominence on consumer choices, seller pricing, and entry. We find that the platform can indeed steer demand as 95% of consumers consider only the Buybox offer. The Buybox is highly price‐elastic (−21), but skews toward Amazon's own offers, which are featured as frequently as observably similar offers priced 5% cheaper. Still, as consumers prefer these offers, this skew does not amount to self‐preferencing in the sense of harming consumers: consumer surplus is roughly maximized at the estimated Amazon Buybox advantage, which balances higher prices against showing consumers their preferred offers.

Title: An Exact t ‐Test
Authors: Guillaume A. Pouliot
Affiliations: Department of Economics, Rice University
Abstract: Multivariate linear regression and randomization‐based inference are two essential methods in statistics and econometrics. Nevertheless, the problem of producing a randomized test for the value of a single regression coefficient that is exactly valid when errors are exchangeable, and which is asymptotically valid for the best linear predictor, has remained elusive. In this paper, we produce a test that is exactly valid with exchangeable errors and which allows for general covariate designs; covariates may be continuous as well as discrete and may be correlated. The test is asymptotically valid when the errors are not exchangeable, in particular in the presence of conditional heteroskedasticity.

Title: From Predictive Algorithms to the Automatic Generation of Anomalies
Authors: Sendhil Mullainathan, Ashesh Rambachan
Affiliations: Department of Economics and Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, MIT; NBER; Department of Economics, MIT
Abstract: How can we extract theoretical insights from machine learning algorithms? We take a familiar lesson: researchers often turn intuition into theoretical insight by constructing “anomalies”—specific examples highlighting hypothesized flaws in a theory, such as the Allais paradox. We develop procedures that replace researchers' intuitions with predictive algorithms: given a predictive algorithm and a theory, our procedures automatically generate anomalies for that theory. We illustrate our procedures by generating anomalies for expected utility theory. Based on a neural network that accurately predicts lottery choices, we recover known anomalies for expected utility theory and discover novel ones. In incentivized experiments, subjects violate expected utility theory on these algorithmically generated anomalies at rates similar to the Allais paradox and common ratio effect.

Title: Why Are the Wealthiest so Wealthy? New Longitudinal Empirical Evidence and Implications for Theories of Wealth Inequality
Authors: Joachim Hubmer, Elin Halvorsen, Sergio Salgado, Serdar Ozkan
Affiliations: Department of Economics, University of Pennsylvania; Research Department, Statistics Norway; The Wharton School, University of Pennsylvania; Research Division, FRB of St. Louis; Department of Economics, Southern Methodist University
Abstract: We study the lifecycle dynamics of wealth inequality using 1993–2019 Norwegian administrative panel data on wealth and income. Employing a novel budget‐constraint approach, we decompose the excess wealth of the top 0.1% households relative to the median between ages 45 and 64 into higher saving rates (36%), inheritances (31%), returns (28%), and labor income (5%). One‐quarter of the wealthiest—the “New Money”—start with negative wealth on average but accumulate rapidly through high labor income and exceptionally high saving rates and returns. The “Old Money” inherit substantial wealth and grow it through above‐average though more modest saving and returns. We use these dynamic facts to evaluate five standard wealth inequality models. Although these models match cross‐sectional wealth concentration, they fail to reproduce the distinct dynamics of New and Old Money. A heterogeneous entrepreneurship model with decreasing returns to scale technology and nonhomothetic preferences is consistent with the observed dynamics.

Title: Coalitions in Repeated Games
Authors: S. Nageeb Ali, Ce Liu
Affiliations: Department of Economics, Pennsylvania State University; Department of Economics, Michigan State University
Abstract: This paper proposes a framework and solution concept for repeated coalitional behavior. We model history‐dependent schemes that use continuation promises and punishments to deter coalitions from blocking. We evaluate the effectiveness of these schemes with and without transferable utility, and apply the framework to study the implications of wage transparency in labor markets.

Title: Putting the ‘Finance’ Into ‘Public Finance’: A Theory of Capital Gains Taxation
Authors: Mark Aguiar, Benjamin Moll, Florian Scheuer
Affiliations: Department of Economics, Princeton University; Department of Economics, London School of Economics; Department of Economics, University of Zurich
Abstract: Standard optimal capital tax theory abstracts from modeling asset prices, making it unsuitable for thinking about capital gains and wealth taxation. We study optimal redistributive taxation in an environment with asset‐price movements, adopting the modern finance view that asset prices fluctuate not only because of changing cash flows, but also due to other factors (“discount rates”). We show that a combination of realization‐based capital gains and cash flow taxes implements the optimal allocation regardless of the source of asset‐price fluctuations. Moreover, the capital gains tax avoids distortions in portfolio choice (the so‐called lock‐in effect) by targeting total net trades rather than gains from selling individual assets. These results stand in contrast to the classic Haig–Simons comprehensive income tax concept as well as recent proposals for wealth or accrual‐based capital gains taxes.

Title: Optimal Formula Instruments
Authors: Kirill Borusyak, Peter Hull
Affiliations: Department of Agricultural and Resource Economics, University of California, Berkeley; Department of Economics, Brown University
Abstract: When estimating the effects of treatments defined by complex formulas, researchers often use simple functions of exogenous shocks as instruments. A leading example is “simulated instruments” for public policy eligibility, which capture variation in state‐level policy generosity. We show how more powerful instruments can be constructed by incorporating heterogeneous shock exposure while using a recentering procedure to avoid bias. We characterize the asymptotically efficient instruments in this class and propose an algorithm for constructing feasible approximations to them. Compared to a simulated instrument approach, our approach yields a 44% smaller standard error on the private insurance crowd‐out effect of Medicaid enrollment from the 2014 Affordable Care Act expansions.

Title: The Social Learning Barrier
Authors: Florian Brandl
Affiliations: Institute for Microeconomics, Department of Economics, University of Bonn
Abstract: Long‐lived agents interact repeatedly in a social network. In each period, each agent observes a private signal, chooses an action, and then observes the actions of her neighbors. We show that the learning rate of the slowest‐learning agent is capped by a constant that depends only on the distribution of the most informative private signal, but not on the number of agents, the network structure, correlations between the private signals, or the agents' strategies. For equilibrium learning with rational agents, the same result bounds the learning rate of every agent in any equilibrium under a broad class of conditions. The result is driven by an information‐theoretic tradeoff between optimal action choices and information revelation.

Title: Correction to ‘Dynamic Spatial General Equilibrium’ by Benny Kleinman, Ernest Liu, and Stephen Redding
Authors: Benny Kleinman, Ernest Liu, Stephen J. Redding, Tomohiro Uchiyama
Affiliations: Department of Economics, Stanford University; NBER; Department of Economics, Princeton University; CEPR; Faculty of International Liberal Arts, Soka University

Title: Correction to ‘General Equilibrium Effects of Cash Transfers: Experimental Evidence From Kenya’ by Dennis Egger, Johannes Haushofer, Edward Miguel, Paul Niehaus, and Michael Walker
Authors: Dennis Egger, Johannes Haushofer, Edward Miguel, Paul Niehaus, Michael Walker
Affiliations: Department of Economics, Oxford University; Department of Economics, Brooks School of Public Policy, Cornell University; NBER; Busara Center for Behavioral Economics; Department of Economics, University of California, Berkeley; CEGA, University of California, Berkeley; Department of Economics, University of California, San Diego

Title: Backmatter of Econometrica Vol. 94 Iss. 6
Frontmatter of Econometrica 94 Iss. 6
Measuring Socioemotional Wealth Using Content Analysis: A SEWi-Based Approach
Authors: Shane W. Reid, Chelsea Sherlock, Erik T. Markin, R. Gabrielle Swab
Affiliations: Department of Management, McCoy College of Business, Texas State University, San Marcos, TX, USA; Department of Management & Information Systems, College of Business, Mississippi State University, Mississippi State, MS, USA; Department of Management, Parker College of Business, Georgia Southern University, Statesboro, GA, USA
Abstract: Socioemotional wealth (SEW) is a foundational construct in family business research; however, its empirical measurement remains limited by reliance on proxy variables and survey data. This study addresses these challenges by developing a computer-aided text analysis method to measure SEW using the SEWi framework. Our approach enables direct, scalable, and multidimensional assessment of SEW through organizational narratives. We detail the development and validation of the measure, demonstrating its reliability and construct validity. This method expands the methodological toolkit for family business scholars and enhances SEW measurement precision, offering a pragmatic solution for broader, comparative, and longitudinal research.

Title: Measuring Entrepreneurial Activities in the U.S.: Introducing the Entrepreneurship in the Population Survey
Authors: Quentin Brummet, Diana Hechavarria, Katie Johnson, Anthony Washburn
Affiliations: Methodology and Quantitative Social Sciences Department, NORC at the University of Chicago, Chicago, IL, USA; Entrepreneurship Department, Babson College, Wellesley, MA, USA
Abstract: This paper introduces the Entrepreneurship in the Population (EPOP) survey, a nationally representative data source for understanding entrepreneurial activities across the United States since 2022. The EPOP survey is distinguished by its focus on a broad set of entrepreneurial activities and collects a wealth of information on the behaviors, challenges, and resources available to entrepreneurs. This data brief provides information on the design and measurement approach of the survey, discusses how to work with EPOP data, and outlines future plans for the survey, including a longitudinal data collection to support research on trajectories of current and prospective entrepreneurs.

Title: Angel Investors’ Reinvestment Decisions: Escalating Commitments and Conflict Management Beyond Venture Performance
Authors: Alexander Narh Tetteh, Haibo Zhou, Dan K. Hsu, Qingxiong (Derek) Weng
Affiliations: University of Science and Technology of China, Hefei, China; University of Nottingham Ningbo China, China; North Dakota State University, Fargo, ND, USA
Abstract: Angel investment research has grown rapidly; yet, when and under what conditions angel investors recommit remains understudied. Integrating escalation of commitment (EOC) theory with the conflict management styles (CMSs) perspective, we examine these conditions through archival data investigation, a conjoint experiment (2,368 decisions by 148 angel investors), and a field study (214 ventures by 112 angel investors). We show that prior commitment increases angel investors’ reinvestment likelihood, contingent on entrepreneurs’ CMSs. We advance EOC theory by identifying relational boundary conditions and conflict management research by theorizing its moderating role in reinvestment decision-making, revealing escalation as a socially embedded process shaped by investor–entrepreneur interactions.

Title: Resource Orchestration, Team Faultlines, and Entrepreneurial Resilience
Authors: Jian Guan, Shengyuan Lin, Justin Tan, Jiamin Dong
Affiliations: Central South University, Changsha, China; York University, Toronto, ON, Canada
Abstract: This study develops an integrated resource orchestration framework to examine how internal resource configurations shape entrepreneurial resilience in new ventures under crisis conditions. Specifically, we focus on bundles of social and technological resource slack and constraints and conceptualize entrepreneurial resilience as comprising two dimensions: stability (severity of loss) and flexibility (time to recovery). We argue that stability is primarily driven by a resource compensation logic, whereas flexibility is driven by a crisis-induced resource reconfiguration logic. Extending resource orchestration theory (ROT), we conceptualize entrepreneurial teams as the central actors of resource orchestration and introduce entrepreneurial team task-related faultlines (ETTF) as a key structural mechanism shaping how effectively resources are mobilized under disruption. Using a sample of 345 Chinese listed new ventures, we find that dual resource slack reduces severity of loss but slows recovery, whereas among constrained bundles, social resource slack combined with technological constraints enables both lower loss and faster recovery. Response surface analyses further show that greater misalignment between social and technological resources increases loss severity but shortens recovery time. In addition, ETTF moderates the effects of resource bundles on resilience outcomes by strengthening both compensatory coordination and reconfiguration capacity. This study advances ROT by showing that internal resource configurations shape entrepreneurial resilience through both bundle composition and misalignment, contingent on team structural conditions.

Title: Doing bad by doing good? The impact of philanthropy on perceptions of organizational leader morality and organizational trust and support
Authors: Haley Gandy, Cristiano Guarana, Blake Mathias, Shelby Solomon

Title: The entrepreneur as ecosystem architect: Economic foundations for strategic entrepreneurship in the age of AI
Authors: David J. Teece
Affiliations: Graduate School University of California, Berkeley Berkeley California USA; Berkeley Research Group Emeryville California USA
Abstract: Abstract Research Summary This paper develops an alternative foundation for understanding strategic entrepreneurship in the age of artificial intelligence (AI) by joining entrepreneurship research with the profiting from innovation model and the dynamic capabilities framework. It argues that the economic function of the entrepreneur is increasingly that of an ecosystem architect, exercising judgment under uncertainty to orchestrate complementary assets and capabilities across organizational boundaries. AI dramatically lowers the cost of building software thereby lowering product development costs but may raise the barriers to scaling and sustaining competitive advantage. Value capture depends not simply on innovation, but on a compelling value proposition and access to and control over critical complementary assets, architectural control points, and shifting ecosystem bottlenecks. The paper emphasizes that entrepreneurial success requires dynamic capabilities and human judgment to configure and reconfigure ecosystems as technologies and competitive conditions evolve. Managerial Summary AI makes it easier to start a business as it lowers the cost of software development; but building a durable competitive advantage still requires more than a good product or technology. It requires a compelling value proposition to the customer and participation in ecosystems first as tenant and later as anchor. Accordingly, entrepreneurs need to become sophisticated ecosystem players and aspire to be architects, coordinating partners, platforms, data, technology, capital, and other capabilities they may not own. They should identify early which complementary assets are critical to creating and capturing value, understand where control and bottlenecks lie in their ecosystem, and continually reassess these as technology and competition change. AI can help small teams move faster and operate at greater scale, but it does not replace human judgment. Successful entrepreneurs must combine AI with strong ecosystem relationships, domain expertise, governance, and the ability to adapt as their businesses scale.

Title: Silent female representation and tech entrepreneurial project evaluation: The role of evaluators' genders
Authors: Yan “Anthea” Zhang, Lun Li, Jizhen Li, Xiwei Yi
Affiliations: School of Business Rice University Houston Texas USA; Business School Beijing Normal University Beijing China; School of Economics and Management Tsinghua University Beijing China; Guanghua School of Management Peking University Beijing China
Abstract: Abstract Research Summary We examine how the nature of female representation in tech entrepreneurial projects may be related to the evaluations of the projects. We argue that silent female representation —i.e., women are present but do not speak in representing projects—may reinforce the stereotyped view of women, resulting in lower project evaluations relative to male‐only projects, whereas active female representation may not lead to evaluation penalty. We further predict that the negative association between silent female representation and project evaluation is stronger when the evaluators are women than when they are men. Conducted in a unique setting wherein female and male evaluators on panels, independently and confidentially, rated funding applications represented by various mixes of male and female entrepreneurs, our study provides evidence that is consistent with these predictions. Managerial Summary It is widely recognized that female entrepreneurs face greater challenges than their male counterparts when seeking external financial resources in the tech sector. This funding disparity may start from evaluation disparity. We find that projects with silent female representation—i.e., women are present but do not speak—receive lower evaluations than male‐only projects, whereas projects with active female representation receive evaluations comparable to male‐only projects. We also find that female evaluators are more likely than male evaluators to penalize projects with silent female representation. Our research offers valuable insights into strategies for fostering gender equality in traditionally male‐dominated fields.

Title: Should birds of a feather flock together: How public criticism shapes pressures for sustainability conformity and differentiation
Authors: Nareuporn (Bell) Piyasinchai, Matthew Grimes
Affiliations: Department of Organization Studies Tilburg University Tilburg the Netherlands; Cambridge Judge Business School University of Cambridge Cambridge UK
Abstract: Abstract Research Summary While firms face pressure to engage in Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) practices, it is unclear how they should specifically engage given the breadth of sustainability‐related concerns. Drawing on optimal distinctiveness and social evaluations research, we argue that public criticism directed toward an industry creates oscillating pressures for firms to conform with or deviate from industry ESG norms. Using data on 8176 global companies from 2013 to 2022, we find that although ESG conformity benefits investor evaluations, once industry peers' public criticism accumulates beyond a threshold, ESG differentiation is rewarded, particularly when firms increase material ESG practices and reduce immaterial ones. Our study reveals how public criticism dynamically reshapes the evaluative processes by which investors determine firm legitimacy, bridging optimal distinctiveness and social evaluations literatures. Managerial Summary Our research indicates that firms often adopt similar ESG practices as their industry peers, which usually enhances investor evaluations. However, this conformity can backfire and become a liability when industry peers face significant criticism. In such scenarios, firms that adopt distinctive ESG practices compared to the industry tend to receive greater rewards, especially when differentiation involves increasing material ESG practices and reducing immaterial ones. Therefore, while adopting ESG norms can be beneficial, managers should be vigilant of public opinion and ready to deviate from those norms when necessary.

Title: Earnings Instability
Authors: Peter Ganong, Pascal Noel, Christina Patterson, Joseph Vavra, Alexander Weinberg
Affiliations: University of Chicago and National Bureau of Economic Research; University of Chicago
Abstract: Abstract This paper uses high-frequency administrative data to show that most U.S. workers experience substantial month-to-month fluctuations in pay, even within ongoing employment relationships. Monthly earnings instability is pervasive but is masked in annual data. Moreover, this instability is unequally distributed: lower-income, hourly workers face more instability than higher-income, salaried workers. Firm-driven fluctuations in hours account for a large share of this instability. Monthly earnings instability, in turn, increases spending volatility and job separations. Short-term earnings risk is therefore a significant feature of the labor market and falls disproportionately on the most financially fragile workers.

Title: From Design to Disclosure
Authors: S Nageeb Ali, Andreas Kleiner, Kun Zhang
Affiliations: Pennsylvania State University; University of Bonn; Auburn University and University of Queensland
Abstract: Abstract We study the role of hard information in contractual and market settings in which the receiver can flexibly adjust allocations and transfers in response to the sender's disclosure. These settings include monopoly pricing, insurance contracting, and policy negotiations. Across these settings, the sender is worst off if she reveals her type completely because the receiver would then adjust the terms of trade to extract her surplus. Taking this feature as our central departure from the literature, we characterize the entire set of equilibrium payoffs in these disclosure games. We prove an equivalence result: a payoff profile can be approximated by an equilibrium of the disclosure game if and only if it can be achieved through information design. Thus, there exist equilibria in which the sender obtains approximately her commitment payoff.

Title: The Impact of Mandatory Audit Firm Rotation on Competitive Pricing Strategies for New Audit Engagements: Evidence From the European Union
Authors: Ditmir Sufaj, Simon Dekeyser, Marleen Willekens
Affiliations: KU Leuven Leuven Belgium
Abstract: ABSTRACT Mandatory audit firm rotation was introduced in the European Union (EU), in part, to make the audit market more dynamic by bringing audit engagements to market more frequently. However, it creates a countervailing economic force: By limiting the duration of auditor–client relationships, mandatory rotation shortens the period over which auditors can recoup first‐year fee discounts through fees earned in subsequent years. Consistent with this argument, we find that first‐year fee discounts decline substantially after mandatory firm rotation took effect in the EU, particularly in countries with stricter limits on auditor tenure. Thus, greater opportunities to compete for new engagements do not necessarily translate into greater first‐year fee discounts. Our findings highlight that regulators should consider not only how frequently audit engagements are brought to market but also how limits on auditor tenure shape the pricing incentives associated with competing for new clients.

Title: Place Matters: A Dynamic Multilevel Perspective on Stigma Management in French Elderly Care
Authors: Claire Le Breton, Frédéric Bally, Albane Grandazzi, Hélène Picard
Affiliations: Grenoble Ecole de Management; KEDGE Business School
Abstract: Abstract This article interrogates how ‘place’ contributes to managing stigma and its associated multilevel processes. In doing so, it addresses a literature that often treats stigma as a static attribute, overlooking the spatial and material dynamics of managing it. Drawing on a 2.5‐year case study of Help@hom, a French national initiative aimed at restructuring elderly care, we examine how spatial and material arrangements actively shape stigma management processes. We identify three interrelated mechanisms – expanding , enclosing , and fragmenting – through which Help@hom reconfigures the meanings, locations, and materialities of care. Building on these mechanisms, we theorize place as producing, sustaining, and distributing the dynamics of stigma management: place produces stigma management strategies rather than merely providing their setting, sustains stigma by relocating rather than dissolving it, and distributes it across organizational, occupational, and individual levels. Our study demonstrates that place is constitutive of stigma management, shaping how organizations enact and experience multilevel stigma processes, and that spatial and material interventions can produce unexpected cross‐level consequences. In doing so, it advances recent efforts to conceptualize stigma as relational, dynamic, and systemic, and offers a more integrated understanding of how organizations navigate complex stigma management landscapes.

Title: May I Have Your Attention, Please? Debating the Ontology of Attention in Organizational Research
Authors: Paolo Aversa, Christopher Wickert
Affiliations: King's Business School, King's College London; School of Business and Economics Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam
Abstract: Abstract Few constructs in management research have proved as generative as organizational attention, and few have been left so largely unexamined at their core. This Point‐Counterpoint debate brings a dormant question into the open: what exactly is attention? The Point argues for an ontological reorientation of the Attention‐Based View from attention quantity to attention quality, reconceptualizing attention as a set of sociomaterial practices of attending that are crescive and differentiated rather than limited and homogeneous. One Counterpoint defends the ontological integrity of attention as scarce, selective, and situated, warning that a crescive ontology dissolves the very constraint from which attention derives its explanatory power. The other Counterpoint charts an expansive third way, tracing the contested assumptions to Herbert Simon's legacy and proposing to broaden the Attention‐Based View towards competition, thicker situations, and possible attentional abundance. In this introduction to the debate, we present the three positions and reflect on what their disagreement teaches us about ontological disputes in management theory more generally. We distil three tests – of phenomena, of explanation, and of genealogy – that scholars can apply when deciding whether a construct's ontology deserves revision, defence, or expansion.

Title: Decision Considerations Influencing Information Systems Modularity: A Multimethod Study of LEGO
Authors: Stefan Henningsson, Ben Eaton, Lorenz Törmer, Suprateek Sarker
Affiliations: Copenhagen Business School, Digitalization, Frederiksberg, Capital Region, Denmark; Copenhagen Business School, Department of Digitalization, Frederiksberg, 2000, Denmark; University of Virginia McIntire School of Commerce, Information Technology, Charlottesville, Virginia, United States
Abstract: Abstract. The maturing of concepts such as microservices and open application programming interfaces (APIs) has radically increased the practicality of fine-grained modularization in Information Systems (IS) architecture. These are critical technical advancements, given the central role of modularity in the ability of IS to transform and meet future organizational needs efficiently. Nevertheless, reports from practice suggest that, when presented with new opportunities for modularization, organizations face multifaceted decision criteria and do not necessarily embrace new approaches as may be expected. While emergent IS literature observes that organizations’ decisions on modularity in IS may involve competing concerns, understanding of the considerations involved and how they influence such decisions remains limited. To examine these considerations, we intensively study the experience of LEGO, a global toy company. Specifically, we sequentially apply multiple methods consisting of an exploratory inductive analysis of LEGO’s approach to IS modularity decisions over 36 months, which then informs a crisp-set qualitative comparative analysis (QCA) of 31 episodes of LEGO’s situated decision-making on IS modularity. Through the analysis, we find the rationale for a purposeful choice between two forms of modularity that differ in granularity of decomposition, rather than a linear pursuit of maximizing decomposability in IS architecture. We bring to the fore a perspective of IS modularity as situated decisions reconciling competing demands in pursuit of the right type of modularity, in the right place to achieve the right effect. Our findings add nuance to modularity in the context of IS architecture and explain the complex causality of IS modularity decisions.

Title: Online Review Generation in the Digital Age: A Meta-Analytic Study of Online Review Behavior
Authors: Hong Hong, DaPeng Xu, Xiaoquan (Michael) Zhang
Affiliations: Harbin Institute of Technology, School of Management, Harbin, China; Tsinghua University, Shenzhen International Graduate School, Shenzhen, China; Chinese University of Hong Kong, Decision Sciences and Managerial Economics, Shatin, N.T., CUHK Business School, Hong Kong
Abstract: A large body of literature on online review generation has investigated various antecedents to online review characteristics. However, the mixed and even contradictory findings in this domain have hampered a clear understanding of consumers’ online review behavior for both researchers and practitioners, thereby complicating actionable strategies. To address this issue, we conduct a comprehensive meta-analysis of 154 independent samples from 152 empirical papers, synthesizing the relationships between 28 antecedent factors and 12 review features, which we categorize into rating-based (evaluative) and non-rating (expressive) dimensions. Our results indicate that rating attributes are dominantly driven by stable reviewer tendencies and market-level reputation cues, whereas non-rating features—such as text length and image inclusion—are primarily influenced by reviewer social embeddedness and platform engagement. Crucially, we identify that inconsistencies in prior literature can be explained by critical boundary conditions, including platform type (business-hosted vs. third-party), goods type (service vs. tangible), and cultural background (Asia vs. North America). By distinguishing between evaluative and expressive review components, our study reconciles mixed findings and uncovers underlying mechanisms such as expectation-based evaluation and self-presentation. The findings provide a robust theoretical foundation for empirical model specification and offer actionable insights for retailers and platforms to optimize reputation management and system design. Ultimately, our work offers a holistic framework for understanding online review behavior and proposes a rich agenda for future research in the digital marketplace.

Title: Influence Without Authority: Bottom-Up Normalization of Organizational Corruption
Authors: Patricia Helena Hein, Shahzad (Shaz) Ansari
Affiliations: Western University, Ivey Business School, London, Canada; University of Cambridge, Judge Business School, Cambridge, Cambridgeshire, United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland
Abstract: Research on organizational corruption has largely portrayed normalization as a top-down, management-driven process. We know less about how employees with limited formal authority can escalate wrongdoing beyond isolated acts and drive its normalization. Drawing on a qualitative study of a German recruitment firm’s practices during the COVID-19 pandemic, we develop a three-phase model of bottom-up normalization of organizational wrongdoing. Less powerful actors first engage in tolerated rule-bending to demonstrate competence and indispensability and build influence through informal networks. When disruption threatens this influence and legitimate alternatives are unavailable, they may escalate to more serious wrongdoing to safeguard their standing by framing new opportunities as extensions of familiar rule-bending. Normalization then depends on their ability to sustain a cohesive coalition, secure support from actors with formal authority, and contain resistance. We make three contributions. First, we advance a relational view of corruption by showing how central positions in informal networks enable actors lacking formal authority to mobilize support across hierarchical levels and normalize wrongdoing. Second, we show how organizational corruption can become a means of building and preserving social influence, fostering a sense of accomplishment rather than guilt or shame. Third, we identify a disruption-driven pathway to normalization in which threats to less powerful actors’ social influence precipitate abrupt escalation from tolerated rule-bending to more serious wrongdoing.

Title: The Consequences of Pay Standing under Pay Range Transparency
Authors: Meredith Woehler, Tae-Youn Park
Affiliations: Purdue University; Sungkyunkwan University

Title: Role conflict, growth mindset, and financial misreporting
Authors: Eddy Cardinaels, Oliver Hegers, Anil Kshatriya
Abstract: Business unit (BU) controllers often face role conflicts between their fiduciary duty to report accurately and role expectations of their superiors or colleagues that put pressure on controllers to engage in misreporting. We develop theory that the positive relation between role conflict and misreporting is strengthened for business controllers with a growth mindset. While a growth mindset can be beneficial for learning and overcoming challenges, it can also lead to a flexible attitude toward rule-breaking, which might be dysfunctional in environments where a BU controller's fiduciary duties clash with role expectations of their business unit. Through a survey of BU controllers and an experiment, in which we manipulate mindset, we find that role conflict leads to more misreporting. We further find that a growth mindset relative to a fixed mindset strengthens the positive relation between role conflict and misreporting. Our results are relevant for practice: encouraging a growth mindset in business unit controllers can backfire and can lead to more misreporting, particularly when role conflict increases.

Title: Government‐funded experimentation: How startups use R&D contracts to resolve uncertainty
Authors: Larisa Cioaca
Affiliations: Freeman School of Business Tulane University New Orleans Louisiana USA
Abstract: Abstract Research Summary Startups use experimentation to reduce technological and market uncertainty, but experimentation is costly and unevenly funded. This paper examines how government‐funded experimentation relates to subsequent performance among high‐tech startups that receive federal awards. Using data on $32 billion in US government R&D contracts awarded to high‐tech startups between 2001 and 2018, I distinguish between technology experimentation, measured by the value of R&D contracts, and market experimentation, measured by the number of agencies awarding the R&D contracts. Market experimentation is positively associated with subsequent employment, sales, and acquisition, while technology experimentation shows weaker associations with these outcomes. The findings are consistent with startups using information from multiple government buyers to learn about market opportunities and improve subsequent performance. Managerial Summary High‐tech startups need to test both whether their technology works and where demand exists, but venture capital often leaves this experimentation unfunded. Using data on $32 billion in US government R&D contracts awarded to high‐tech startups from 2001 to 2018, this paper shows that startups funded by more government agencies subsequently have higher employment and sales and are more likely to be acquired. Larger R&D contract amounts have less consistent relationships with these outcomes. For managers, the findings suggest considering what different government customers can help the firm learn. For policymakers, they suggest that the diversity of a startup's public customer base is a vital margin to consider alongside the overall size of its R&D awards.

Title: Nonpredictive approaches in marketing
Authors: Masoud Karami, Stuart Read
Abstract: Abstract Much academic research is focused on the application of predictive data, forecasts, and models to inform practical marketing decision-making. Such work offers powerful insights to marketers directing their firms and interacting with the environments in which they operate. The present study is devoted to the smaller, alternative, and equally potent body of work that seeks to enable decision-making without reliance on prediction. We term this category of approaches ‘nonpredictive’ because their operative basis for action does not depend on prior estimation of future states or outcomes. Instead, decision paths are generated and revised through mechanisms of action, interaction, commitment, recombination, experimentation, and imagined direction. This foundation enables nonpredictive approaches to function across a wide variety of marketing decisions, including truly uncertain situations where prediction cannot reliably guide action. Interest in nonpredictive approaches is emerging but has yet to be consolidated. We inventory and synthesize nonpredictive approaches in the marketing literature, contributing to academic discussion at the foundation of marketing decision-making. In the process, we clarify conceptual specifics of nonpredictive approaches, construct a taxonomy that distinguishes among them, and develop a series of propositions to inform future research. The payoff from our work lies in bringing attention to a class of approaches for making decisions in an increasingly uncertain world.
Journal: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science

Title: Joint optimization of condition-based maintenance and load adjustment for a performance-based 1-out-of-2 pairs balanced system
Authors: Haojun Fang, Rui Zheng, Xinyue Wang, Zhiming Liu, Xinbao Liu

Title: Capacity relocation and pricing to cope with customs tariffs
Authors: Ramzi Hammami, Moutaz Khouja, Imen Nouira, Meihan Chen

Title: Meritocracy and Homophily in Collegial Organizations
Authors: Paul-Henri Moisson, Jean Tirole
Affiliations: Paris School of Economics and Ecole des Ponts ParisTech; Toulouse School of Economics (TSE)
Abstract: Abstract In collegial organizations, homophily jeopardizes the recruitment of the most talented (“meritocracy”). We analyze the dynamics and welfare properties of an organization whose incumbent members coopt new ones in a forward-looking manner. We identify organizations in which meritocracy is likely to give way to favoritism and entrenchment, and investigate policy interventions (such as affirmative action, quality-based or diversity-based funding, discretionary overruling of majority decisions, blind hiring processes) and their unintended consequences.

Title: Partisan Banks and Creditor Coordination Within Loan Syndicates
Authors: Robert M. Bushman, Sang Woo Sohn, Jianxin (Donny) Zhao
Affiliations: University of North Carolina; City University of Hong Kong; Emory University
Abstract: ABSTRACT We investigate how firm‐level partisanship influences interactions between banks in the syndicated loan market. Because politically divergent banks hold conflicting perceptions of economic conditions, ideological distance between banks impedes consensus and elevates expected coordination costs. We find that greater political distance between a lead arranger and a participant reduces the participant's likelihood of joining a syndicate and lowers its retained loan share relative to the lead. The relation between political distance and loan share differences intensifies during periods of high national political polarization. Moreover, greater political diversity within a syndicate is associated with less restrictive loan covenants and higher interest spreads, reflecting a trade‐off where lenders sacrifice contingent control to avoid costly renegotiation gridlock. Validating our disagreement mechanism, we show that following presidential elections, banks politically misaligned with the incoming administration issue significantly more pessimistic macroeconomic forecasts than aligned banks.

Title: The Impacts of Host Culture Heterogeneity on Learning from Success Versus Failure in Foreign Direct Investments
Authors: Yuping Zeng, Sangcheol Song, Soonkyoo Choe
Affiliations: Southern Illinois University Edwardsville; Saint Joseph's University; Yonsei University
Abstract: Abstract This study examines the differentiated influences of host culture heterogeneity on the learning outcomes of multinational enterprises' (MNEs) success and failure experiences in foreign direct investments (FDI). We posit that host culture heterogeneity among prior successful FDIs reduces the beneficial effect of an MNE's success experience on a subsequent FDI, particularly when the cultural differences between the subsequent FDI and the MNE's prior successes are significant. In contrast, host culture heterogeneity among prior failed FDIs enhances the learning benefits of failure experience, and this effect is more pronounced when the subsequent FDI is culturally distant from the prior failures. Using FDI data of South Korean MNEs between 1990 and 2016, we find support for our hypotheses, demonstrating that host culture heterogeneity has divergent impacts on the learning outcomes of MNEs' success versus failure FDI experiences. This study enhances our understanding of the conditions under which host culture heterogeneity may weaken or strengthen the learning benefits of an MNE's FDI experience.

Title: Human Performance at Solving 0-1 Knapsack Problems: Results from a Large-Scale Field Experiment
Authors: Sumit Agarwal, Joel Goh, Wenlan Qian, Xin Zou
Affiliations: NUS Business School, National University of Singapore, Singapore 119245; and NUS Global Asia Institute, National University of Singapore, Singapore 119076; and NUS Institute of Operations Research and Analytics, National University of Singapore, Singapore 117602; and NUS Institute of Real Estate and Urban Studies, National University of Singapore, Singapore; School of Business, Hong Kong Baptist University, Kowloon Tong, Hong Kong SAR
Abstract: The 0-1 knapsack problem is a fundamental problem of discrete choice that permeates many diverse fields and applications, but relatively little is known about what instances human solvers find more difficult than others. This paper reports the results of the first large-scale randomized controlled field experiment investigating this question, conducted in partnership with a global mobile gaming platform. A total of 100,000 different knapsack instances were predesigned for this study and randomly assigned to each player attempt at the knapsack problem. For our base-case analysis, there were 17,950,838 distinct player accounts who made a total of 150,284,195 submitted solution attempts. Contrary to expectations, players performed better on problems that were rated as more difficult by two traditional measures of knapsack difficulty (the Pearson correlation between value and weight vectors and Sahni complexity), but performed worse on problem instances that featured large optimality gaps from a suite of heuristic solution algorithms. These suggest that optimality gaps can serve as promising measures of human-perceived knapsack difficulty and potentially could be used to measure human-perceived problem difficulty for other types of discrete choice problems. We found evidence that players improved their performance with repeated attempts at the knapsack task overall, but less-experienced players of the mobile game improved more quickly than more-experienced players. Through the construction of a new measure of human-perceived difficulty rating for each knapsack instance, we found evidence that players who were assigned to instances with a higher difficulty rating in the past tended to perform better on future attempts. This paper was accepted by Manel Baucells, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Funding: S. Agarwal’s research is supported by the Ministry of Education, Singapore, under its Social Science and Humanities Research Thematic [Grant SSRC2024-SSHRTG-022] and the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grant 72495154]. J. Goh’s research is supported by a Startup [Grant R-314-000-110-133] and a 2021 Humanities and Social Sciences Faculty Research Fellowship from the National University of Singapore. Title: Whiplash: Congestion Dissipation in a Disrupted Circulatory Shipping System
Authors: Ming Hu, Chaoyu Zhang
Affiliations: Rotman School of Management, University of Toronto, Toronto, Ontario M5S 3E6, Canada; College of Business, City University of Hong Kong, Kowloon, Hong Kong
Abstract: The (post)pandemic period was marked by numerous port disruptions, leading to delays and rising costs for shippers. We build a fluid model in transient states to investigate how a disruption at one port can affect the disrupted port and its counterpart in another country in a circulatory container shipping system, where a stream of fleets moves goods back and forth between the two ports. Port disruption leads to two types of congestion: the inbound backlogs, which occur when ships are unable to enter the port, and the outbound backlogs, which arise when goods are unable to be loaded onto ships for transport to other ports. We analytically characterize the system’s recovery time, measured from the onset of the port closure until normal operations are restored, and the dynamics of inbound and outbound backlogs during recovery. We identify a whiplash effect in which outbound backlogs alternate between ports, creating oscillatory congestion patterns because of the disruption-induced uneven spatial distribution of ships. Our analysis reveals that simply increasing ship capacity may not expedite system recovery, highlighting the importance of coordination between port authorities and shipping companies when jointly planning capacity expansions. Furthermore, we examine several extensions of the model. We use the two-port system as a building block to analyze bipartite and cyclic network structures, and we also consider scenarios in which a port experiences multiple disruptions. In all cases, the whiplash effect persists, thereby demonstrating the robustness of our findings. Finally, we use the prediction from our theoretical model as a feature and apply machine learning techniques to predict the time that vessels spend in Shanghai Port after a typhoon disruption and show that using the predictor derived from our theoretical model, alongside all relevant vessel and voyage attributes as raw features, significantly reduces prediction errors by roughly 10%–30% on average compared with not using it. This paper was accepted by Elena Katok, operations management. Funding: This work was supported by the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada [Grant RGPIN-2021-04295]. Title: Corporate Contributions to Ballot Measure Campaigns: Real Effects and Valuation
Authors: Rüdiger Fahlenbrach, Alexei Ovtchinnikov, Philip Valta
Affiliations: Ecole Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne, 1015 Lausanne, Switzerland; and Swiss Finance Institute, 8006 Zürich, Switzerland; and European Corporate Governance Institute, 1000 Brussels, Belgium; HEC Paris, 78350 Jouy-en-Josas, France; University of Bern, 3012 Bern, Switzerland
Abstract: We analyze novel data on corporate contributions to ballot initiatives at the U.S. state level. Firms make large contributions to ballot measure campaigns in favor of or against specific initiatives. They contribute significantly more to business initiatives compared with ideological initiatives. Corporate campaign spending is systematically associated with the likelihood that a ballot measure passes. Contributing firms experience changes in sales growth following the passage of important ballot measures. Following successful (failed) initiatives, all firms in affected industries exhibit significantly more positive (negative) cumulative abnormal returns around the election, but contributing firms do more so than peers. This paper was accepted by Bo Becker, finance. Funding: R. Fahlenbrach gratefully acknowledges financial support from the Swiss Finance Institute. Title: The Asymmetry in Responsible Investing Preferences and Beliefs
Authors: Jacquelyn Humphrey, Shimon Kogan, Jacob S. Sagi, Laura T. Starks
Affiliations: Business School, The University of Queensland, Brisbane, Queensland 4072, Australia; Arison School of Business, Reichman University, Herzliya 4610101, Israel; Kenan-Flagler Business School, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, Chapel Hill, North Carolina 27599; McCombs School of Business, University of Texas at Austin, Austin, Texas 78712
Abstract: Empirical stylized facts in the literature concerning “sin” versus “angel” stocks display marked asymmetries in investor behavior. Through a set of experiments, we examine whether such biases can be micro-founded via individuals’ preferences and belief formations. With respect to portfolio allocation decisions, we find that the responses to negative environmental and social externalities are several times larger in magnitude than their responses to comparable positive externalities, ceteris paribus. Negative externalities also modestly increase pessimism about future investment performance, whereas positive externalities have little discernible effect on beliefs. This asymmetry is pervasive across our sample, exhibits heterogeneity across individuals, and is comparable to or greater in magnitude than estimates observed in loss aversion analyses. These findings help rationalize several existing stylized empirical facts documented in the responsible investing literature and carry implications for the growing body of theoretical work modeling the role of nonpecuniary investor preferences in asset pricing. This paper was accepted by Marie Claire Villeval, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Title: Connectors and Influencers
Authors: Frédéric Moisan, Syngjoo Choi, Sanjeev Goyal
Affiliations: Emlyon Business School, CNRS, Université Lumière Lyon 2, Université Jean Monnet Saint-Etienne, GATE, 69007 Lyon, France; Department of Economics, Seoul National University, Seoul 08826, Republic of Korea; Faculty of Economics, University of Cambridge, Cambridge CB3 9DD, United Kingdom
Abstract: We study a setting in which personal acquisition of information is costly and maintaining personal contacts to share information socially is also costly. The theory predicts star networks, with small groups sustaining an active hub and large groups allowing in addition for an inactive hub equilibrium. Experiments with small (8 subjects) and large (50 subjects) groups show star-like networks throughout. In small groups, behavior matches the active hub prediction. In large groups, hubs are inactive or engage in activity far in excess of the active hub equilibrium depending on how much information subjects are given on their own and others’ earnings. The hub’s activity level shapes relative earnings of subjects and the overall performance of the group. This paper was accepted by Roberto Weber, behavioral economics and decision analysis. S. Goyal acknowledges financial support from the Center of Behavioural Institutional Design and Tamkeen [New York University Abu Dhabi Research Institute Award CG005]. Title: Biodiversity Risk in the Corporate Bond Market
Authors: Sevgi Soylemezgil, Cihan Uzmanoglu
Affiliations: Binghamton University, Binghamton, New York 13902
Abstract: We show that a biodiversity risk premium has emerged in the U.S. corporate bond market following the United Nations Biodiversity Conference (COP15) in October 2021. COP15 placed biodiversity on the global regulatory agenda and raised transition risks for exposed firms. After COP15, a one standard deviation increase in a firm’s biodiversity footprint is associated with a 7% increase in its secondary market yield spreads, whereas this relation is insignificant before COP15. The biodiversity effect is also present in primary bond markets, most pronounced for medium-term bonds and distinct from climate-related mechanisms. Furthermore, a higher biodiversity footprint is associated with a lower likelihood of issuing medium-term bonds after COP15, consistent with firms managing their biodiversity-related risks. Evidence from firms’ biodiversity dependencies suggests that physical biodiversity risks are also priced in the bond market. This paper was accepted by Bo Becker, finance. Title: Advertising by Recruiting Influencers
Authors: Maya Jalloul, Vasiliki Kostami
Affiliations: Paris School of Business, 75005 Paris, France; HEC Paris, 78351 Jouy-en-Josas, France
Abstract: The rise of social media platforms has enabled customers to rely on influencers and peer reviews to guide their purchasing decisions. As products increasingly focus on experiences, firms are leveraging influencer marketing as a crucial tool. This paper addresses key challenges of influencer marketing by considering different types of influencers and partnership schemes alongside the impact of social learning. We introduce a two-period model wherein, in the initial period, the firm unveils a new product experience of unknown quality alongside an influencer marketing campaign. The campaign relies on two types of influencers that differ in popularity and engagement levels and two partnerships: sponsored advertising and public relations. Customers base their purchasing decisions on their original (heterogeneous) beliefs, influencer-driven information, and reviews from early adopters in the second period. When customers are equally likely to follow any given influencer, the firm should choose a single influencer type and partnership. Consumer reviews complement influencer marketing when products are initially undervalued, increasing the returns to influencer investment. Moreover, within a societal structure characterized by distinct classes, in which followers and influencers often belong to the same class, a mix of influencer types and partnership schemes may become optimal. Our study provides guidance on selecting influencer types, partnership schemes, and social media platforms based on engagement, popularity, audience composition, and platform characteristics. This paper was accepted by Jeanette Song, operations management. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.07919 .

Title: Do Fund Managers’ Commitments to Responsible Investing Affect Private Information Acquisition, Information Environment, and Corporate Sustainability?
Authors: Sumit Agarwal, Johan Sulaeman, Yue Zhang, Zhe Zong
Affiliations: NUS Business School and Sustainable and Green Finance Institute (SGFIN), National University of Singapore, 119245, Singapore; International School of Business & Finance and Advanced Institute of Finance, Sun Yat-sen University, Zhuhai 519082, China; China Zheshang Bank, Hangzhou 310020, China
Abstract: We investigate the effects of mutual funds’ commitments to responsible investing on their information acquisition activities and the corresponding externalities for other stakeholders. After committing to responsible investing (via United Nations Principles for Responsible Investment (UNPRI)), fund managers increase private information acquisition activities, that is, corporate site visits, particularly focusing on environmental and social issues. These visits generate negligible private investment value for the visiting funds. However, the information environment at the stock level improves following these visits with lower consensus analyst forecast errors. In addition to the information production role of these visits, they also generate positive externalities for other stakeholders through incremental improvements in the sustainability practices of the firms receiving sustainability-focused site visits from UNPRI fund managers. Collectively, the paper highlights the private costs and social benefits of responsible investing. This paper was accepted by Will Cong, finance. Funding: S. Agarwal and J. Title: Does Feedback Enhance Diversity in Selection Decisions?
Authors: Jose A. Cervantez, Sophia L. Pink, Linda W. Chang, Aneesh Rai, Katherine L. Milkman
Affiliations: The Wharton School, University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania 19104; Robert H. Smith School of Business, University of Maryland, College Park, Maryland 20742
Abstract: Some organizations provide employees with feedback on the demographics of people they have chosen to spotlight, hire, and promote, hoping to spur more diverse future selections. However, it is an open question whether purely descriptive feedback accomplishes this. We theorize and show that descriptive feedback highlighting low past selection rates of women or racial minorities (e.g., “5% of previous experts interviewed were women”) triggers a motivation to respond without prejudice, increasing the subsequent selection of members of underrepresented groups. Conversely, providing descriptive feedback about low selection rates of people with other attributes (e.g., areas of expertise, geographical location) that do not evoke image or reputational concerns has less influence on future decisions. We demonstrate these patterns across seven preregistered experiments (total n = 6,502), including one framed field experiment (Study 2). One study identifies motivation to respond without prejudice as a mediator of the effect of descriptive feedback about past choices on future selections of women and racial minorities. Another study shows that when women are overrepresented, the effect of descriptive feedback reverses in direction, increasing the subsequent selection of men (due to concerns about fairness), but this effect is significantly smaller in magnitude than the feedback effect produced when women are underrepresented. Practically, the effects of descriptive feedback were 45%–80% as large as simulating a strict quota requiring that at least one woman or racial minority be selected for a given opportunity, highlighting that descriptive feedback is a light-touch but potentially powerful intervention for promoting diversity. This paper was accepted by George Wu, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.01479 .

Title: Opinion Trumps Fact: Entry and Competition in Online Political News
Authors: Aaron Chatterji, Sharique Hasan, William D. Miles, Dror Shvadron
Affiliations: Fuqua School of Business, Duke University, Durham, North Carolina 27708; and NBER, Cambridge, Massachusetts 02138; Rotman School of Management, University of Toronto, Toronto, Ontario M5S 3E6, Canada
Abstract: This paper examines how new entrants influenced content strategies in the U.S. online political news business from 2014 to 2021. Using a novel measure of article opinionation that captures the extent to which an article displays editorializing and persuasive language, we provide correlational evidence that new entrants produce articles that are more opinionated than those of incumbents, even when reporting on the same event. We then show that there is an economic rationale for this content strategy: opinionated articles receive more engagement on Twitter, and this engagement translates to increased webpage visits, crucial for advertising revenue. Consistent with these incentives, we provide evidence that news providers increase the average opinion level in their articles in response to competition and advertiser pressure. These shifts are accompanied by a possibly unintended consequence: opinionated content is associated with greater anger and hate speech in social media engagement. This paper was accepted by Alfonso Gambardella, business strategy. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.01487 .
