Title: Learning from success but not from failure in digital experimentation
Authors: Berk Deniz, Quang Nguyen, Pedro Sequeira
Abstract: Digital experimentation platforms translate continuous statistical evidence into categorical labels such as Win, Loss, and Inconclusive. We ask whether the label itself, rather than the underlying estimate, shapes a team's next search. We develop a model in which a single label-contingent wedge on the marginal value of distant search captures how a label reshapes behaviour. The wedge combines aspiration satisfaction with the action map attached to each label, and from this building block we derive an asymmetry: a Win narrows search, whereas a Loss has no determinate effect. Because our data do not record distances between successive ideas, we derive conditions under which narrower search produces a tighter distribution of realised outcomes. Using a large sample of A/B tests and a local regression-discontinuity design at the default threshold, we examine post-treatment outcomes including the variance, interquartile range, maximum and minimum lift, the share of large effects, the selected mean lift, and testing intensity. Within 15 days, a marginal Win is followed by lower variance, a narrower range, and fewer large effects, while the selected mean lift does not change significantly. Marginal Losses are not followed by detectable broadening. Platform feedback design thus shapes high-frequency organisational learning, though these measures reveal only part of what it means for innovation.

Title: Unveiling the J-curve: How intangibles drive productivity mismeasurement
Authors: Gert Bijnens, Jozef Konings, Aaron Putseys
Abstract: This paper identifies a firm-level Productivity J-curve induced by intangible investment. Using novel microdata on business-to-business transactions for Belgian firms, we construct a comprehensive measure of intangibles covering software, R&D, design, training, and organizational capital. Because these investments are expensed instead of capitalized, conventional TFP measures misclassify them as intermediate inputs, overstating inputs relative to output. Exploiting their lumpy timing in a difference-in-differences event study, we show that TFP is underestimated by about 1.7%–3.0% over seven years. Intangible investment spikes are followed by higher profits and lower marginal costs, indicating that the J-curve reflects mismeasured, rather than absent, returns to intangible investment. Linking intangible capital to systematic mismeasurement provides new evidence on the productivity slowdown and highlights intangibles as a source of downward measurement bias.

Title: Porter might be right: environmental policy, innovation, and product differentiation
Authors: Wensi Xie
Affiliations: Chinese University of Hong Kong CUHK Business School, , Hong Kong SAR
Abstract: Abstract We evaluate the effects of environmental regulation on corporate innovation and real outcomes. Exploiting plant-level regulatory shocks induced by the 1990 Clean Air Act Amendments, we identify firms’ exposure to stricter environmental standards based on whether their plants emit newly regulated pollutants in counties designated as nonattainment. We show that firms more heavily exposed to the regulatory shock increase green innovation, including green process and green product patents, with no corresponding changes in nongreen patenting. The innovation-enhancing effects are concentrated among firms in industries with low external finance dependence and are stronger in areas with more intensive environmental enforcement. In addition, employment declines in response to the regulatory shock, and the effects are more pronounced among firms relying heavily on external finance. Overall, the results support the Porter hypothesis while highlighting the roles of financial capacity and enforcement intensity in shaping firms’ innovation and labor responses to environmental regulation.

Title: Tail risk and asset prices in the short-term
Authors: Caio Almeida, Gustavo Freire, René Garcia, Rodrigo Hizmeri
Affiliations: Department of Economics, Princeton University , 20, Washington Rd, Room 207 , Princeton, NJ, 08540; Nova School of Business and Economics, Universidade NOVA de Lisboa , Campus de Carcavelos , Carcavelos, 2775-405; Department of Economics, Université de Montréal , 2900 Edouard Montpetit Boulevard , Montreal, H3T 1J4; Toulouse School of Economics , 1 Esplanade de l'Universite , Toulouse, 31080; University of Liverpool Management School, University of Liverpool , Chatham Street , Liverpool, L69 7ZH
Abstract: Abstract We combine high-frequency stock returns with risk-neutralization to extract the daily common component of tail risks perceived by investors in the cross-section of firms. Our tail risk measure significantly predicts the equity premium and variance risk premium at short horizons. Furthermore, a long–short portfolio built by sorting stocks on their recent exposure to tail risk generates abnormal returns with respect to standard factor models. Incorporating investors’ preferences via risk-neutralization is fundamental to our findings: the predictive power of the physical tail risk is weaker and generally subsumed by its risk-neutral counterpart.

Title: Behavioral messages and debt repayment
Authors: Giorgia Barboni, Juan Camilo Cárdenas, Nicolás de Roux
Affiliations: Warwick Business School and CAGE, University of Warwick , Coventry, CV47AL; Department of Economics, Universidad de Los Andes , Bogotá; Department of Economics, University of Massachusetts Amherst , Amherst, MA
Abstract: Abstract We conduct a randomized experiment involving 7,063 late-paying clients of a large Colombian bank to compare the effects of text messages that leverage different behavioral motives on loan delinquency. Our results show that receiving a message decreases the likelihood of borrowers being late by 4 percent. The effects are more pronounced and persistent when messages leverage social norms. Using machine learning tools, we find that the effects are higher among borrowers with higher credit scores and unsecured loans. A second experiment shows that this type of message is ineffective in preventing on-time borrowers from falling into loan delinquency.

Title: High-end IPO prices
Authors: Clemens Mueller, Patrick Verwijmeren
Affiliations: Erasmus School of Economics, Erasmus University Rotterdam , Rotterdam; University of Melbourne, Melbourne, Australia
Abstract: Abstract Many initial public offerings (IPOs) are priced at exactly the high-end of the pricing range. Investing in IPOs priced at the high-end leads to first-day returns that are substantially higher than investing in IPOs that are priced just below or above the high-end. We argue that these results are in line with issuing firms settling for positively perceived salient pricing points in negotiations with underwriters.

Title: The unintended impact of the Volcker rule on primary market bond pricing: evidence from the Rule 144A bond market
Authors: Eric Powers, Donghang Zhang, Yafei Zhang
Affiliations: Darla Moore School of Business, University of South Carolina , Columbia, SC 29208; School of Business Administration, American University of Sharjah, University City , Sharjah, UAE; Manchester University Alliance Manchester Business School, , Booth Street West , Manchester, M15 6PB, England
Abstract: Abstract We study how the Volcker rule affects bond pricing in the pritmary market. Following implementation, Volcker-affected bonds have greater credit spreads at issuance than non-affected bonds. Bond liquidity in the year after issuance is also negatively affected by the Volcker rule. These effects are concentrated in the Rule 144A bond market. The Volcker rule’s impacts on credit spreads and liquidity are stronger for bonds with lower expected liquidity. The results suggest that expected liquidity deterioration due to the Volcker rule increases the liquidity premium demanded by primary market investors.

Title: Opacity, signaling, and bail-ins
Authors: Kentaro Asai, Bruce Grundy, Ryuichiro Izumi
Affiliations: Center for Interdisciplinary Studies of Law and Policy, Graduate School of Law, Kyoto University , Kyoto 606-8501; Department of Finance, University of Melbourne , Victoria 3010; Department of Economics, Wesleyan University , Middletown, CT 06457
Abstract: Abstract Should banks be transparent during a bail-in? Banks suffering losses may bail-in creditors to optimally allocate resources between early and late withdrawers. However, if losses are private information, then bail-ins may signal asset quality. In the absence of signaling, banks can sell assets at a pooled price, effectively insuring creditors against asset risks. However, when bail-ins signal quality, banks may delay bail-ins and sell assets at higher prices than otherwise, but this incentive can trigger inefficient bank runs. To prevent such runs, banks should choose to be either fully transparent or entirely opaque, ensuring asset quality is not private information.

Title: Stress tests by an informed regulator
Authors: Markus Parlasca
Affiliations: WU Vienna University of Economics and Business Institute of Finance, Banking and Insurance, , Vienna, Vienna 1020; Vienna Graduate School of Finance , Vienna, 1020; Leibniz Institute for Financial Research SAFE, Frankfurt am Main, 60323; Finance Theory Group
Abstract: Abstract This article studies the disclosure of stress test results by a regulator who is privately informed about bank health when she chooses the stress scenario. I show that the regulator’s choice of the stress scenario depends on how heterogeneous health is across banks. There can be fewer runs than under transparency. However, there are more runs than when the regulator chooses the scenario before becoming informed, highlighting a time-inconsistency problem. Moreover, disclosure can become a source of informational contagion, as changes in the health of one bank affect beliefs about other banks. The model explains the empirical puzzle that a bank’s share price can fall even though it passes the stress test.

Title: Sectoral comovement and conglomerate networks
Authors: Kenneth R. Ahern, Lei Kong, Xinyan Yan
Affiliations: Marshall School of Business and National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER), University of Southern California , Los Angeles, CA 90089; Culverhouse College of Business, University of Alabama , Tuscaloosa, AL 35487; Muma College of Business, University of South Florida , Tampa, FL 33620
Abstract: Abstract We study the influence of multi-sector conglomerate firms on sectoral comovement. Using an innovative network model of firms and industries, we derive a novel measure of the co-concentration of industries in which two industries are more co-concentrated if they share greater exposure to the same conglomerate firms. Using time-series, cross-sectional, and longitudinal tests on establishment-level data from nearly all US firms over 1991 to 2019, we find that industries with higher co-concentration exhibit stronger comovement in employment, sales, and asset growth. Controlling for alternative explanations, a 1-SD increase in co-concentration corresponds to a 0.32-SD increase in the comovement of employment growth. In variance–covariance decompositions, we find that firm-specific shocks explain nearly half of aggregate volatility and industry comovement and that conglomerates play a significant role in sectoral comovement. Our framework helps explain how idiosyncratic, firm-level shocks contribute to aggregate fluctuations and influence business cycles.

Title: Joint supply boat and drone scheduling for shore-to-ship delivery considering battery constraints
Authors: Baoli Liu, Qinghe Sun, Zhi-Chun Li, Jianfeng Zheng, Lingrui Kong

Title: Sequential supplier selection in grocery collection operations
Authors: Daniel Cuellar-Usaquén, Marlin W. Ulmer, Florentin D. Hildebrandt, Camilo Gomez, David Álvarez-Martínez
Abstract: We study sequential resource-allocation problems in which uncertain information must be actively collected, resources are committed after information is revealed, and these commitments affect subsequent operational decisions. Our focal application is grocery collection from small farmers, where a company sequentially contacts suppliers to reveal uncertain price–quantity offers, decides whether to accept or reject them, and subsequently routes vehicles to collect the accepted purchases. Effective decisions therefore require jointly coordinating information collection, post-revelation commitment, and downstream routing. We develop the Stochastic Look-Ahead with Penalized Perfect Information policy (SLAPPI), which uses scenario-based optimization to anticipate future purchasing and routing consequences while reinforcement learning calibrates a state-dependent correction for the optimism introduced by perfect-information scenarios. This correction accounts for the fact that scenario solutions can exploit future information that is unavailable to the actual decision maker. Using real procurement data from the Colombian agricultural sector, SLAPPI achieves the best overall performance across all evaluated settings, reducing the average gap by 6.5–13.6 percentage points relative to rule-based benchmarks and by 10.9 percentage points relative to the uncorrected lookahead. Its largest gains occur when uncertainty creates meaningful differences among alternatives and sufficient flexibility remains to exploit them by adapting both commitment and subsequent selection decisions.

Title: Dangerous Liaisons? Debt Supply and Convenience Yield Spillovers in the Euro Area*
Authors: Cristian Arcidiacono, Matthieu Bellon, Matthias Gnewuch
Affiliations: University of Bern; International Monetary Fund; European Stability Mechanism
Abstract: Abstract The literature established that a sovereign bond’s “convenience yield” premium diminishes when that country issues more debt. But how is this convenience yield affected when another country issues sovereign debt? Using high-frequency identification and debt management offices’ communication, we find that an increase in German or French debt reduces convenience yields across the eurozone. Spillovers to low-risk countries are one-for-one while those to riskier countries are smaller. To rationalize these findings, we develop a model with heterogeneous credit risk. Safe sovereign bonds are close substitutes to hedge against idiosyncratic risk, explaining large spillovers, while risky bonds are poor substitutes.

Title: How Gig Sellers Do the Hustle
Authors: Eileen Fischer, Sandy D. Jap
Abstract: We conceptualize and develop theoretical insights related to a neglected category of market actors: gig sellers. Gig sellers are independent agents who sell products on behalf of a specific brand with marketing support. They face semi-entrepreneurial opportunities, meaning that while they are entirely responsible for managing the customer sales funnel, they do not develop new products or services like conventional entrepreneurs. They are compensated solely by sales commissions and do not receive salaries or benefits like organizational salesreps. Drawing on a large set of qualitative data from effective agents, we inductively and abductively draw inspiration both from literature and our analyses to unpack how these agents seize the opportunity to accomplish what is important to them. We find prominent reliance on effectual versus predictive practices is crucial to satisfactory achievement of outcomes. We expand our understanding of the range of outcomes that gig selling may result in, whether it be to remain in gig sales (enacting long-term loyalty, switching teams, or enriching) or enter alternative opportunity corridors (pursuing entrepreneurship, seeking employment). Our theoretical insights contrast with findings regarding salespeople in institutional settings and other categories of independent agents. Practical implications for agents and organizations are developed.

Title: Slim Shading in Ad Auctions: Adjustment of Bidding Strategies to First-Price Rules
Authors: Robert Zeithammer, Miguel Alcobendas
Abstract: We study how bidders adjusted to a switch from second-price to first-price auction rules on a large online advertising exchange. Under first-price rules, bidders should strategically reduce (“shade”) their bids. To assess whether observed bid reductions were sufficient given the competition each bidder faced, we develop a nonparametric estimator of a lower bound on the valuation underlying each bid. The estimator relies on localized measures of competition and does not require assumptions of bidder symmetry, valuation independence, or equilibrium bidding. Applying the method to more than 40 million auctions involving eight major demand-side platforms, we find pervasive insufficient bid shading after the switch. The implied lower bounds on valuations remain substantially above pre-switch levels for at least three months after the transition, indicating that none of the bidders we study shaded sufficiently. This finding is robust to alternative definitions of local competition, richer conditioning information, and variations in the assumptions underlying the estimator. The results suggest that adjustment to major auction-design changes can be surprisingly slow even among sophisticated algorithmic bidders, with implications for marketplace design and the interpretation of short-run “A/B test” experiments.

Title: Exploration Optimization for Dynamic Assortment Personalization under Linear Preferences
Authors: Fernando G. Bernstein, Sajad Modaresi, Denis Saure
Affiliations: Duke University, The Fuqua School of Business, Durham, North Carolina, United States; University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill Kenan-Flagler Business School, Chapel Hill, North Carolina, United States; University of Chile, Industrial Engineering, Santiago, Chile
Abstract: We study dynamic assortment personalization, where an online retailer adaptively selects assortments based on customer attributes to learn preferences and maximize revenue. We assume that product utilities depend linearly on customer attributes through an unknown coefficient matrix, leading to an exploration–exploitation trade-off. We identify price-driven and linearity-driven exploration efficiencies, showing that not all products need to be offered to all customer profiles to recover optimal assortments. We establish an instance-dependent regret lower bound characterized by a linear program, which we call the Regret Lower Bound (RLB) problem. Because the RLB has a complex structure and depends non-trivially on unknown parameters, we introduce an alternative formulation, called the Exploration-Optimization problem, that yields an interpretable exploration structure and can be formulated as a tractable mixed-integer linear program. We develop learning policies that select efficient exploration sets by solving either problem and establish a regret upper bound for the Exploration-Optimization policy. Using data from a large Chilean retailer, we demonstrate that our policies substantially outperform Thompson sampling in terms of both regret and computational efficiency, while remaining scalable in practice.

Title: Reducing shrinkage in diversity tradeoff curves for personnel selection: Comparing local validity studies, meta-analysis, and Bayes analysis.
Authors: Chen Tang, Daniel A. Newman, Q. Chelsea Song, Serena Wee
Abstract: For reducing adverse impact, the diversity-validity tradeoff curve approach (De Corte et al., 2007) provides sets of selection predictor weights that can often substantially enhance diversity (i.e., increase adverse impact ratio and number of minority job offers), with no loss of job performance in comparison to unit weights (Wee et al., 2014). A key limitation of this diversity-enhancing approach is the tendency for tradeoff curves to shrink, leading to lesser job performance and diversity outcomes upon cross-validation (Song et al., 2017). The current article evaluates and compares tradeoff curve shrinkage (both validity shrinkage and diversity shrinkage) using three types of validity evidence/calibration studies: (a) a local validity study, (b) a meta-analysis (Schmidt & Hunter, 1977), and (c) a Bayes analysis with empirical priors, which is a weighted combination of a local study with a meta-analysis (Newman et al., 2007). Using simulation, we show conditions where each approach performs best, offering recommendations on ideal methods for diversity improvement (reducing shrinkage and maximizing cross-validity) in local selection settings. Results guide selection practitioners in novel methods (integrating the advantages of meta-analysis, Bayes analysis, and Pareto-optimal weighting) to best combine predictors to simultaneously achieve job performance and diversity objectives in local selection settings. Title: Bridging a gap in meta-analytical practices: A superior approach for converting standardized beta weights to correlations.
Authors: Piers Steel, Hadi Fariborzi, Patrick D. Dunlop
Abstract: , correctly identify error variance. Due to imputation error, reporting beta weights alone typically destroys 95% to over 99% of the information originally held by a full correlation matrix. For fields that almost exclusively report betas, such as economics, it necessarily hampers them from becoming cumulative sciences. We recommend that all previous uses of Peterson and Brown be reevaluated, future aggregations of standardized beta weights use our provided imputation techniques, and correlation matrices be routinely reported. Title: They’ll conform anyway: A motivation stereotype perspective on the exploitation of Asian employees.
Authors: Liuxin Yan, Anjier Chen
Abstract: Perceptions of motivation play a critical role in shaping workplace treatment, yet little is known about how such perceptions are socially constructed. Drawing on social exchange theories and perspectives on interdependent versus independent self, we propose an ethnic-stereotype perspective of perceived motivation, suggesting that Asian employees are perceived as having higher controlled motivation-being driven by external pressures and expectations rather than personal volition-which leads supervisors to anticipate greater conformity from Asian employees and subsequently exploit them. Across one experiment (Study 1), one multiwave survey (Study 2), and one preregistered experiment with a behavioral measure (Study 3a), we consistently found that Asian employees were perceived as having higher controlled motivation compared to White and Black employees, leading to greater anticipated conformity and exploitation. A second preregistered experiment (Study 3b), in which we directly manipulated perceived controlled motivation, provided causal evidence that higher perceived controlled motivation increased exploitation through anticipated conformity, whereas lower perceived controlled motivation reversed this effect relative to a neutral baseline. We conclude by discussing theoretical implications for research on workplace mistreatment, Asian employees' work experiences, and motivation. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

Title: Resocialization as a lens to understanding workplace reentry transitions: An integrative conceptual review.
Authors: Jamie J. Ladge, Gabriel R. Sala, Audrey L. Holm
Abstract: Workplace reentry affects millions of workers annually, with over 15 million Americans supported by the Family and Medical Leave Act in 2024 alone. Yet research remains fragmented across contexts and lacks theoretical coherence. This integrative conceptual review synthesizes 264 articles spanning diverse reentry contexts following career breaks or leaves of absence, including family, medical, military redeployment, unemployment, retirement, sabbaticals, expatriation, and incarceration. We develop a unified theoretical framework grounded in resocialization theory that addresses the unique complexity of workplace reentry, where individuals must simultaneously unlearn outdated information, update existing knowledge, and navigate changed relationships while managing their dual insider-outsider status-processes fundamentally different from newcomer socialization. Our framework includes a five-stage recursive process: anticipatory resocialization, encountering, coping, assimilating, and evaluation. Four contextual factors-societal expectations, workplace practices, professional resources, and personal circumstances-influence all stages. We provide a comprehensive research agenda emphasizing stage-specific priorities while also noting important methodological challenges and opportunities. As the workforce becomes increasingly diverse and work-life integration more complex, understanding workplace reentry transitions is essential for advancing research and practice in the hopes of influencing organizational success and individual well-being. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

Title: Reciprocal relationships between personality traits and job satisfaction? A continuous time approach with two investigations.
Authors: Kaili Yu, Wen-Dong Li, Weiwen Yang, Yanglei Zheng, Zhen Zhang, Christian Dormann, Huanxi Zhang, Hannes Zacher
Abstract: > 2,000). Convergent results demonstrated that within-person changes in job satisfaction were positively related to subsequent changes in conscientiousness and emotional stability, and increases in these two traits were associated with subsequent increases in job satisfaction. Sample characteristics and job contexts moderated the within-person relationships between job satisfaction and personality traits. The magnitudes of the socialization effects of job satisfaction on personality traits and the selection effects of personality traits on job satisfaction evolved in an inverted U-shaped manner across long and intermediate timescales. Our findings highlight reciprocal within-person relationships between job satisfaction and personality traits and the important role of time in shaping these effects. Title: Transformational leadership in context: A meta-analysis of 40 years of research.
Authors: Dustin Maneethai, Robert Eisenberger, Thomas Rockstuhl, Dongyuan Wu, Blaine A. Lewis
Abstract: = 200,732), we meta-analytically assess whether TFL's foundational assumptions of generalizability hold or whether its use and effectiveness depend on broader contextual features. Results show that while TFL continues to positively predict attitudinal (e.g., commitment, trust) and performance (e.g., task, creative) outcomes, significant contextual differences exist. Specifically, TFL levels and effects vary by occupational (i.e., leader position and job type), cultural, and temporal contexts, with mixed support for compensation versus congruence perspectives. Notably, moderator effects vary across outcome domains, with occupational and cultural moderators exerting stronger effects on attitudinal outcomes than on performance outcomes. These patterns suggest that the mechanisms underlying TFL effects differ across outcome domains and challenge the assumption that transformational leaders universally motivate followers to go beyond expectations. These findings extend TFL theory by clarifying its boundary conditions and highlighting the importance of integrating omnibus contextual features into TFL models. Practically, our study informs evidence-based leadership development by underscoring that transformational approaches are not universally applicable and require contextual tailoring to maximize their effectiveness. Title: Understanding the intersection of gender and cognitive ability on interpersonal outcomes: A multistudy investigation.
Authors: Nitya Chawla, Trevor M. Spoelma, Seo-Hyun Kwon, Allison S. Gabriel, Aleksander P. J. Ellis, Wen Wu
Abstract: lowered communality by their peers; these perceptions, in turn, are theorized to be associated with greater levels of victimization and lower levels of received task- and person-focused help from teammates. Across two multisource studies comprised of 826 individuals nested within 140 work groups, utilizing objective cognitive ability ratings and a mixture of round robin and self-report data, results demonstrated the detrimental interpersonal ramifications associated with higher cognitive ability for women but not for men. Our results paint an important, and difficult, picture for higher cognitive ability women, highlighting several theoretical issues that warrant further investigation and practical challenges to be addressed by organizations. Title: From road to rage: Why commute demands are associated with interpersonal counterproductive work behaviors (and what to do about it).
Authors: Jake Gale, Trevor A. Foulk, Amir Erez, Satish Krishnan, Hae-Lyeng Rose Kim, Binyamin Cooper
Abstract: Previous literature on commute demands, or the presence of stressors during a commute, has largely concluded that affective processes do not account for the impact of commuting on employees' work behavior. In this article, we challenge this conclusion by showing that when the specific affective state aligned with the distinctive characteristics of commute demands is identified, it spills over into counterproductive work behaviors. Based on core affect theory (Russell, 2003), we propose that commute demands are specifically linked to irritability, a negative, high-arousal affective state without a clear, identifiable cause. We further posit that elevated morning irritability will be associated with higher levels of interpersonal counterproductive work behaviors during the workday. In a field-experimental experience sampling study, where we captured naturally occurring commute demands daily, we found support for these relationships. Further, we consider two interventions, listening to relaxing music and perspective taking, to weaken the indirect effect of commute demands on interpersonal counterproductive work behaviors via irritability. We found evidence that listening to relaxing music after commuting to work weakens the positive association between commute demands and irritability. Overall, these findings show that in contrast to previous assertions, demanding commutes spill into negative affective states and, in turn, to behaviors at work. However, there is a quick, low-cost way to mitigate these associations. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

Title: Acknowledgment
A “bad beta, good beta” anatomy of currency risk premiums and trading strategies
Authors: I-Hsuan Ethan Chiang, Xi Nancy Mo
Affiliations: Finance Department, University of North Carolina at Charlotte, Charlotte, NC 28277
Abstract: Abstract The article introduces a novel two-beta currency pricing model, which decomposes the conventional dollar factor beta into a beta with risk-premium news and a beta with real-interest-rate news. These betas capture distinct features of currency returns and explain cross-sectional variations in currency risk premiums. The risk-premium beta is associated with an unconditionally positive price of risk, while the real-rate beta has an unconditionally negative price of risk due to precautionary savings. The prices of these beta risks exhibit conditional variations tied to economic conditions. Furthermore, the model explains the abnormal performance of various currency trading strategies.

Title: Retail limit orders
Authors: Amber Anand, Mehrdad Samadi, Jonathan Sokobin, Kumar Venkataraman
Affiliations: Whitman School of Management, Syracuse University, Syracuse, NY, USA; Rutgers Business School, Rutgers University, Newark, NJ, USA; FINRA, Washington D.C., USA; Cox School of Business, Southern Methodist University, Dallas, TX, USA
Abstract: Abstract Using a large sample of orders from nineteen active US retail brokers, we analyze retail traders’ use of marketable and limit orders, brokers’ order handling practices, and order execution quality. Limit orders play a significant role in retail trading, accounting for 25.5 percent of orders and 30 percent of submitted shares. They incur lower trading costs than marketable orders: a result robust to controls for differences across stocks, order placement time, order size, trade direction, and brokerages. Retail limit orders are often placed behind the best quotes, stay open longer, and have higher fill rates than previously reported in market-level statistics. Overall, limit orders help retail traders reduce trading costs by being patient and supplying liquidity in the current market structure.

Title: The Bin Packing Problem with Setups: Formulations, structural properties and computational insights
Authors: Roberto Baldacci, Fabio Ciccarelli, Valerio Dose, Stefano Coniglio, Fabio Furini

Title: Understanding multi-level dynamics in rural entrepreneurial ecosystems: A conceptual framework and research agenda
Authors: Ana Joana Candeias Fernandes, João J. Ferreira, Luís Farinha
Abstract: Rural regions occupy vast territories and often exhibit spatial dispersion, limited institutional support, constrained resources, and scarce market opportunities. Yet entrepreneurial activity develops under these conditions. This coexistence creates a theoretical puzzle for entrepreneurial ecosystem (EE) research, as rural EE operate despite several conditions commonly associated with effective ecosystem functioning being comparatively weak or dispersed. We conduct a bibliometric–systematic review of 71 articles on rural EE, identifying four thematic clusters and synthesizing them into a multi-level conceptual framework and eight research propositions. Grounded in complex adaptive systems theory and informed by a multi-level mechanisms perspective, we conceptualize rural EE as compensatory cross-level systems operating under conditions of structural thinness. We theorize that structural thinness changes the functional logic of EE as available ecosystem elements assume broader, more interdependent, and compensatory roles. Whereas denser EE, often associated with urban environments, may rely comparatively more on abundant and specialized ecosystem elements, rural EE functioning becomes relatively more dependent on adaptive alignment. We conceptualize adaptive alignment as an emergent system-level mechanism through which ecosystem elements continually adjust their roles and relationships via recurring processes of coordination, feedback, resource recombination, and mutual adjustment across analytical levels. Adaptive alignment sustains rural EE functioning, thereby supporting entrepreneurial activity and shaping regional value creation. By theorizing that structural thinness changes not merely the availability of ecosystem elements but the functional logic through which they become connected and collectively sustain ecosystem functioning, we extend the boundary conditions of prevailing EE explanations and inform more context-sensitive research, policy, and practice in rural regions worldwide.

Title: From incidents to outcomes: consumer reactions and firm responses to negative environmental and social practices
Authors: Zhanbing Xiao, Xin Zheng, Yuxiang Zheng
Abstract: We examine how negative environmental and social (E&S) incidents affect consumer behavior and firms’ responses. Using high-frequency store-visit data from SafeGraph linked to firm E&S incidents from RepRisk, we find that negative incidents lead to a modest decline in store visits on average, with substantially larger reductions among more environmentally and socially conscious consumers in Democratic-leaning areas. The effects are stronger for more severe and influential incidents, among younger and more educated consumers, for firms with higher pre-incident advertising intensity and E&S ratings, and in more competitive markets. Following these incidents, firms temporarily reduce discretionary disclosures and increase advertising expenditures over the longer run. Together, the results highlight consumer behavior as a way in which E&S incidents affect firm cash flows and suggest that firms adjust disclosure and advertising following these incidents.

Title: Controlling perceived competitive balance in sports leagues through scheduling
Authors: Estéfano B. Vassoler, Pedro O.S. Vaz-de-Melo
Abstract: This paper investigates how scheduling influences the perceived competitive balance in sports leagues. By analyzing 1,236 seasons across 172 professional leagues in basketball, handball, soccer, and volleyball, we observe that a tournament’s behaviour eventually diverges from what would be expected from a perfectly balanced tournament. We propose novel heuristic algorithms that leverage team rankings to control this divergence. Our findings demonstrate that these heuristics can significantly extend the period of perceived competitive balance in a large majority of the tournaments analyzed, potentially enhancing audience engagement and complementing existing strategies for maintaining interest throughout the season.

Title: Integer linear programming formulations for a multiple bin size dual bin packing problem to optimize wood reuse
Authors: Pauline Bessemans, Célia Paquay, Morgane Dumont
Abstract: We consider the two-stage two-dimensional multiple bin size dual bin packing problem applied to wood reuse optimization. Unsplittable wooden slats are assembled into strips of minimum length to build as many wooden panels of different sizes as possible. The dual bin packing problem is also known in the literature as the bin covering problem. Moreover, we study a one-dimensional simplification of the problem where the wooden slats can be split over two strips, which is a variable-sized bin covering problem. This article proposes an extensive literature review of the closest cutting and packing problems and some methods used to solve them, in addition to a binary linear formulation and an arc-flow formulation for both versions of the problem. Computational experiments are performed on realistic field data to assess the impact of the cuts proposed and to compare the formulations with respect to the proportion of wood reused, the runtimes, and the gaps of the solution after the given time limit. The arc-flow formulation for the two-dimensional dual bin packing problem achieves the best performance overall, although it is sensitive to the input data because of its pseudo-polynomial complexity.

Title: Dynamic programming for exact time-slot scheduling within heuristic routing: A matheuristic for the multi-profit orienteering problem
Authors: Farouk Hammami

Title: The Welfare Effects of Price Shocks and Household Relief Packages: Evidence from an Energy Crisis
Authors: Peter Levell, Martin O'Connell, Kate Smith

Title: Noisy Global Value Chains
Authors: Ha Bui, Zhen Huo, Andrei Levchenko, Nitya Pandalai-Nayar

Title: Daddy’s Girl: Daughters, Managerial Decisions, and Gender Inequality
Authors: Maddalena Ronchi, Nina Smith
Affiliations: Northwestern University, CESifo, and IZA , USA; Aarhus University and IZA , Denmark
Abstract: Abstract Using Danish registry data, we study how managers’ gender attitudes shape gender inequality in the workplace by exploiting the birth of a daughter—as opposed to a son—as a plausibly exogenous shock to male managers’ gender attitudes. Comparing within-firm changes in women’s labour outcomes depending on the gender of the manager’s newborn child, we find that women’s relative earnings and employment increase by 4.4% and 2.9%, respectively, following the birth of the manager’s first daughter. These effects are driven by an increase in managers’ propensity to substitute male hires with female hires that have comparable education, hours worked, and earnings. Consistent with this substitution channel, we do not detect any significant effect on firm performance. Because these effects emerge rapidly and persist over time, we can rule out the need for prolonged exposure to gender issues or for personal incentives tied to improving conditions for their own daughters as prerequisites for managers to promote gender equality within their firms.

Title: Exploring the Dark Side of the Coopetition Paradox: Unintentional Knowledge Leakage, Capital Structure, and Organizational Decline in Small‐Firm Coopetition
Authors: Tatbeeq Raza‐Ullah, Saouré Kouamé, Baback Yazdani
Affiliations: Nottingham Business School; Telfer School of Management
Abstract: Abstract While paradox theory's generative view implicitly assumes that actors possess the agency to navigate contradictory pursuits productively, an emerging dark‐side perspective suggests that power relations and material constraints may transform such pursuits into pragmatic paradoxes. Building on this perspective, we explore how constrained paradox navigation manifests in behavioural dysfunction and contributes to organizational decline. We study this process in small‐firm coopetition, where boundary‐spanning managers experience the paradoxical tension of coopetition while juggling persistent, contradictory demands. We propose that this tension is positively associated with unintentional knowledge leakage (UKL), a boundary‐regulation failure whereby managers inadvertently disclose sensitive knowledge to a competing partner. In turn, UKL relates to organizational decline, thereby mediating the tension–decline relationship, while capital structure (financial leverage) amplifies the tension–UKL association. Using survey and archival data from 236 Swedish small technology‐manufacturing firms, we find support for these relationships. We advance paradox theory by identifying boundary‐regulation failure as a distinct dark‐side dysfunction and financial leverage as a material boundary condition that exacerbates the constraining effects of paradox navigation. We also reorient coopetition research from intentional partner appropriation toward inadvertent disclosure by the focal firm's own managers. Practically, we highlight the importance of financial resilience in preserving managers' discretion when navigating coopetition's dark side.

Title: Rigorous Engaged Scholarship
Authors: Amanda Williams, Ali Aslan Gümüşay, Andrew J. Hoffman
Affiliations: Emlyon Business School; LMU Munich and Humboldt Institute for Internet & Society Berlin; University of Michigan
Abstract: Abstract Scholars are increasingly asked to address societal grand challenges. Yet forms of scholarship that pursue these aims through engagement with practice are often treated with suspicion. In this Point, we intend to zoom in on this paradox. We argue that engaged scholarship requires rethinking what it means to be rigorous when working closely with practitioners. We advance this conversation by defining a novel set of six principles to guide its rigor: articulating positionality, orienting prospectively, collaborating critically, experimenting systematically, appearing visibly, and reflecting inwardly. These principles enhance current norms in management studies regarding knowledge production, leading us to suggest how the institutional environment will need to change to support rigorous engaged scholarship.

Title: Dynamic Principal-Agent Problem in Queueing Systems with Customer Abandonment
Authors: Tan Yu, Tiaojun Xiao, Xiang Zhong, Xiaohan Zhu
Abstract: Service systems in which demand, congestion, and worker incentives evolve jointly are ubiquitous in modern operations. We study a dynamic principal–agent problem in a queueing system with customer abandonment, where the principal controls arrivals through pricing and the agent privately chooses a costly service rate. Modeling workload as a controlled reflected diffusion, we characterize the centralized and decentralized Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equations and construct a representative two-part contract consisting of an access charge and a completion payment. Under unrestricted transfers, the contract coordinates pricing and service to attain the first-best joint payoff. Whenever participation is feasible, it makes the agent's participation constraint bind and allocates the remaining surplus to the principal. Implementation is robust to misspecification of the service-rate function used by the principal. We also establish conditions under which the representative payment schedules are nonmonotone in workload. Extensions consider multiple agents, general patience distributions, and information disclosure in a reduced Bayesian-persuasion benchmark. Numerical examples illustrate how the effects of customer impatience on optimal pricing and service can vary with congestion.

Title: Digital platforms meet artificial intelligence: Implications for POM research and practice
Authors: Edward Anderson, Nitin Joglekar, Sunil Mithas, Geoffrey Parker, Yinliang (Ricky) Tan
Affiliations: The University of Texas at Austin; Villanova University; University of South Florida; Dartmouth College; China Europe International Business School (CEIBS)
Abstract: Digital platforms are changing how firms design, coordinate, and govern operations by integrating artificial intelligence, blockchain, digital sensing and digital twins, data infrastructure, and additive manufacturing. This article develops a forward-looking research agenda for production and operations management by distinguishing enabling technologies from the platforms, workflows, and business models through which they are deployed. We organize the agenda around a sequence linking technological capability, operational manifestation, mechanism, outcomes, and boundary conditions. The relevant mechanisms include prediction, information visibility, verification, orchestration, monitoring, human override, and decision rights. We articulate how these mechanisms may create operational value through improvements in productivity, quality, responsiveness, resilience, compliance, and customer experience, enabling firms to capture financial value through revenue growth, cost reduction, risk avoidance, and improved asset utilization. We identify enduring operations management themes that emerging technologies may reshape, and develop five forward-looking paths involving artificial intelligence-enabled business-to-business platforms, physical–digital integration, agentic service workflows, data and artificial intelligence governance, and platform-enabled resilience under geopolitical disruption. Finally, we discuss theoretical and methodological approaches that can support cumulative research.

Title: Benefits of extreme political stability and instability of supplier countries for firms: The U-shaped relationship
Authors: Jafar Namdar, Sachin Modi, Arash Azadegan, Milad Baghersad
Affiliations: Michigan State University; University of Cincinnati; The State University of New Jersey; Florida Atlantic University
Abstract: Using a large-scale panel dataset of U.S. buyer firms and their global supplier networks from 2010 to 2020, we examine how global political instability (GPI), a firm's weighted exposure to political instability across the countries where its international suppliers operate, is associated with firm performance. We find a U-shaped relationship: buyer firm performance is highest when a firm's overall sourcing exposure reflects either very low or very high levels of GPI. At the low-GPI end, the results align with transaction-cost economics, as political stability is associated with lower uncertainty and fewer coordination frictions. At the very high-GPI end, we identify bargaining power as a key mechanism: buyers exposed to politically unstable supplier countries exhibit greater bargaining power and more favorable contractual terms, particularly favorable trade credit, which may partially offset the costs of political instability. We further show that this nonlinear relationship varies across industries. It is more pronounced in productive industries, where buyers have greater bargaining power to negotiate favorable trade credit and lower switching costs to reallocate sourcing during periods of political instability. However, it is flatter in durable-goods industries, where asset specificity and higher switching costs are associated with weaker bargaining power and a more limited ability to secure favorable trade credit from suppliers in politically unstable countries. Finally, we document an important managerial trade-off: while higher exposure to unstable supplier countries is associated with improved performance, it is also associated with more negative media coverage related to supply chain issues and ethical risks. Our results remain robust across multiple complementary identification strategies, strengthening confidence that the documented nonlinear effect and its underlying mechanism are not driven by spurious correlations or a single empirical approach.

Title: An Exploratory Analysis of Variation in Payback Periods of Emissions Reduction Projects Using CDP Disclosures
Authors: Christian C. Blanco, Felipe Caro, Charles J. Corbett
Abstract: Firms continue to engage in projects to reduce their greenhouse gas emissions. Based on their disclosures to CDP, many such projects have relatively short payback periods of 2-3 years. Earlier work by Blanco et al. (2020) found that payback periods appeared stable over time between 2010-2016. The current paper extends that work in several directions: by using a substantially longer time horizon, and exploring several factors that contribute to the variation in payback periods and trends. With the longer horizon of data now available, we find that paybacks are lengthening slowly but significantly over 2010-2024, by an average of about 2 weeks per year, or approximately one half year over our 14-year horizon. Firms with greater liabilities relative to their assets report faster payback, though the effect is only marginally significant. Firms in Europe that are subject to a carbon tax or an emissions trading scheme report shorter paybacks than in the US or elsewhere. Firms that are more consumer-facing report lengthening payback periods, while upstream firms do not. This analysis is exploratory, but prior firm-level research on these effects is mixed and surprisingly limited.

Title: Bounded rationality in public healthcare competition
Authors: Yu Zhang, Hao Wu, Zhongbin Wang
Affiliations: University of Science and Technology Beijing; Dongbei University of Finance and Economics; Tianjin University
Abstract: Fiscal pressure forces public healthcare systems to reduce waiting times via hospital competition, yet patients’ bounded rationality weakens this policy. We develop a Hotelling-type queueing model that incorporates the strategic interaction between two budget-constrained public hospitals and patients with heterogeneous preferences and bounded rationality. Our analysis yields the following results. First, we show that bounded rationality can incentivize hospitals to increase service rates, thereby alleviating congestion and leading to an inverted-U relationship between patient welfare and the degree of bounded rationality. Moreover, the effect of bounded rationality on hospital revenue is also non-monotonic: when the capacity constraint is tight and the budget is sufficiently high, hospital revenue may be maximized at an intermediate level of bounded rationality rather than under full rationality. Second, higher reimbursement does not necessarily enhance patient welfare; instead, we identify an optimal reimbursement level that rises with the available public budget. Third, extending the framework to a multi-hospital environment within a Salop model shows that total market share, patient welfare, and hospital revenue are all maximized at a moderate level of competition. Overall, from a managerial perspective, healthcare managers should carefully account for patients’ bounded rationality when designing capacity and information disclosure policies. Meanwhile, excessive hospital expansion may undermine both operational efficiency and financial sustainability. We further confirm the robustness of our main insights under alternative objectives (profit maximization and social welfare), systematic bias, heterogeneous hospital objectives, and other cost specifications.

Title: The Digital Journey of Health Insurance Marketing: Narrative Ads and Product Page Design
Authors: Yin Bai, Rui Wang, Xingyao Ren, Rajdeep Grewal
Affiliations: College of Management and Economics, Tianjin University, Tianjin 300072, China; Guanghua School of Management, Peking University, Beijing 100871, China; Business School, Nankai University, Tianjin 300071, China; Kenan-Flagler Business School, The University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, Chapel Hill, North Carolina 27599
Abstract: Selling health insurance through digital advertising is fundamentally different from selling most consumer products online: health insurance protects against abstract future risks, and regulatory constraints prohibit transactions from closing on third-party platforms, forcing consumers to transition from the ad platform to the insurer’s own product page. We examine how aligning narrative ad content with product page design sustains persuasion across this mandatory handoff. In a randomized field experiment with a leading Chinese insurer on Douyin, we study 335 ads that generated nearly 17 million impressions and 777,412 click-throughs. Users who clicked were randomly routed to either a fact-based product page or one incorporating a customer experience exemplar. Purchase conversion rises most when narrative ads are paired with the exemplar page, increasing from 1.51% to 2.05%, implying roughly 8,400 additional policies per month at campaign scale. Neither element is effective in isolation. A causal mediation analysis confirms that sustained engagement on the product page accounts for more than 80% of the total effect. To address algorithm-driven selection in ad delivery and self-selection into clicking, we employ a sequential endogeneity correction strategy and confirm robustness with causal forests. Aligning ad design with product page design significantly improves conversion in regulated digital markets. History: Catherine Tucker served as the senior editor. Funding: X. Title: Rethinking Distribution Shifts: Empirical Analysis and Modeling for Tabular Data
Authors: Tianyu Wang, Jiashuo Liu, Peng Cui, Hongseok Namkoong
Affiliations: Department of Industrial Engineering and Operations Research, Columbia University, New York, New York 10027; Department of Computer Science and Technology, Tsinghua University, Beijing 100190, China; Decision, Risk, and Operations Division, Columbia University, New York, New York 10027
Abstract: Different distribution shifts require different interventions, and algorithms must be grounded in the specific shifts they address. However, methodological development for robust algorithms typically relies on structural assumptions that lack empirical validation. Advocating for an empirically grounded data-driven approach to algorithm development, we build an empirical testbed comprising natural shifts across 8 tabular data sets, 172 distribution pairs over 45 methods, and 90,000 method configurations encompassing empirical risk minimization and distributionally robust optimization (DRO) methods. We find that Y|X-shifts are most prevalent in our testbed, in stark contrast to the heavy focus on X (covariate)-shifts in the machine learning literature, and that the performance of robust algorithms is no better than that of vanilla methods. To understand why, we conduct an in-depth empirical analysis of DRO methods and find that underlooked implementation details—such as the choice of underlying model class (e.g., LightGBM) and hyperparameter selection—have a bigger impact on performance than the ambiguity set or its radius. We illustrate via case studies how a data-driven understanding of distribution shifts can provide a new approach to algorithm development. This paper was accepted by Wolfram Wiesemann, data science. Title: The Economics of Waste Valorization
Authors: Yuefeng Li, Zhongbin Wang, Shenghai Zhou
Affiliations: School of Economics and Management, University of Electronic Science and Technology of China, Chengdu 611731, China; College of Management and Economics, Tianjin University, Tianjin 300072, China; School of Business, Central South University, Changsha, Hunan 410083, China; and Laboratory of Intelligent Governance for Complex Social Systems, Changsha, Hunan 410083, China
Abstract: As the spread of waste imposes substantial environmental and economic burdens, a newer operational strategy, waste valorization, is gaining attention. This approach transforms production-generated byproduct waste into valuable, distinct products, creating intricate production and demand interdependencies that traditional strategies like remanufacturing and coproduction cannot fully capture. In this study, we examine the impacts of these interdependencies within a two-stage stochastic production decision model to determine optimal production quantities under waste valorization. Our findings reveal that a higher waste valorization rate does not always benefit the manufacturer, especially if the waste incurs disposal costs. When product demands are uncorrelated, the manufacturer’s optimal profit can exhibit an inverse U-shaped relationship with the valorization rate, attaining its maximum at a moderate level that maintains a perfect balance in production. Conversely, when product demands are correlated, the manufacturer employs a “pool-to-center” strategy, using different pooling policies to smooth production quantities and minimize disparities with respect to the valorization rate. Surprisingly, as demand randomness or correlation intensifies, the optimal profit becomes M-shaped, with profit maximum shifting toward either low or high valorization rates, a phenomenon we term “go-to-extreme.” Although waste valorization can yield both economic and environmental benefits, we caution that a more efficient waste valorization process may lead to negative outcomes for both the manufacturer and the environment. This analysis not only sheds light on how waste valorization contributes to waste reduction and economic value, but also provides insights for production decision making. This paper was accepted by Caroline Flammer, sustainability. Title: The Data-Driven Censored Newsvendor Problem
Authors: Chamsi Hssaine, Sean R. Sinclair
Affiliations: Department of Data Sciences and Operations, University of Southern California, Marshall School of Business, Los Angeles, California 90089; Department of Industrial Engineering and Management Sciences, Northwestern University, Evanston, Illinois 60208
Abstract: We study a censored variant of the data-driven newsvendor problem, where the decision maker must select an ordering quantity that minimizes expected overage and underage costs based only on offline censored sales data rather than historical demand realizations. Our goal is to understand how the degree of historical demand censoring affects the performance of any learning algorithm for this problem. To isolate this impact, we adopt a distributionally robust optimization framework, evaluating policies according to their worst-case regret over an ambiguity set of distributions. This set is defined by the largest historical order quantity (the observable boundary of the data set), and contains all distributions matching the true demand distribution up to this boundary while allowing them to be arbitrary afterward. We demonstrate a spectrum of achievability under demand censoring by deriving a natural necessary and sufficient condition under which vanishing regret is an achievable goal. In regimes in which it is not, we exactly characterize the information loss due to censoring: an insurmountable lower bound on the performance of any policy, even when the decision maker has access to infinitely many demand samples. We then leverage these sharp characterizations to propose a natural robust algorithm that adapts to the historical level of demand censoring. We derive finite-sample guarantees for this algorithm across all possible censoring regimes and show its near-optimality with matching lower bounds (up to polylogarithmic factors). We moreover demonstrate its robust performance via extensive numerical experiments on both synthetic and real-world data sets. This paper was accepted by Wolfram Wiesemann, data science. Title: Insurers’ Investments and Insurance Prices
Authors: Benjamin Knox, Jakob Ahm Sørensen
Affiliations: Division of International Finance, Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, Washington, District of Columbia 20551; Finance Department, Bocconi University, Milan 20136, Italy
Abstract: We develop a theory in which stable funding from insurance underwriting allows insurers to earn the liquidity premium on illiquid assets and pass part of it back to policyholders through lower prices. Consistent with the model’s predictions, we show empirically that (1) insurance prices are lower when the liquidity premium is higher, for both life insurers and property and casualty insurers. (2) In the cross-section, insurers with more stable funding earn higher expected returns and set lower prices. (3) It is specifically the part of expected returns driven by stable funding that passes through to prices. The findings highlight the value of insurance underwriting as a stable source of funding, with benefits that flow back to policyholders. This paper was accepted by Bo Becker, finance. Title: What’s at Stake? Understanding the Role of Home Equity in Flood Insurance Demand
Authors: Yanjun (Penny) Liao, Philip Mulder
Affiliations: Resources for the Future, Washington, District of Columbia 20036; Department of Risk and Insurance, University of Wisconsin–Madison, Madison, Wisconsin 53715
Abstract: Changing flood insurance demand shifts climate risk across homeowners, lenders, and governments. We show that flood insurance take-up follows rising and falling home equity over the housing boom and bust across markets with different price dynamics. To isolate the causal effect of risk shifting on insurance demand, we study flood insurance policy renewals over the housing bust, exploiting granular differences in purchase timing that led policyholders to experience differential changes in skin-in-the-game exposure to flood risk for the same change in home equity. When homeowners have less equity exposure to flood losses, they are less likely to renew their policies. Lenders, in turn, have little incentive to require flood insurance when they can sell their mortgages to federally backed mortgage purchasers. This paper was accepted by Tomasz Piskorski, finance. Title: Banking on a Corporate Rebrand
Authors: Matthew Jaremski, Kris James Mitchener, Kilian Rieder
Affiliations: Department of Economics and Finance, Huntsman School of Business, Utah State University & NBER, Logan, Utah 84322; Department of Economics, Leavey School of Business, Santa Clara University, NBER, CEPR, CESifo & CAGE, Santa Clara, California 95053; Economics and Research Department, Oesterreichische Nationalbank (Eurosystem) & CEPR, Vienna 1090, Austria
Abstract: Firms often rebrand to counter negative shocks, but can it work? Using a historical natural experiment, we analyze a large sample of companies from the same industry (banking) that shared very similar names, but overwhelmingly decided to change them in response to a common, negative news shock. U.S. entry into World War I in 1917 created a sudden anti-German backlash against anything that invoked an association with the now enemy. The shock itself was thus orthogonal to bank fundamentals and pre-existing trends, but pushed banks to reconsider their brands. After 1917, the few German-named banks that kept their tainted names saw significant declines in assets, deposits, and market share relative to other banks. However, German-named banks that rebranded mitigated much of the negative shock. Specifically, German-named banks that adopted a new non-ethnic brand name avoided between 75% and 85% of the anti-German effect, and those that adopted a new patriotic brand name were able to neutralize it completely. Overall, we find that “crisis rebranding” paid off in our historical setting regardless of the chosen brand, with patriotic rebranding proving the most effective at offsetting the exogenous shock. Title: Comparing Factor Models Under Regime Switching
Authors: Shamim Ahmed, Cesare Robotti, Daniel Tsvetanov, Xiaoxia Ye
Affiliations: University of Liverpool Management School, University of Liverpool, Liverpool L69 7ZH, United Kingdom; Warwick Business School, University of Warwick, Coventry CV4 7AL, United Kingdom; Norwich Business School, University of East Anglia, Norwich NR4 7TJ, United Kingdom; Nottingham University Business School, University of Nottingham, Nottingham NG8 1BB, United Kingdom
Abstract: We compare factor pricing models using the “test-asset irrelevance” result but under regime switching. We show that the unconditional squared Sharpe ratio measure is no longer appropriate for model comparison when returns are subject to regime shifts. However, conditional on a given regime, model comparison can be performed using the conditional squared Sharpe ratio metric. We find that the Fama-French six-factor model that employs a cash-based profitability factor, the Barillas-Shanken six-factor model, and the Stambaugh-Yuan four-factor model are jointly the best-performing models under the bull regime. However, no model performs significantly better than others under the bear regime. Importantly, these findings are robust to regime uncertainty. We also find that unconditional model rankings closely mirror those in bull markets, overstating the superiority of the models identified as best performing in expansions by ignoring the performance convergence across models that emerges in downturns. This underscores the importance of evaluating factor models conditional on market regimes. This paper was accepted by Lukas Schmid, finance. Title: Who Will be Assigned Unreasonable Tasks by Supervisors: A Conjoint Survey Experiment
Authors: Haien Ding, Bård Kuvaas
Affiliations: Business School The University of Edinburgh Edinburgh UK; Department of Leadership and Organizational Behavior BI Norwegian Business School Oslo Norway
Abstract: ABSTRACT Supervisors sometimes assign employees tasks that employees may perceive as unreasonable because they fall outside their formal job duties. Prior research has mostly focused on the negative effects of unreasonable tasks on employee outcomes, without examining the fundamental question of who is more likely to be assigned such tasks by their supervisors. To answer this question, we examined three distinct logics underlying the assignment of unreasonable tasks based on employee attributes (i.e., age, gender, task performance, helping behavior, recent workload, and relationship closeness): stereotype‐driven logic, efficiency‐driven logic, and exchange‐driven logic. In a fully randomized conjoint survey experiment, we asked 464 supervisors to allocate an unreasonable task based on evaluations of 4640 hypothetical employee profiles, with profiles varying randomly on six employee attributes. Results show that supervisors are more likely to assign unreasonable tasks to younger employees who perform better on tasks, exhibit more helping behavior, currently have lighter workloads, and maintain closer relationships with their supervisor. The relatively stronger effects of employees' recent workload, task performance, and helping behavior suggest that the efficiency‐driven logic plays the most influential role in shaping supervisors' unreasonable task assignments. We discuss the theoretical, methodological, and practical implications of our findings.

Authors: Zebiao Feng, Weidong Huang, Yizhong Ma, Jianjun Wang

Title: How interval-dependent profits affect team orienteering problems with two visits
Authors: Jiaojiao Li, Jianjiang Wang, Jianghan Zhu, Zhe Liang, Kai Yang, Zeqiang Hou
Abstract: Motivated by real-world applications such as earth observation satellite scheduling and perishable goods delivery, this study investigates a variant of the Team Orienteering Problem (TOP) in which each customer requires two visits and the collected profit depends on the inter-visit interval. Unlike existing studies that mainly rely on fixed profits or simplified representations, a stepwise interval-dependent profit function is proposed to explicitly capture the relationship between inter-visit intervals and collected profits. Based on this setting, a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) formulation is developed for the proposed problem. To efficiently solve the resulting problem, this study proposes the Profit-Guided Greedy Randomized Iterated Local Search (PG-GRILS), a structured extension of GRILS that explicitly accounts for paired-visit dependency and interval-dependent profit structures. The proposed framework consists of three interacting components: a UCB-guided multi-heuristic initialization mechanism for generating diversified initial solutions, a problem-specific perturbation and repair mechanism for reconstructing paired visits, and a temporal refinement mechanism for further optimizing service schedules and temporal profit allocation. Extensive computational experiments show that PG-GRILS consistently obtains high-quality solutions and outperforms baseline algorithms on a wide range of benchmark instances. Additional neighborhood structure analysis, temporal refinement analysis, and initialization strategy analysis provide useful insights into the structural characteristics of the problem and further support the effectiveness of the proposed framework.

Title: When shifts matter for hybrid teams: The moderating role of location predictability.
Authors: Trevor M. Spoelma, Daniel M. Ravid, Ke Michael Mai, Yuan Jiang

Title: From patient to purpose: How a cancer diagnosis creates existential liminality to motivate crafting for work-related generativity.
Authors: Wendy J. Casper, Ariane Froidevaux, Sabrina D. Volpone, Jamie J. Ladge

Title: Aspiring to a Better Future: Can a Simple Psychological Intervention Reduce Poverty?
Authors: Kate Orkin, Robert Garlick, Mahreen Mahmud, Richard Sedlmayr, Johannes Haushofer, Stefan Dercon
Affiliations: University of Oxford; Emory University , USA; University of Exeter, U K; The Agency Fund , USA; Cornell U niversity, USA; University of Oxford , UK
Abstract: Abstract Do higher aspirations for the future motivate people living in poverty to make long-term investments? Do their aspirations increase when economic conditions improve? To answer these questions, we run a 415-village field experiment with 8,300 women living in poverty in rural Kenya. We design an 80-minute workshop to help people set higher aspirations and plan to achieve them. We cross-randomise this with large unconditional cash transfers. The workshop substantially raises aspirations, labour supply, investment, revenue, and living standards 17 months later, relative to a placebo workshop. Increases in aspirations are the most likely mechanism to explain the economic effects. Cash transfers also raise aspirations, which might help to explain why transfers increase labour supply and investment. We conclude that aspirations respond to both economic and psychological interventions, contribute to investment decisions and living standards, and are important considerations for development policy.

Title: The Impact of Commercial Real Estate Regulations on U.S. Output
Authors: Fil Babalievsky, Kyle F Herkenhoff, Lee E Ohanian, Edward C Prescott
Affiliations: Census Bureau; University of Minnesota; University of California, Los Angeles; Arizona State University
Abstract: Abstract Commercial real estate accounts for about 20% of the U.S. capital stock and is highly regulated. Yet relatively little is known about how these regulations affect economic activity or consumer welfare. This paper develops a spatial general equilibrium model of the U.S. economy with commercial real estate regulations and congestion effects, the latter providing a rationale for such regulations. The model constructs a panel of commercial real estate regulation indices for major U.S. metropolitan areas by exploiting variation in the share of parcel value attributable to land versus structures in tax assessor records compiled by Cotality. We find that a moderate relaxation of commercial real estate building regulations across U.S. cities generates large allocative efficiency gains, increasing output by 2.7% to 5.3% and welfare by 2.8% to 8.0% of lifetime consumption. We then extract the component of our regulatory indices that covaries with specific zoning attributes in LightBox data, including zoning height limits, and use it to simulate local deregulation policies. Relaxing height limits in New York City raises its output by 2.9%.

Title: Climate Risk Disclosure and Risk Sharing in Financial Markets
Authors: Kevin Smith
Abstract: Abstract In this paper, I model how climate risk disclosure impacts climate risk sharing among investors. I show that this disclosure can improve risk sharing by helping investors identify stocks that effectively hedge climate risk, and I analyze the disclosure’s impact on investors’ equilibrium portfolio choices. I then study firms’ voluntary disclosure incentives and analyze when disclosure mandates enhance risk sharing. Finally, I demonstrate that, by facilitating risk sharing, climate risk disclosure reduces the climate risk premium among stocks held by climate-focused investors. Hence, disclosure can lower the valuations of firms with low climate exposures and the overall market. (JEL: D82, D84, G12, G14)

Title: Government Guarantees and Dynamic Debt Runs
Authors: Jacopo Magnani, Yabin Wang
Affiliations: Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU) , Department of Economics
Abstract: Abstract This study quantifies the impact of public guarantees on the stability of bank wholesale funding. We study the Chinese market for negotiable certificates of deposit (NCDs) around the first bank failure in two decades, the Baoshang event, which struck investors’ belief in government guarantees on wholesale bank debt. We document a sharp increase in NCD spreads, issuance failures, and runs, with weaker banks becoming more exposed to rollover risk after the event. Using a model of dynamic debt runs, we estimate that the perceived guarantee fell from 54% of creditor losses before the event to approximately zero after the event. The decline is largest for small banks, low-rated banks, and rural commercial banks. Our structural model also allows us to compare alternative policies aimed at stabilizing creditors’ willingness to roll over short-term debt.

Title: Constant Connectivity as Everyday Practice: Theorizing Through Problematization
Authors: Matthew B. Perrigino, Roshni Raveendhran, Ji Woon Ryu
Affiliations: Baruch College; University of Virginia; Portland State University
Abstract: Abstract Despite a significant amount of research on constant connectivity , defined as the opportunity to remain connected to work at any time, from any place, we assert that there remains a disconnect between how constant connectivity is studied and how it unfolds in everyday occurrences. Using the miner‐prospector continuum, we problematize the extant literature to evaluate this assertion and develop new theory. Our mining reveals that constant connectivity studies rely on notions of time and place that insufficiently demarcate work–nonwork boundaries; prescribe constant connectivity as either wholly incompatible with enacting nonwork roles or inherently interfering with specific nonwork activities; and operationalize constant connectivity with vague ‘technology use’ constructs. In prospecting, we conceptualize constant connectivity as a set of sociomaterial practices that capture how: technology affords opportunities to engage in, and disengage from, work activity; constant connectivity and nonwork role enactment are compatible via the pursuit of work and nonwork activities in parallel or sequentially; and work–nonwork boundaries are socially constructed in ways that transcend time and place. Taken together, we extend considerations of constant connectivity beyond knowledge workers to any occupation (skilled trades; physical labour) in which individuals use technology to conduct aspects of work at any time, from any place.

Title: Explaining Coexisting Trust and Distrust Transitions: The Case of Senior Doctors in the UK NHS
Authors: Branko Božič, Stacey Bushfield, Graeme Martin
Affiliations: NEOMA Business School; Edinburgh Napier University Business School; University of Dundee School of Business
Abstract: Abstract The emergence of distrust in organizations damages working relationships and leads to poor organizational performance. We examine how senior doctors in the UK NHS transitioned from low trust/low distrust to low trust/high distrust in their managers and employer. Drawing on qualitative data from three time periods, we show, counter‐intuitively, how a positive crisis response by doctors' leaders during COVID‐19 intensified a long‐term downward trust–distrust trajectory. This response temporarily restored confidence and elevated expectations of a renewed psychological contract among doctors. When those expectations were later violated, scepticism and value incongruence grew, inciting negative expectations and a descent into distrust. We make three contributions to trust–distrust theory. First, we identify a previously unexplained pathway from coexisting low trust/low distrust to low trust/high distrust through a temporary state of high trust/low distrust. Second, we explain how ideological contract violations, perceived betrayals of core values and professional identities, drive the development of distrust. Third, we extend punctuated‐threshold explanations of distrust emergence by demonstrating that distrust can arise not only from accumulating negative experiences but also from the collapse of newly restored positive expectations. This has broader implications for the leadership of change, particularly the management of hope and expectations during crisis.

Title: Spatial Competition in Fast-Charging Networks
Authors: Philipp Artur Artur Kienscherf, Yixin Lu, Long He, Wolfgang Ketter
Affiliations: University of Cologne, Faculty of Management, Economics and Social Sciences, Koln, Nordrhein-Westfalen, Germany; The George Washington University, School of Business, Washington, District of Columbia, United States; University of Notre Dame Mendoza College of Business, Information Technology, Analytics, and Operations, Notre Dame, Indiana, United States
Abstract: Despite the steady growth of fast-charging networks under government subsidies, the impact of spatial and ownership structures of charging points on pricing strategies of charging point operators (CPOs) and consumer welfare is poorly understood. Given EVs’ limited range, the competition in a fast-charging network is inherently regional. It is unclear whether and under what circumstances CPOs’ competition can lead to regional monopoly, which may hinder the transition to electric mobility. In this paper, we develop a novel framework to examine the competitive dynamics in fast-charging networks that serve regional demand, incorporating delay costs arising from congestion and locational attractiveness of charging stations. At the core of our framework is a spatial competition model, which characterizes the strategic interactions between CPOs and consumers.
