Title: Board–CEO Trust and Concealing Adverse News
Authors: Kee-Hong Bae, Sadok El Ghoul, Zhaoran Gong, Omrane Guedhami, Lixin Su
Affiliations: York University; The University of Texas at El Paso; University of South Carolina
Abstract: ABSTRACT We investigate how generalized trust, a culturally rooted belief in the trustworthiness of unfamiliar others, influences board oversight. Using an ancestry-based measure of board–CEO trust based on ancestral origins and bilateral trust scores across countries, we find a significant positive relation between board–CEO trust and stock price crash risk, indicating higher bad-news hoarding. This relation remains robust across alternative crash risk measures, sample specifications, and trust measures. Firms with high board–CEO trust exhibit more asymmetric stock market reactions to good news versus bad news and a higher likelihood of material restatements. Analyses of insider trading patterns show that directors in high-trust firms are less informed than CEOs about adverse developments, supporting lax board monitoring rather than collusion between directors and CEOs. Overall, the evidence suggests that culturally inherited trust can weaken board oversight and reduce corporate transparency, consistent with an underexplored governance friction even within well-structured boards. Data Availability: Data used in this study are available from public sources identified in the study. JEL Classifications: G14; G34; G41; M12.

Title: Resilient drone-enabled logistics: integrating truck-and-drone planning with disruption response
Authors: Mehmet Kurt, Daniel F. Silva, Alice E. Smith

Title: Political uncertainty, social legitimacy, and nonmarket strategy
Authors: Jonathan Doh
Abstract: Abstract The Decade Award–winning article by Darendeli and Hill (2016) presents a novel yet nuanced approach to the question of whether and how foreign firms can strategically navigate a volatile and unpredictable political environment. Their 2026 retrospective builds on their earlier contribution by showing how their insights have contributed to a number of contemporary IB research streams, including those addressing political risk, political action, and political ties. Going beyond their earlier contribution, in the retrospective, they describe the relational and physical pillars of social legitimacy (Darendeli & Hill, 2026). They then assess the efficacy of their original perspective in an environment characterized by heightened geopolitical conflict and political polarization. Finally, they develop a model that delineates four strategic approaches to legitimacy building in host countries. In this commentary, I offer perspectives that complement and extend their contributions by discussing (1) the nature of political uncertainty and the use of real options in responding to that uncertainty, (2) the literature on substantive versus symbolic CSR and how that might further extend some of their insights, and (3) research regarding when and how multinational enterprises provide public goods and services typically provided by government. I conclude by outlining how Darendeli and Hill’s (2016, 2026) insights have relevance for contemporary practice and policy.

Title: Large Funds and Corporate Bond Market Fragility
Authors: Yong Chen, Mengqiao Du, Zheng Sun
Affiliations: Texas A&M University; National University of; University of California , Irvine
Abstract: Abstract The corporate bond fund industry is characterized by a high concentration of capital, with a substantial portion of assets managed by large funds. We examine the relation between large-fund trading exposure and corporate bond volatility across market conditions. Using a comprehensive sample of U.S. bond funds and corporate bonds, we show that bond return volatility decreases (increases) with trading fund size when market liquidity is high (low). Exploring the underlying mechanisms, we find that large funds are more likely to reach for yield by holding illiquid bonds. Further analysis suggests that while large funds supply liquidity during normal times, their liquidity-supplying activity weakens during market stress. Finally, large funds tend to sell illiquid bonds when facing investor outflows during illiquid markets. Overall, our findings reveal an important yet subtle relation between fund size and bond market fragility, akin to a “dam effect.” JEL Classification: G10, G12, G23

Title: Using Financial Accounting Information to Estimate the Income Shifting of US Multinationals
Authors: Scott D. Dyreng, Robert Hills, Kevin S. Markle
Affiliations: Duke University Durham North Carolina USA; University of Georgia Athens Georgia USA; Michigan State University East Lansing Michigan USA
Abstract: ABSTRACT Existing estimates of how much income US multinational corporations (MNCs) shift out of the United States differ dramatically, and most cannot identify which specific firms do the shifting. We use data from firms' public financial reports to derive firm‐year estimates of US MNCs' outbound income shifting. We find that aggregate US outbound income shifting is substantially lower than widely cited macroeconomic‐based estimates, with the gap driven primarily by double counting of foreign income in macroeconomic data rather than by differences in firms' sensitivity to tax rates. Income shifting is also highly concentrated among a small number of firms, primarily in intangible‐intensive industries such as computers and pharmaceuticals, while most MNCs shift little or no income. This concentration implies that size‐based thresholds embedded in the OECD's Pillar 2 and the US corporate alternative minimum tax will capture the most active income shifters but may also impose compliance burdens on many firms that shift minimal income. These findings have direct implications for policy‐makers designing international tax rules, tax authorities prioritizing audit resources toward high‐risk income shifters, and investors and lenders assessing MNCs' tax‐related exposures.

Title: Book Review: Wang, D. Breakneck: China’s Quest to Engineer the Future WangD. (2025). Breakneck: China’s quest to engineer the future. W. W. Norton. 288 pp. ISBN 9781324156956
Authors: Adam K. Frost
Affiliations: Assistant Professor of Entrepreneurship, University of Southern Denmark Business School, Danish Institute of Advanced Studies, Odense, Denmark

Title: The Enjoy-Able Effect: Consumer Enjoyment Inflates Self-Evaluations of Ability
Authors: Jacob D. Teeny, Daniel M. Zane, Anna Paley, Robert W. Smith
Abstract: This research establishes the enjoy-able effect . Enjoyment (whether experienced, anticipated, or relative) increases consumers’ self-evaluated ability, leading them to act more like self-perceived experts (e.g., choose more expert-targeted products) and exhibit better-than-average biases for more enjoyable activities. Two waves of archival data (Ns = 559,370 and 491,791), normed associations across 100 consumer activities (N = 397), and six experiments (Ns = 251–593) document these outcomes of consumer enjoyment, establish that they operate independently of actual ability, and provide evidence that consumers’ inferences about their ability are driven by their overgeneralization of a lay theory about the relationship between enjoyment and expertise. The enjoy-able effect therefore depends on the diagnosticity of enjoyment as an input to subjective expertise, relative to other accessible inputs. Accordingly, this work highlights when and for whom other accessible inputs (e.g., an alternate lay theory associating effort and expertise) reduce reliance on the “enjoyment = expertise” lay theory. Overall, this research documents a previously unrecognized influence of enjoyment on consumer behavior, offers new insights on classic theories (e.g., flow and self-determination theory), and identifies a new and robust antecedent to subjective expertise. Managerial implications for product development and promotion, consumer targeting, and gamification are discussed.

Title: So Near Yet So Far: The Unexpected Role of Near Misses for Salesperson Turnover
Authors: Arpit Agrawal, Michael Ahearne, Yashar Atefi, Johannes Habel, Mohsen Pourmasoudi, Praveen Punia
Abstract: Quota attainment is critical for salespeople because it determines their income, recognition, and career progression. Accordingly, salespeople who frequently fail to meet quota may become more inclined to turn over and try their luck elsewhere. However, not all quota failures carry the same weight. Drawing on the expected utility model of turnover, we argue that salespeople who repeatedly miss quota by a narrow margin are especially likely to turn over. This is because such near misses erode a salesperson’s confidence that they will yield valued outcomes in their current job while increasing the perceived attainability of those outcomes elsewhere. We validate these predictions using a seven-year cross-industry panel of 13,277 salespeople across 44 companies, three experiments, and multiple auxiliary studies. The effect is stronger when hitting quota is more important due to high variable pay and group performance homogeneity. Furthermore, we establish expected utility of switching as the mechanism underlying these effects. Our research introduces near misses as a novel antecedent of turnover and as a new trigger that can reshape expected utilities. Furthermore, our research allows managers to implement targeted interventions to retain valuable talents, such as preventing near misses or reframing salespeople’s expected utility once near misses occur.

Title: Are Exposure Bucks Worth It? Evidence from Instagram
Authors: Daniel Goetz, Andrew T. Ching
Abstract: We estimate the benefit to creators of making collaborative posts with brands on Instagram, a feature that allows brands and creators to co-author shared posts. We link all collaborative posts from 260 leading fashion and beauty brands to a daily panel of follower counts for small-to-mid-tier collaborating creators, match treated and control posts on visual content, and exploit rigidity in brands' posting schedules to identify causal treatment effects in a difference-in-differences design. Collaborative posts increase a creator's cumulative follower count by 0.52% on average—roughly equivalent to one week of organic growth—with no effect on follower engagement or creators' propensity to partner with other brands. Heterogeneity analyses suggest that the primary benefit stems from audience exposure rather than quality signaling. While brands with larger follower bases yield larger gains all else being equal, they also have less engaged audiences and publish collaborative content that deviates further from creators' typical styles; as a result, treatment effects remain roughly constant across brands ranging from 0.7 to 8.6 million followers. Overall, collaborative posts provide relatively small exposure benefits to creators on average, but partnerships with brands that have highly engaged audiences and grant creative freedom deliver substantially greater value.

Title: Securing supply chains: Subsidies, insurance, and hybrid incentives under costly verification
Authors: Mohammad Nikoofal, Manaf Zargoush, Saeed Beheshti, Mehmet Gümüş, Mahsa Madani-Hosseini
Affiliations: Toronto Metropolitan University; McMaster University; McGill University
Abstract: The rising frequency of supply-chain disruptions—driven by physical shocks and cyber intrusions—underscores the need for coordinated action between governments and private firms. Firms may underinvest in security because they do not internalize the broader social losses generated by supply-chain disruptions. Public intervention is complicated, however, because firms privately know their baseline network security, choose unobservable preventive effort, and are subject to costly and imperfect verification. We develop a game-theoretic framework to compare three policy approaches: an ex-ante, audit-based subsidy; an ex-post, inspection-based insurance mechanism; and hybrid mechanisms that combine preventive support with contingent protection. Insurance performs better in lower-security environments, where incidents under shirking remain sufficiently likely for claims inspection and denied coverage to provide credible deterrence. Subsidies perform better in moderate-to-high-security environments, where pre-incident verification remains effective even as disruptions become less frequent. In regions where both instruments are feasible, we use an efficiency index—prevention per unit of agency cost—to identify the preferred mechanism. We then analyze two hybrid designs. Under delayed inspection, the government provides an up-front subsidy but conditions coverage on post-incident verification. Under early audit, the government verifies compliance before activating both subsidy and coverage. These hybrids can outperform pure mechanisms when effective verification friction is high or when firms face a large investment-benefit gap. The results provide three policy implications. First, governments should segment firms by baseline network security rather than apply a uniform program. Second, improving verification accuracy can be as important as reducing its direct cost. Third, hybrid mechanisms are most appropriate when their stronger incentives justify the additional administrative and compliance burden of layered verification.

Title: Code and Data Repository for Disjunctive Branch-and-Bound for Certifiably Optimal Low-Rank Matrix Completion
Authors: Dimitris Bertsimas, Ryan Cory-Wright, Sean Lo, Jean Pauphilet
Abstract: The software and data in this repository are a snapshot of the software and data that were used in the research reported on in the paper Disjunctive Branch-and-Bound for Certifiably Optimal Low-Rank Matrix Completion by D. Bertsimas, R. Cory-Wright, S. Lo, and J. Pauphilet. The snapshot is based on this SHA in the development repository.

Title: Overall Evaluation Criteria for A/B Tests: A Meta-Analytic Approach
Authors: Easton Huch, Stephanie A. Nail, Terran Melconian, Xan Vongsathorn, Fred Feinberg
Affiliations: Department of Statistics, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, Michigan 48109; Applied Science and Data Science, Zillow Experimentation Platform, Zillow, Seattle, Washington 98101; Applied Science, Zillow Experimentation Platform, Zillow, Seattle, Washington 98101; Stephen M. Ross School of Business and Department of Statistics, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, Michigan 48109
Abstract: This paper discusses meta-analytic methods for estimating the value of marketing interventions given a database of historical A/B tests with multiple outcome variables.

Title: Scaling up to the cloud: Cloud technology use and growth rates in small and large firms
Authors: Bernardo Caldarola, Luca Fontanelli
Abstract: Using a unique combination of micro-level data sources on French firms, this paper explores the relationship between cloud technologies and firm growth. Whereas digital technologies have generally been found to disproportionately benefit larger firms, we document that cloud use is positively associated with firm growth, and this association is significantly stronger for smaller firms. Distinguishing cloud services between Infrastructure-as-a-Service (IaaS) and Software-as-a-Service (SaaS), we find that the size-contingent association is driven entirely by SaaS. Crucially, this small firm advantage is conditional on complementary assets as it emerges only among firms endowed with ICT capabilities. Our results are robust across a range of specifications, including instrumental variable strategies. SaaS cloud use is further associated with internal workforce reorganisation toward ICT, managerial, and intermediate occupations and away from manual and clerical ones, particularly among smaller firms, consistent with SaaS cloud operating as an organisational innovation enabling digitalisation and scaling. Finally, we present descriptive sectoral evidence of a negative correlation between cloud and market concentration.

Title: Staying on topic: How research knowledge spills over via university education to regional entrepreneurial activity
Authors: Frank J. van Rijnsoever, Jip Leendertse, Iris Wanzenböck, Yvette Baggen
Abstract: Innovative entrepreneurship is an important driver of regional economic development. According to the Knowledge Spillover Theory of Entrepreneurship (KSTE), universities contribute directly to innovative entrepreneurship by conducting state-of-the-art research and educating talent. A key assumption of the KSTE is that human interactions play a pivotal role in transferring knowledge from universities to entrepreneurship, implying that educating students on research topics provides an indirect route for knowledge to spill over into innovative entrepreneurship. Yet this mechanism has not been tested at the level of knowledge specificity where such human interactions actually occur. In this paper, we introduce topics as a novel level of analysis to examine these processes empirically. We define topics as knowledge organized around a coherent theme or problem orientation, making them understandable, transmittable, and usable across institutional contexts through human interaction. Using this topic-level approach, we answer the following question: What is the direct and indirect influence of the amount of university research and education on the level of regional innovative entrepreneurial activity on a topic? We apply Latent Dirichlet Allocation to different documents to extract the amount of educational, research, and entrepreneurial activity per topic in two university regions in the Netherlands. We then connect these activities on a topic through a series of regression models. Our results show that education on a topic has a strong direct effect and largely mediates the positive effect of research on innovative entrepreneurial activity on that topic. Our results further suggest that spillovers to innovative entrepreneurial activity mostly take place within topics rather than between them. Finally, we find evidence that research on related topics can pull talent away from innovative entrepreneurship on a topic. In practical terms, our results suggest that education on state-of-the-art research topics is an important mechanism for promoting innovative entrepreneurship.

Title: When the music changes, so must your dance: Technology-forcing regulation and the shifting geography of automotive invention
Authors: Seyyed Milad Shirvani, Ari Van Assche, Ekaterina Turkina
Abstract: Technology-forcing regulations can compel incumbent firms to develop capabilities in technologies that lie outside their established knowledge bases. We examine how firms respond to this challenge by reconfiguring the geography and organization of invention. Focusing on the automotive industry's transition toward low-emissions technologies, we investigate whether more stringent environmental policies increase incumbent firms' reliance on technological hotspots—locations with specialized knowledge in low-emissions vehicle technologies. We examine two mechanisms through which firms can access this geographically concentrated knowledge: locating inventive activity in hotspots and collaborating with hotspot inventors. Using a comprehensive panel dataset covering more than half a million patent families from incumbent automotive manufacturers and their first-tier suppliers across 311 regions from 1990 to 2020, we find that technology-forcing regulation increases firms' propensity both to locate invention in low-emissions technology hotspots and to collaborate with inventors located there. These findings reveal an important spatial dimension of technology-forcing policy: by increasing firms' need to access specialized knowledge, regulation can reshape not only the direction of technological change but also where and with whom incumbent firms innovate.

Title: Financial constraints and the transmission of monetary policy: Evidence from relaxation of collateral constraints
Authors: Nishant Vats
Abstract: Do financial constraints determine the transmission of monetary policy? I examine this question using the staggered enactment of anti-recharacterization legislation as a source of exogenous variation in creditor rights that loosens firm-financial constraints. A 25 basis-point expansionary monetary policy shock results in a 2 percentage-point higher investment growth among treated (unconstrained) firms. This reflects their flatter marginal cost curves for financing, which amplifies responses to shifts in the marginal benefit curve. The relationship, however, reverses during economic downturns when investment opportunities are scarce. I rationalize these findings in a static model and quantify the channels using a Heterogeneous Agent New Keynesian model.

Title: Are the Hedges of Funds Green?
Authors: Huan Kuang, Bing Liang, Mila Getmansky Sherman, Tianyi Qu
Affiliations: Bryant University College of Business; University of Massachusetts Amherst Isenberg School of Management Finance; Baylor University Finance Department
Abstract: Abstract Over the past decade, hedge funds have increasingly embraced green investing. We develop a novel return-based measure of fund greenness and find that greener funds earn higher average returns, consistent with capturing a positive green premium, and are associated with lower risks, especially during adverse periods. We further show that performance gains are greatest among directional funds, whereas risk reduction is most pronounced among nondirectional funds. We also provide evidence that managers of these funds exhibit superior green investment skills through green stock selection and green factor timing. Finally, investors reward greener hedge funds only when they demonstrate strong performance.
Journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis

Title: Learning‐by‐twinning: Organizational digital twins and the future of search
Authors: Prithwiraj (Raj) Choudhury, Yingxin Du, Megan Lawrence
Affiliations: London School of Economics and Political Science London UK; Indiana University Bloomington Indiana USA
Abstract: Abstract Research Summary Entrepreneurs and managers often need to evaluate strategic choices, such as redesigning an incentive plan or entering an unfamiliar market, before committing scarce resources. Existing offline search tools, including mental models, analogical reasoning, model building, and simulation, allow managers to weigh alternatives without acting, but each is limited by what a single decision maker can specify, recall, or imagine. We argue that advances in generative AI, combined with the growing availability of firm‐specific digital trace data, are transforming this tradeoff. We introduce the organizational digital twin (ODT), an infrastructure combining firm‐specific data, AI‐based behavioral simulation models, and governance rules which facilitates a new form of offline search that we call learning‐by‐twinning: search conducted by observing how a strategic choice unfolds within a digital replica of the firm. We identify three mechanisms through which learning‐by‐twinning creates value, namely expanded search, safer experimentation, and richer system‐level feedback as well as specify certain conditions under which these benefits may attenuate. Managerial Summary Strategic entrepreneurship depends on discovering and refining opportunities through search and experimentation under uncertainty. Enabled by advances in generative artificial intelligence and organizational data infrastructures, we theorize that a new form of entrepreneurial search—learning‐by‐twinning—allows managers to conduct systematic virtual experimentation prior to real‐world implementation. We introduce the concept of the organizational digital twin (ODT) as the technological infrastructure that makes this search and experimentation possible: an evolving simulation environment built from firm‐specific digital trace data and multi‐agent AI models capable of reproducing organizational routines, interactions, and decision processes. We argue that learning‐by‐twinning alters the traditional tradeoffs of offline search by expanding the set of alternatives managers can explore, enabling low‐risk experimentation, and revealing second‐order organizational consequences before strategic commitments are made.

Title: A polyhedral study on unit commitment with a single type of binary variables
Authors: Bin Tian, Kai Pan, Chung-Lun Li
Abstract: Efficient power production scheduling is a crucial concern for power system operators aiming to minimize operational costs. Previous mixed-integer linear programming formulations for unit commitment (UC) problems have primarily used two or three types of binary variables. The investigation of strong formulations with a single type of binary variables has been limited, as it is believed to be challenging to derive strong valid inequalities using fewer binary variables, and the reduction of the number of binary variables is often accompanied by a compromise in tightness. To address these issues, this paper considers a formulation for unit commitment using a single type of binary variables and develops strong valid inequality families to enhance the tightness of the formulation. Conditions under which these strong valid inequalities serve as facet-defining inequalities for the single-generator UC polytope are provided. For those large-size valid inequality families, the existence of efficient separation algorithms for determining the most violated inequalities is also discussed. The effectiveness of the proposed single-binary formulation and strong valid inequalities is demonstrated through computational experiments on network-constrained UC problems. The results indicate that the strong valid inequalities presented in this paper are effective in solving UC problems and can also be applied to UC formulations that contain more than one type of binary variables.

Title: Why Do Union Jobs Pay More? New Evidence from Matched Employer-Employee Data
Authors: Pierre-Loup Beauregard, Thomas Lemieux, Derek Messacar, Raffaele Saggio
Affiliations: Université de Montréal; University of British Columbia and NBER; Memorial University
Abstract: Abstract We use Canadian matched employer-employee data to assess the sources of the union pay premium. After controlling for worker heterogeneity using the two-way fixed effects approach of Abowd, Kramarz, and Margolis (AKM), we find that unionized firms pay about 15 log points more than non-unionized firms. Forty percent of this gap is linked to productivity differences between unionized and non-unionized firms as measured by value added per worker. The remaining gap reflects unions’ ability to extract more rents for workers. Our estimates imply that unions raise pay among unionized workers by around 9 log points, with considerable heterogeneity by industry and firm birth cohorts. The union effect grows to about 11 log points in an extension of the AKM approach where unions also affect the returns to unobservable worker characteristics.

Title: The DNA of neuroticism and financial decisions
Authors: Richard Sias, Laura T Starks, Harry J Turtle
Affiliations: Eller College of Management, University of Arizona , Tucson, AZ 85721; McCombs School of Business, University of Texas at Austin , Austin, TX 78712; College of Business, Colorado State University , Fort Collins, CO 80523
Abstract: Abstract A polygenic score (PGS) capturing genetic predisposition toward neuroticism predicts heterogeneity in risk aversion, return beliefs, and stock market participation. This approach addresses key methodological and interpretive concerns associated with phenotypic measures of neuroticism. Risk aversion and return beliefs are important, but incomplete, channels linking the neuroticism PGS to stock market participation. The neuroticism PGS also predicts heterogeneity in demographic and behavioral characteristics previously shown to influence financial choices. These characteristics serve as key channels through which the genetic propensity for neuroticism shapes financial choices.

Title: The Anti‐SLAPP Statutes and Corporate Environmental Policies
Authors: Kevin C.W. Chen, Zhihong Chen, Chengzhu Sun
Affiliations: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology; Hong Kong Polytechnic University
Abstract: ABSTRACT We examine whether legal protection for civic participation affects corporate pollution. Polluters may deter public discipline through strategic lawsuits. Anti‐SLAPP (Strategic Lawsuit Against Public Participation) statutes mitigate this threat by enabling prompt dismissal and recovery of legal costs. Using a difference‐in‐differences design, we find that enacting an anti‐SLAPP statute in a state significantly reduces toxic emissions from that state by increasing local public pressure. The reduction is greater when the statutes provide stronger protection, when local stakeholders have stronger incentives and abilities to discipline polluters, and when local public pressure increases more after the enactment. Plants lower emissions by improving abatement rather than by reducing output or relocating emissions. Our paper underscores the role of legal protection in environmental governance and informs policy debates over anti‐SLAPP legislation.

Title: The Ubiquity of Business Groups around the World: A Property‐Rights Theory
Authors: Ruth V. Aguilera, Rafel Crespi‐Cladera, Alfredo Martín‐Oliver, Bartolomé Pascual‐Fuster
Affiliations: Northeastern University; Universitat de les Illes Balears
Abstract: Abstract Business groups (BGs) are collections of legally independent firms connected by ownership ties and are widely present in both developing and developed economies. We develop property‐rights theory (PRT) to explain this prevalence, extending its scope from the allocation of rights over a bundle of assets to the legal partitioning of assets as another allocative mechanism of property rights. Our conceptual framework complements traditional theories understanding BGs primarily as responses to institutional voids. Drawing on a large global dataset of firms, we examine how firm asset specificity and ownership sharing influence the controlling owners' decision to organize their economic activities as a BG or as a standalone firm. We find that the likelihood of adopting a BG organizational form over a standalone entity increases when (1) controlling owners rely on more firm‐specific assets, and (2) ownership is shared or potentially shared. Moreover, our findings are robust across three commonly observed firm strategic configurations: focused, vertically integrated, and diversified. Our study expands the PRT by developing a theory of property‐rights architecture, moving forward from the institutional voids perspective to explain BGs as efficient governance responses to asset and ownership complexities, hence contributing also to the strategic management and international business literatures.

Title: Co‐Constructing the Illusion of Progression: How Boundary Blurring and Affirming Reproduce Social Exclusion in Elite Professions
Authors: Stefanie Gustafsson, Laura Empson
Affiliations: University of Bath; City University London; Copenhagen Business School
Abstract: Abstract Social exclusion is a persistent problem in elite professions. While scholarship has emphasized structural and cultural barriers, less is known about the relational practices and mechanisms through which social exclusion is sustained. Drawing on interviews with 84 lawyers, paralegals, and managers in elite UK law firms, we develop a conceptual model of how the blurring and affirming of social and symbolic boundaries between higher‐status and lower‐status groups reproduces social exclusion. We show how both groups blur and affirm boundaries across three domains: professional work, professional space, and systems of professional advancement. Boundary blurring makes symbolic boundaries more permeable, positioning lower‐status actors as prospective professionals, while boundary affirming maintains social boundaries around professional membership. We identify and theorize the illusion of progression as a relational mechanism emerging from intertwined blurring and affirming, constructing lower‐status roles as pathways into the profession even though progression is rare. The illusion perpetuates liminality by sustaining hope, individualizing failure and undermining lower‐status groups' collective challenge to social exclusion. Our findings advance understanding of the relational mechanism through which social exclusion persists in elite professions, show how boundary blurring can sustain rather than threaten status distinctions, and help explain why organizational diversity and inclusion efforts have produced little substantive change.

Title: The Gambler’s Fallacy Fallacy Fallacy (Commentary on Xiang et al., 2025)
Authors: Daniel Banki, Uri Simonsohn
Affiliations: Esade Business School, Universitat Ramon Llull, Barcelona, Spain
Abstract: Xiang et al. concluded that the gambler’s fallacy does not originate in biased beliefs. Reanalyzing their data, we arrived at the opposite conclusion. We show, more generally, that their main analysis—examining whether the median belief is biased—is not diagnostic of the presence of the gambler’s fallacy, whereas our test of the share of probability estimates for the streak ending above or below 50% is diagnostic. We also report results from a new study in which at least 80% of gambler’s-fallacy predictions originated in biased beliefs.

Title: Selective industrial policy for the EU open strategic autonomy: The role of products' relatedness
Authors: Filippo Bontadini, Valentina Meliciani
Abstract: The European Union has adopted the concept of Open Strategic Autonomy (OSA) to reduce strategic dependencies while preserving openness to international trade. An important policy question is therefore which countries are best positioned to develop new trade advantages in strategic products. Building on the literature on relatedness and export diversification, we address this question by complementing the standard notion of product distance, measuring how close a country is to a product compared to other countries, and how close a product is to a country's productive structure compared to other products. We term these concepts absolute and relative distance advantages. We argue that relative distance advantages reflect countries' incentives to diversify into a product, whereas absolute distance advantages capture their ability to successfully develop new trade advantage in that product. Using trade data for EU countries, we show that both dimensions significantly predict the emergence of new export specializations in products identified by the EU as strategic.

Title: Shadow banks on the rise: Evidence across market segments
Authors: Kim Fe Cramer, Pulak Ghosh, Nirupama Kulkarni, Nishant Vats
Abstract: This paper examines the comparative advantages of shadow banks across market segments. Combining credit bureau data on retail loans in India with weather shocks as a proxy for credit demand, we show that Fintechs respond more in uncollateralized markets. In contrast, non-Fintech shadow banks exhibit stronger responsiveness in collateralized markets. Exploiting geographic heterogeneity in the adoption of digital payments, we identify technology as the key advantage for Fintechs. Leveraging four natural experiments, we document the significance of lower regulation for non-Fintech shadow banks. Our results suggest that the comparative advantage of shadow banks differs across market segments.

Title: China Walls
Authors: Tomy Lee, Daniel Nathan, Chaojun Wang
Abstract: We evaluate the enforcement of China Walls—information barriers within conglomerates. We focus on July 2018, when the SEC tightened enforcement around broker-dealer subsidiaries, and on the 25 million Israeli Shekel trades over 2018–2024. Our difference-in-differences design compares a dealer’s affiliate, connected, and unrelated funds on days when the dealer likely obtained valuable information. Before July 2018, dealers share information with their affiliate and connected funds. After July 2018: the sharing ceases only with the affiliate funds; price discovery slows; trading costs fall for affiliate funds and rise for other funds. Tightly enforced walls eliminated 99.0% of affiliate funds’ event-day profits.

Title: Choosing Outcomes-Based Reimbursement Policies: Should We Worry About Collusion?
Authors: Saša Zorc, Stephen E. Chick, Sameer Hasija
Affiliations: Darden School of Business, University of Virginia, Charlottesville, Virginia 22903; INSEAD, Boulevard de Constance, 77300 Fontainebleau, France; INSEAD, Singapore 138676, Singapore
Abstract: Outcomes-based reimbursement rewards health providers with better health outcomes with higher payments. Such reimbursement policies require several design choices, including the type of contract (e.g., capitation or fee-for-service), measure (e.g., population- or provider-level outcomes), and whether to contract with individual providers or larger groups. We explore which outcomes-based reimbursement policies may be vulnerable to potentially illegal collusion, and whether collusion issues can be averted through incentive design. We present a game-theoretic model a chronic care pathway in a two-tier healthcare system. We identify differences in the impact of collusion on health, costs, and system efficiency under different reimbursement policies. Theoretical and numerical results (calibrated to data from two pathways for diabetes) show that whether an outcomes-adjusted reimbursement system is vulnerable to collusion depends critically on one trait: whether the income of physicians who receive referrals scales with volume. In systems where it does, as with fee-for-service models in the United States, there exist financial incentives to collude, underlining the importance of addressing collusion through laws. Systems that lack this trait (e.g., the UK NHS) are more resistant to collusion. Exploring theoretically optimal contracts, we find evidence of strong performance of outcomes-adjusted capitation contracts with individual providers using population-level data. This paper was accepted by Terry Taylor, operations management. Funding: S. E. Chick acknowledges research support through the Novartis Chair for Healthcare Management. Title: Tobin Tax Policy, Housing Speculation, and Property Market Dynamics
Authors: Sumit Agarwal, Kwong Wing Chau, Maggie Rong Hu, Wayne Xinwei Wan
Affiliations: National University of Singapore, Singapore 119077; The University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong; Baruch College, City University of New York, New York, New York 10010; Monash University, Clayton, Victoria 3800, Australia
Abstract: Hong Kong introduced a Tobin property tax—the Special Stamp Duty (SSD)—in 2010, which substantially increased the selling costs of short-term residential property holders. This study examines the effectiveness of this Tobin tax in curbing speculation and cooling down the housing market. We find that the SSD effectively curtails flippers who hold homes for less than two years and reduces their market presence from 23.2% in 2009% to 2.4% in 2011 and 0.9% in 2013. However, one year after implementing the tax, housing prices grow by 12.64% and 15.76% in the primary and secondary markets, respectively, indicating a lack of a market cooling effect. Flippers strategically defer sales to circumvent the SSD charges, resulting in the sharp bunching of urgent sales immediately after the lock-in period ends. Further, the SSD effectively increases selling costs and prolongs potential sellers’ holding periods, thereby significantly reducing liquidity and driving up prices in the secondary market. The unintended externality is that the unmet housing demand from the secondary market triggers a buying frenzy in the primary market, which increases the prices in the primary market as well. Our findings have policy implications for the viability of Tobin taxes for regulating real estate markets. This paper was accepted by Agostino Capponi, finance. Funding: S. Title: Dealer Funding and Market Liquidity
Authors: Max Bruche, John Chi-Fong Kuong
Affiliations: Humboldt University of Berlin, 10117 Berlin, Germany; and Berlin School of Economics, Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin, 10117 Berlin, Germany; CUHK Business School, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong
Abstract: We analyze a model where dealers provide market liquidity by intermediating trades between clients. They exert unobservable search effort to improve intermediation profit. This moral-hazard friction limits their ability to raise external finance and compete with each other, constraining market liquidity even for safe assets and more so for those with higher search costs. Dealers mitigate this friction by using debt financing and intermediating across multiple markets, making leverage endogenous and linked to liquidity variations in otherwise unrelated markets. Capping leverage reduces dealer external financing and has mixed effects on welfare. It worsens liquidity but encourages effort. Our findings illuminate how postcrisis regulations impact bond market liquidity. This paper was accepted by William Cong, finance. Funding: J. C.-F. Title: The Role of Physician Integration in Alternative Payment Models: The Case of the Comprehensive Joint Replacement Program
Authors: Christopher J. Chen, Kraig Delana
Affiliations: Kelley School of Business, Indiana University, Bloomington, Indiana 47405; IE Business SchoolIE University, 28006 Madrid, Spain
Abstract: U.S. health system reform simultaneously promotes alternative payment models (APMs) and integrated provider organizations, where integration is assumed to better enable providers to coordinate and manage the risks introduced by APMs. While the interaction of these two changes has implications for both APM design and regulation of provider integration, it is not well studied. In this paper, we offer empirical evidence on the role of horizontal and vertical integration of orthopedic surgeons in driving heterogeneity in the impact of the Comprehensive Joint Replacement (CJR) APM. Using a quasi-experimental generalized difference-in-differences approach, we find that, relative to similar control hospitals, CJR hospitals with fully horizontally and vertically integrated orthopedic surgeons receive a 5.83% increase in CMS payments to hospitals but do not differ in CJR quality measures. Further analysis shows that the increase in payments stems from changes in physicians’ clinical decision-making that reduce penalties (increase CMS payments) to hospitals for low-value care and reduces CMS payments to postacute care (PAC) providers. Consequently, these hospitals also receive greater CJR reward payments. Overall, our findings suggest that integrated providers are likely to perform better under APMs, providing novel insights for policymakers, payors, and healthcare providers as they design, implement, and evaluate value-based reforms. This paper was accepted by Carri W. Chan, healthcare management. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2022.02547 .

Title: Building Careers in Project-Based Organizations: Breadth, Fit, and the Path to Advancement
Authors: Federica De Stefano, Matthew Bidwell
Affiliations: Saïd Business School, University of Oxford, Oxford OX1 1HP, United Kingdom; Wharton School, University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania 19104
Abstract: Project-based organizations allow employees in ostensibly similar roles to acquire very different experiences by working on different kinds of projects. We study how people build careers in these contexts, examining when employees choose to diversify their experience—both in terms of project content and collaborators—and how the resulting diversification affects their career advancement. Using longitudinal project data from a services organization, our results suggest that employees initially explore different kinds of work by moving across project types, but then go on to find their fit in a particular area. This process is quicker for high-performing employees and for those with longer tenure and more diverse collaborator networks. We also find that promotion rates and compensation are lower for employees who worked on a broader portfolio of content types and collaborators in the most recent year, but higher for employees who had worked on broader project portfolios in prior years. Title: Transportation and Inventory Planning in Serial Supply Chain with Heterogeneous Capacitated Vehicles
Authors: Kartik Kulkarni, Manish Bansal
Affiliations: Department of Industrial and Systems Engineering, Virginia Tech, Blacksburg, Virginia 24061
Abstract: We study serial supply chain problems where a product is transported from a supplier to a warehouse (inbound transportation), and then from the warehouse (outbound transportation) to a retailer such that demand for a given planning horizon is satisfied. We consider heterogeneous vehicles of varying capacities for transportation in each time period, and the objective is to plan inbound and outbound transportation along with inventory in each time period so that overall inventory and transportation costs are minimized. These problems belong to the class of two-echelon lot-sizing (2-ELS) problems with the warehouse and retailer as the first and second echelons, respectively. We address an open question raised in van Hoesel et al. [van Hoesel S, Romeijn HE, Morales DR, Wagelmans APM (2005) Integrated lot sizing in serial supply chains with production capacities. Management Sci. 51(11):1706–1719]: Does there exist a polynomial-time algorithm for 2-ELS with a single capacitated vehicle for each of the inbound and outbound transportation? Specifically, we introduce polynomial-time algorithms for this problem and its three generalizations with multiple capacitated vehicles for inbound and/or outbound transportation, thereby generalizing the results of Kaminsky and Simchi-Levi [Kaminsky P, Simchi-Levi D (2003) Production and distribution lot sizing in a two stage supply chain. IIE Trans. 35(11):1065–1075] and Sargut and Romeijn [Sargut FZ, Romeijn HE (2007) Capacitated production and subcontracting in a serial supply chain. IIE Trans. 39(11):1031–1043] for 2-ELS with a single capacitated vehicle for inbound transportation and uncapacitated outbound transportation. We showcase the practical applications of these approaches in efficiently solving discrete two- and multiechelon lot-sizing problems that arise in freight transportation, the international shipping industry, and the tire manufacturing industry. Based on our computational experiments, we observe that the algorithm for discrete 2-ELS with a capacitated vehicle for inbound and outbound transportation is computationally efficient in comparison with solving the mixed binary formulations of two- and multiechelon lot-sizing problems using an off-the-shelf optimization solver. Title: Frozen-State Value Iteration: Faster Reinforcement Learning by Freezing Slow States
Authors: Yijia Wang, Daniel R. Jiang
Affiliations: University of Pittsburgh, Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania 15260; and Meta Platforms, Menlo Park, California 94025
Abstract: We study infinite-horizon Markov decision processes (MDPs) with fast–slow structure, in which some state variables evolve rapidly (fast states), whereas others change more gradually (slow states). This structure commonly arises in practice when decisions must be made at high frequencies over long horizons and when slowly changing information still plays a critical role in determining optimal actions. Examples include inventory control under slowly changing demand indicators or dynamic pricing with gradually shifting consumer behavior. Modeling the problem at the natural decision frequency leads to MDPs with discount factors close to one, making them computationally challenging. We propose a novel approximation strategy that freezes slow states during phases of lower level planning and subsequently applies value iteration to an auxiliary upper level MDP that evolves on a slower timescale. Freezing states for short periods of time leads to easier to solve lower level problems, whereas a slower upper level timescale allows for a more favorable discount factor. On the theoretical side, we analyze the regret incurred by our frozen-state approach, and this leads to simple insights on how to trade off regret versus computational cost. Empirically, we benchmark our new frozen-state methods on three domains: (i) inventory control with fixed order costs, (ii) a grid world problem with spatial tasks, and (iii) dynamic pricing with reference price effects. We demonstrate that the new methods produce high-quality policies with significantly less computation, and we show that simply omitting slow states is often a poor heuristic. Title: Observational Learning and Information Disclosure in Search Markets
Authors: Ziying Fan, Xi Weng, Li-An Zhou, Yiyi Zhou
Affiliations: College of Public Finance and Investment, Shanghai University of Finance and Economics, Shanghai 200433, China; Guanghua School of Management, Peking University, Beijing 100871, China; Department of Economics, Stony Brook University, Stony Brook, New York 11794
Abstract: We develop and estimate a structural model of buyers’ observational learning, search, and bidding, using unique data on in-person home viewings and transactions. We use the estimated model to quantify the welfare impact of different information disclosure rules. Our findings indicate that prohibiting the disclosure of home viewing information while permitting only the disclosure of time-on-market would extend the sale time and raise the transaction price, benefiting sellers but harming buyers on average. Title: Private Equity, Consumers, and Competition: Evidence from the Nursing Home Industry
Authors: Ashvin D. Gandhi, YoungJun Song, Prabhava Upadrashta
Affiliations: University of California, Los Angeles, Los Angeles, California 90095; and National Bureau of Economic Research, Cambridge, Massachusetts 02138; Fowler College of Business, San Diego State University, San Diego, California 92182; U.S. Department of Labor, Washington, District of Columbia 20210
Abstract: This paper studies how product market competition shapes the impact of private equity (PE) acquisitions on consumers. We examine nursing home buyouts and observe that PE-owned facilities exhibit greater competitive sensitivity: competing more aggressively when competitive incentives are strong and exploiting market power more aggressively when competitive incentives are weak. We find that PE-owned facilities are more sensitive to local market competition—even when comparing effects only across facilities purchased as part of the same acquisition—and are more responsive to a pro-competitive policy helping consumers compare facilities. This suggests that regulators should attend to the competitive sensitivity of acquirers and the concentration of markets where acquisitions occur, as well as consider pro-competitive policies to mitigate or even reverse PE’s potentially adverse consequences. Title: Comment on “Regulating Gender Diversity: Evidence from California Senate Bill 826”
Authors: Daniel Greene, JiHoon Hwang, Vincent J. Intintoli, Kathleen M. Kahle
Affiliations: Clemson University, Wilbur O. and Ann Powers College of Business, Clemson, South Carolina 29634; School of Business Administration, University of Mississippi, University, Mississippi 38677; Eller College of Management, University of Arizona, Tucson, Arizona 85721; and European Corporate Governance Institute, 1000 Brussels, Belgium
Abstract: Prior studies draw mixed conclusions on the market response to California SB 826, the first board gender diversity mandate in the United States. We find that these discrepancies stem from two factors: confusion about the legislative process and the use of different return methodologies. We find that the response to early dates in the legislative process yields largely insignificant and sometimes conflicting results, depending on the return methodology used. This result is consistent with our finding that many of these dates generated little interest from investors. Returns are mostly negative and significant on the date the bill was signed into law. Additionally, all models show a negative and significant relation between the signing-day return and the number of female directors needed to meet the law. Title: Measuring the Driving Forces of Predictive Performance: Application to Credit Scoring
Authors: Sullivan Hué, Christophe Hurlin, Christophe Pérignon, Sébastien Saurin
Affiliations: Aix Marseille University, Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique (CNRS), Aix-Marseille School of Economics (AMSE), 13205 Marseille, France; University of Orléans, 45067 Orléans, France; and Institut Universitaire de France, 75231 Paris, France; HEC Paris, 78350 Jouy-en-Josas, France
Abstract: Because they play an increasingly important role in determining access to credit, credit scoring models are under growing scrutiny from banking supervisors and internal model validators. These authorities need to monitor the model performance and identify its key drivers. To facilitate this, we introduce the explainable performance (XPER) methodology to decompose a performance metric (e.g., area under the curve (AUC), [Formula: see text]) into specific contributions associated with the various features of a forecasting model. XPER is theoretically grounded on Shapley values and is both model-agnostic and performance metric-agnostic. Furthermore, it can be implemented either at the model level or at the individual level. Using a novel data set of car loans, we decompose the AUC of a machine-learning model trained to forecast the default probability of loan applicants. We show that a small number of features can explain a surprisingly large part of the model performance. Notably, the features that contribute the most to the predictive performance of the model may not be the ones that contribute the most to individual forecasts (Shapley additive explanation). Finally, we show how XPER can be used to deal with heterogeneity issues and improve performance. This paper was accepted by Kay Giesecke, finance. Title: Responsible Investment and Responsible Consumption
Authors: Hendrik Hakenes, Eva Schliephake
Affiliations: Institute for Financial Economics and Statistics, University of Bonn, 53113 Bonn, Germany; Católica Lisbon School of Business & Economics, Center for Sustainable Finance, Palma de Cima, Universidade Católica Portuguesa, 1649-023 Lisboa, Portugal
Abstract: Should households focus on responsible investment (SRI) or responsible consumption (SRC) to mitigate externalities? Using a general equilibrium model linking product and capital markets, we show that neither strategy is efficient on its own—each shifts prices and triggers offsetting market responses. Combining SRI and SRC neutralizes these effects and maximizes impact. This complementarity holds across diverse settings, even when SRI alone would have negligible impact. The effectiveness of green finance, therefore, critically depends on households acting as both investors and consumers. This paper was accepted by Bo Becker, finance. Title: The Task Space: An Integrative Framework for Team Research
Authors: Xinlan Emily Hu, Mark E. Whiting, Linnea Gandhi, Duncan J. Watts, Abdullah Almaatouq
Affiliations: Operations, Information, and Decisions Department, The Wharton School, University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania 19104; and Institute for Data, Systems, and Society, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, Massachusetts 02142; and Pareto AI, Stanford, California 94305; and Department of Computer and Information Science, University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania 19104; and Annenberg School for Communication, University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania 19104; Institute for Data, Systems, and Society, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, Massachusetts 02142; and Sloan School of Management, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, Massachusetts 02142; and Center for Computational Engineering, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, Massachusetts 02139
Abstract: Research on teams spans many contexts, but integrating knowledge from heterogeneous sources is challenging because studies typically examine different tasks that cannot be directly compared. Most investigations involve teams working on just one or a handful of tasks, and researchers lack principled ways to quantify how similar or different these tasks are from one another. We address this challenge by introducing the “Task Space,” a multidimensional space in which tasks—and the distances between them—can be represented formally, and use it to create a “Task Map” of 102 crowd-annotated tasks from the published experimental literature. We then demonstrate the Task Space’s utility by performing an integrative experiment that addresses a fundamental question in team research: when do interacting groups outperform individuals? Our experiment samples 20 diverse tasks from the Task Map at three complexity levels and recruits 1,231 participants to work either individually or in groups of three or six (180 experimental conditions). We find striking heterogeneity in group advantage, with groups performing anywhere from three times worse to 60% better than the best individual working alone, depending on the task context. Critically, the Task Space makes this heterogeneity predictable: it significantly outperforms traditional typologies in predicting group advantage on unseen tasks. Our models also reveal theoretically meaningful interactions between task features; for example, group advantage on creative tasks depends on whether the answers are objectively verifiable. We conclude by arguing that the Task Space enables researchers to integrate findings across different experiments, thereby building cumulative knowledge about team performance. Title: Intangible Liabilities
Authors: Hamid Boustanifar, Arnt Verriest
Affiliations: EDHEC Business School, 06002 Nice, France; KU Leuven, 3000 Leuven, Belgium
Abstract: When liabilities are deemed improbable or cannot be reliably estimated by management, they are not recorded on the balance sheet. Instead, they are disclosed qualitatively in the company’s filings. Examples include obligations related to pending or future lawsuits, product liability, environmental matters, false advertising, or patent and copyright infringements. We refer to these obligations as intangible liabilities. We construct a firm-level, text-based measure of intangible liabilities (IL). IL is positively related to firm size, volatility, and share turnover, and is negatively correlated with accounting performance, abnormal returns, and Tobin’s Q. IL also predictably varies across industries. Moreover, IL predicts future lawsuits against firms and the future deterioration of their reputations. Companies with higher IL trade at lower valuation ratios and have significantly higher future crash risks. A portfolio that is long on high IL and short on low IL yields an annual abnormal return of 3% after accounting for common factors. Overall, the results suggest that intangible liabilities are a significant determinant of firm value and stock returns. This paper was accepted by Bo Becker, finance. Title: Capacity and Pricing Management with Demand Learning
Authors: Jian Chen, Zechao Li, Anyan Qi, Yining Wang

Abstract: In an environment where demand is unknown to the firm, it is important to investigate how capacity adjustment and dynamic pricing can be integrated so that the firm can learn about the demand on the fly while making capacity and pricing decisions. In this paper, we design learning algorithms for the joint capacity and pricing management problem. To evaluate the performance of our algorithms, we consider a large-demand asymptotic regime where the demand and capacity are scaled up with the selling horizon T. We propose a novel double-trisection algorithm that utilizes pricing decisions to collect demand information and tune capacity rate levels safely, attaining an [Formula: see text] regret upper bound that matches the lower bound. We then modify our algorithm to address the issue when the number of capacity adjustment opportunities K is limited and find that only a few opportunities to adjust capacity levels (i.e., [Formula: see text]) are sufficient to achieve the optimal regret rate. We also consider seasonal demands and provide a modified algorithm to incorporate the seasonality. Title: Will the Truth Free Us from Misinformation?
Authors: David Godes
Affiliations: Carey Business School, Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, Maryland 21202
Abstract: We study the impact of truthful revelation mechanisms, like fact checking, on the incentives for media outlets to produce misinformation. The existing literature suggests that such interventions will always reduce this incentive. In this paper, we consider a context in which consumers benefit both, and to varying degrees, from the truth contained in news reports and from sharing, discussing, and reacting to news stories that, independent of their truthful content, reinforce and enhance their social identity. In such a setting, we find that truthful revelation will not always decrease, and may in fact increase, the incentives for biased reporting. We identify two distinct mechanisms behind this effect. First, we show that truthful revelation may improve the ability of a biased media outlet to signal its type to consumers. Second, we find that heterogeneous preferences for misinformation endow the outlet with a demand function that may imply an increase or decrease in the incentives to produce biased news due to the stochasticity implied by the fact checking process. Finally, we provide two empirical examples that offer results that are consistent with the idea that media outlets are unlikely to reduce, and may increase, bias when they expect the truth to be revealed imminently. Title: Collaborative Work Management Technologies and Managerial Intensity in U.S. Corporations: An Examination
Authors: Piyush Gulati, Arianna Marchetti, Phanish Puranam
Affiliations: UCL School of Management, University College London, London E14 5AA, United Kingdom; Lee Kong Chian School of Business, Singapore Management University, Singapore 178899; INSEAD, Singapore 138676
Abstract: Do digital technologies reinforce managerial hierarchies or, instead, make them less relevant? We propose that the answer to this question depends on the nature of the technology: specifically, its relative impact on managers’ capacity to supervise and on subordinates’ need for supervision. Applying this framework to collaborative work management (CWM) technologies that facilitate real-time collaboration, communication, and task coordination, we predict that the adoption of such technologies should reduce managerial intensity and increase decentralization in organizations. To test this prediction, we use a difference-in-differences design on a novel data set built from over 26 million job listings (Lightcast) and over 20 million social profiles (Revelio) matched to 3,017 U.S. public firms in Compustat, which we track over the period from 2010 to 2019. We find that over the observation window, CWM technology adopters show a 3% reduction in managerial intensity and a 5%–7% increase in nonmanagerial skills linked to decentralization in their job postings in the years following adoption. The pattern of results is robust to a battery of validations, alternative measures, and specifications, and it strongly supports the idea that these technologies enable collaboration and make organizations less hierarchical along the dimensions that we studied. Title: Corporate Acquisitions and Bank Relationships
Authors: Steven Poelhekke, Razvan Vlahu, Vadym Volosovych
Affiliations: Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam, 1081 HV Amsterdam, Netherlands; and CEPR, London EC1R 5HL, United Kingdom; and Tinbergen Institute, 1082 MS Amsterdam, Netherlands; De Nederlandsche Bank, 1000 AB Amsterdam, Netherlands; Tinbergen Institute, 1082 MS Amsterdam, Netherlands; and Erasmus University Rotterdam, 3000 DR Rotterdam, Netherlands
Abstract: We study the dynamics of firm-bank relationships following corporate acquisitions using a novel firm-bank data set for 23 European countries over 2008–2014. Our data allows us to track changes in both firm ownership and bank relationships over time. To examine the effect of ownership change on bank relationships, we combine a difference-in-differences approach with matching. We find that the majority of acquisitions are associated with substantial changes in bank relationships of target firms. Acquiring firms actively change the composition of these relationships, incorporating banks with superior knowledge of the target’s local market or with expertise in the target’s industry. This reallocation appears to mitigate informational frictions associated with the acquisition. Our findings are consistent with theories of financial intermediation that emphasize the role of banks in accumulating and providing soft information about the real economy. Title: The Road to Stock Market Participation
Authors: Sumit Agarwal, Meghana Ayyagari, Yuxi Cheng, Pulak Ghosh
Affiliations: National University of Singapore, Singapore 119077; School of Business, George Washington University, Washington, District of Columbia 20052; University of Texas at San Antonio, San Antonio, Texas 78249; Indian Institute of Management, Bengaluru 560076, India
Abstract: This paper examines how infrastructure development affects stock market participation in India using trading data from more than 13 million individuals. Using the phased rollout of a national road construction program as a natural experiment, we find that new road connections lead to significant increases in both trading activity and the number of investors. These effects are driven primarily by new market entrants and are most pronounced in rural and intermediately developed regions as well as among male and middle-aged investors. Two main mechanisms explain these patterns. First is an information channel: improved connectivity reduces information frictions, facilitates portfolio diversification, and encourages investment in geographically distant firms. Second is a financial inclusion channel: road construction spurs new bank branch openings—especially by state-owned banks—expanding access to financial services and enabling portfolio reallocation from savings and consumption to equity markets. We find limited evidence for a third possible channel, risk sharing, whereby participation rises with road connectivity in regions with high income volatility. Whereas initial investor returns are positive, long-term performance declines and risk-taking increases, suggesting that infrastructure expansion promotes market participation but not necessarily optimal investment outcomes. Title: Sourcing with Demand Updates
Authors: Awi Federgruen, Zhe Liu, Jiaqi Lu
Affiliations: Columbia Business School, Columbia University, New York, New York 10027; Imperial Business School, Imperial College London, London SW7 2AZ, United Kingdom; School of Data Science, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen 518172, China; and School of Management and Economics, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen 518172, China
Abstract: We study a two-stage newsvendor model where the initially uncertain mean demand is revealed midstream, allowing for a second, costlier order to be placed. The two-stage process is relevant to many retailers who have access to two supply options: a long-lead, low-cost option where orders need to be placed under much demand uncertainty, and a short-lead, high-cost option after a signal is revealed that updates the mean demand. We introduce a forecast evolution model that describes how the initial forecast for mean demand varies in response to the signal, which generalizes the popular additive and multiplicative martingale model of forecast evolution (MMFE). We show that the optimal first-stage order solves a simple ordinary differential equation (ODE), whereas the second-stage order is analytically available. We characterize asymptotics for the first-stage order and expected profit as the forecasted mean demand grows, and propose a simple, asymptotically optimal heuristic. We apply our study to data from a national retail chain, where we calibrate our model by maximum likelihood estimation (MLE). The comparison of several heuristic policies, as well as two benchmarks, shows the efficacy of our method. When the signal is more uncertain (e.g., for product lines with impulse- and trend-driven purchases), our heuristic with a simple adjusted critical fractile outperforms benchmarks; otherwise, the classic newsvendor solution performs well and is asymptotically optimal. We also extend the approach to distribution-free settings and capacitated systems. This paper was accepted by Jeannette Song, operations management. Title: Does Offshoring Production Reduce Innovation? Firm-Level Evidence from Taiwan
Authors: Lee Branstetter, Jong-Rong Chen, Britta Glennon, Nikolas Zolas
Affiliations: Carnegie Mellon University, Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania 15213; and National Bureau of Economic Research, Cambridge, Massachusetts 02138; and Peterson Institute, Washington, District of Columbia 20036; National Central University, Taoyuan City, Taiwan 320; and Academia Sinica, Taipei City, Taiwan 115; and National Taiwan University, Taipei City, Taiwan 10617; National Bureau of Economic Research, Cambridge, Massachusetts 02138; and University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania 19104; Census Bureau, Washington, District of Columbia 20233
Abstract: Does the offshoring of production degrade or enhance the innovative capabilities of manufacturing firms? We contribute to this debate with causal evidence that offshoring impacts both the level and nature of innovation. Exploiting a policy shock that differentially affected the ability of Taiwanese firms to offshore production of certain goods to China, we find a decline in innovation levels and a shift from product to process innovation in the technologies directly related to product categories that could be offshored more easily after the policy shock. However, we also find evidence that the policy shock led to a reallocation of research effort within the firm, raising innovative effort in product categories not directly impacted by the shock and shifting them toward product innovation. Title: Within–Bank Holding Company Accounting Information and Internal Capital Allocation
Authors: Scott Liao, Allison Nicoletti, Barbara Su
Affiliations: Rotman School of Management, Accounting Department, University of Toronto, Toronto, Ontario M5S 3E6, Canada; The Wharton School, Accounting Department, University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania 19104; Costello College of Business, Accounting Department, George Mason University, Fairfax, Virginia 22030
Abstract: We examine whether loan loss provision validity (i.e., the extent of loan loss provisions mapping into future charge offs) within the bank holding company (BHC) is associated with internal capital allocation efficiency. Exploiting the filing requirements for subsidiary banks, we find that within-BHC provision validity, our measure of internal information quality, is positively associated with internal capital market efficiency. We also find that this association is concentrated in BHCs more likely to allocate capital to take advantage of subsidiary lending opportunities and BHCs with higher internal information asymmetry. These findings suggest that within-BHC accounting information that better reflects subsidiary bank loan performance mitigates information problems between headquarters and subsidiary managers in internal capital allocation. This study contributes to our understanding of how loan loss provision information of lower-level entities within the organization is associated with headquarters capital allocation and helps mitigate internal information asymmetry within banking organizations. Title: Can Reward Uncertainty Encourage Social Referrals? Evidence from a Large-Scale Field Experiment
Authors: Andy Tao Li, Rodrigo Belo, Ting Li
Affiliations: Faculty of Business for Science and Technology, School of Management, University of Science and Technology of China, Hefei 230052, China; Nova School of Business and Economics, Universidade NOVA de Lisboa, 2775-405 Carcavelos, Portugal; Rotterdam School of Management, Erasmus University, 3062 PA Rotterdam, Netherlands
Abstract: Social referral programs, in which individuals recommend products or services within their networks in return for rewards, have been widely adopted across digital platforms. This study explores the impact of incorporating uncertainty into the rewards of such programs, focusing on how senders and recipients perceive and react to uncertain rewards. We run a randomized experiment involving more than 160,000 users of a telecommunications operator in China and examine the effectiveness of different referral reward schemes. We find that referral programs are most successful when senders are incentivized with uncertain rewards and recipients are guaranteed certain rewards. Specifically, introducing uncertainty in the sender’s reward leads to a 20.9% increase in total referrals with recipients of these invitations more likely to engage in subsequent referrals and profitable in-app activities. In contrast, uncertainty in the recipient’s reward results in a 12.3% decrease in total referrals with invited recipients showing a lower propensity to make further referrals and reduced postreferral engagement. Additional online experiments identify distinct mechanisms driving these asymmetric effects: For senders, the uncertainty alleviates feelings of guilt, enhancing referral sharing and, thus, increasing the total number of referrals. For recipients, the adverse effects of uncertainty stem primarily from diminished perceptions of fairness and social pressure, and these deter engagement in the referral process. Our study sheds light on the complex dynamics of reward uncertainty in referral programs, offering novel insights into how it can be optimized to foster more engaged referral networks. Title: Firm-Level Litigation Risk: Measurement and Effects
Authors: Benjamin Bennett, Charles Ham, Todd Milbourn, Zexi Wang

Abstract: Firms are exposed to litigation risk from various stakeholders, including investors, customers, and regulators, and prior research has shown that such risk shapes a range of corporate policies. This measure demonstrates strong predictability for lawsuits, even after controlling for firm characteristics, existing lawsuits, geographic factors, and various fixed effects, including firm fixed effects. Title: The Hidden Costs of Fairness in Platform Markets: The Dynamics of Lowering Developer Royalty Rates
Authors: Annamaria Conti, Juan Santaló
Affiliations: IE University, Madrid, 28046 Community of Madrid, Spain
Abstract: Multisided platforms crucially rely on indirect network effects. When trying to strengthen these effects, platform owners face a fundamental challenge, namely, designing incentives to enhance developer effort and simultaneously ensuring the release of high-quality products on the platform. This paper highlights the costs associated with lowering royalty rates to boost developer effort, as such reductions increase the relative supply of lower-quality offerings, worsening information congestion problems and amplifying the importance of visibility-enhancing investments. We leverage the quasi random announcements made by Apple and Google, declaring their intention to reduce the royalty rate applied to small app developers from 30% to 15%. We analyze the implications of these reforms using a difference-in-differences approach, finding a substantial increase in small developers’ likelihood of releasing lower-quality and less original apps on iOS and Android after the announcements. These effects are neither paralleled by a comparable increase in high-quality app releases nor by an increase in small developers’ likelihood of launching venture-backed apps. Consistent with worsening information congestion problems because of an influx of low-quality apps, our findings show an increase in the marginal value of experienced user certifications and developers’ app store optimization efforts post announcement. Additionally, we observe that venture capitalists are increasingly concentrating their investments in ventures with higher (observable) quality. Title: The Power of Two in Token Systems
Authors: Itai Ashlagi, Süleyman Kerimov, Omer Tamuz, Geng Zhao
Affiliations: Department of Management Science and Engineering, Stanford University, Stanford, California 94305; Jones Graduate School of Business, Rice University, Houston, Texas 77005; Division of the Humanities and Social Sciences, Caltech, Pasadena, California 91125; Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Sciences, University of California, Berkeley, California 94720
Abstract: In economies without monetary transfers, token systems serve as an alternative to sustain cooperation and increase efficiency. This paper studies whether a token-based economy can be effective in marketplaces with thin exogenous supply. We consider a marketplace in which at each time period one agent requests a service, one agent provides the service, and one token (artificial currency) is used to pay for service provision. The number of tokens each agent has represents the difference between the amount of service provisions and service requests by the agent. We are interested in the behavior of this economy when very few agents are available to provide the requested service. Because balancing the number of tokens across agents is key to sustain cooperation, the agent with the minimum number of tokens is selected to provide service among the available agents. When exactly one random agent is available to provide service, we show that the token distribution is unstable. However, already when just two random agents are available to provide service, the token distribution is stable, in the sense that agents’ token balance is unlikely to deviate much from their initial endowment, and agents return to their initial endowment in finite expected time. Our results mirror the power-of-two-choices paradigm in load balancing problems. Supported by numerical simulations using kidney exchange data, our findings suggest that token systems may generate efficient outcomes in kidney exchange marketplaces by sustaining cooperation between hospitals. Title: Improving Cash-Constrained Smallholder Farmers’ Revenue: The Role of Government Loans
Authors: Jimin Park, Somya Singhvi, Yanchong Zheng
